## #2194 - Playback keyframes share the cut bricks that no move changed

**What was decided.** The three cut layers of `SdfField` (`cuts`, `cut_ups`,
`cut_downs`) hold each brick in an `Arc` (`CutLayer` in
`crates/sim/src/stock_sim/field.rs`). A clone of the field copies the keys
and the pointers only. A write goes through `layer_brick_mut`, which uses
`Arc::make_mut`: it copies a brick first when a clone still holds it. The
keyframe store counts a keyframe by `KeyCost::key_bytes_after`: the bricks
that the keyframe before it does not share, and the map entries of the three
layers.

**A visit is not a write.** `claim_record` and `up_record` read the cell
first and take the writable brick only when the value changes. Before, they
took the writable slot first. With shared bricks that copied each brick that
a move reached, also when no cell changed. On the staged 24 mm face the
read-first order holds 9.9 MB for 28 keyframes; without it 16.4 MB; whole
copies cost 45.3 MB. The values that the cut writes are the same, bit for
bit: an absent brick reads NaN, and NaN always took the write.

**Why.** A keyframe was a whole copy of the cut layers (#2181). Two keyframes
one stride apart differ only in the bricks that the moves between them
touched. Sharing the other bricks lets the same 512 MiB budget hold more
keyframes, so the stride stays short on a large program. Copy-on-write keeps
each keyframe an exact prefix of the program: no write can reach a brick that
a keyframe holds. The map entries are counted because a store of fully shared
keyframes would otherwise cost "0 bytes" and escape the budget.

**The count can read high, never low.** The test for "shared" is pointer
identity with the keyframe before. Each brick allocation is counted at the
first keyframe that holds it. A live seek that restores an old keyframe and
cuts again makes equal bricks in new allocations; those count again, which is
what the memory holds. After a thinning the store sums again from the keys
that stay.

**Considered and dropped.**
- A delta chain (each keyframe stores only its changed bricks, a restore
  walks back to key 0). Dropped: a restore would cost a walk over all
  keyframes, and a thinning would need a merge of deltas. Shared pointers give
  the same memory with a restore that is one map clone.
- An exact count with a set of all brick pointers in the store. Dropped: it
  needs the store to know the brick type, and the pairwise count is already
  never low.
- `Arc` on the whole layer map (as the mesh layer has). Dropped: the first
  write after a keyframe would copy every brick again.
- Share the mesh-layer bricks one by one too. Dropped: that map is already
  shared whole and is written only while the field is built.

**Cost.** Each cell write does the `Arc::make_mut` uniqueness check (two
atomic operations, no lock). The swept-distance evaluation of the cell
dominates it. `CostLedger` (the cut region, the full-brick ledger, the dirty
set) is still copied whole by each keyframe and is not counted, as before.

**Cost to change later.** `CutLayer` and `layer_brick_mut` are the only
places that know the brick is shared. A different store (a pool, an arena)
replaces those two and `cut_bytes_after`.

## #2201 - Pick highlight frame cost: input-keyed caches only

**What was decided.** The refresh of PR #2256 against main keeps only the
caches whose key is the input itself (crates/ui/AGENTS.md, "Frame cost",
#2238):

- `frame_cache::FrameCache::world_verts_cached`: each body's world-space
  vertices, keyed by the facet allocation (`Weak<[Triangle]>`, compared by
  pointer, plus the length) and the pose bits.
- `pick_highlight::HighlightCache`: the resolved outlines of the shown
  picks, the viewport hover and the Geometry-row hover. The key is the
  same as the key of `pick_line_memo`: the picks by value, and for each
  picked body its display-off flag, its entity, its `Arc<Features>`
  allocation and its view pose.
- `pick_highlight_mesh`: the batched screen meshes of these outlines,
  in three slots (selected, viewport hover, row hover). The key is
  `MeshKey`: the outline id, the camera matrix, the pane mapping, the
  clip, the pixels per point, the widths and the colours. Each slot
  (`MeshSlot`) has its own build counter. A hit sends a clone of the
  `Arc<Mesh>`, not a deep copy.
- `geometry::feature`: the `[Option<Pos>; 3]` digest (the same hash as the
  `Vec` form) and one `patch_lattice()` call for `patches` and
  `patch_rings`.
- `model::toolpath_nonempty`, in `model/toolpath.rs` (model.rs is past
  400 lines). `toolpath_warning_count` had no caller and is removed.

**Why.** Main now has input-keyed memos for the same work:
`model::features_of` (Weak memo), `model::resolve_chain`, `model::patches`,
`model::patch_rings`, `frame_memo::scene_scope` and `pick_line_memo`. The
PR's other caches keyed on a document counter (`WorldStamp`,
`revision_token`). The frame-cost rule forbids a counter as the only key.

**Hand-resolved hunks (same logic on both sides).**

- `model::features_of` / `features_of_shared`: main's side. The PR's
  `SHARED_FEATURES_CACHE` is dropped; main's Weak memo does the same work.
- `resolve_chain` call sites (state, interact, pick_highlight): main's
  `model::resolve_chain`. The PR's `feature/index.rs` is deleted.
- `world::collect`: main's `frame_memo::scene_scope`. The PR's
  `scene_cache_key` and `collect_shared` are dropped. `world_verts` keeps
  the PR's vertex cache under the new key.
- `pick_ink::paint`: the PR's batched selection and hover meshes, and
  main's start and exit marks as plain strokes between them.
- `shell.rs`: the PR's `paint_row_hover`, inside main's
  `frame_cost::time("ui/viewport.row_hover")`.

**Dropped.** The scene, region and toolpath-line caches, the six panel
caches (`panel_cache.rs`) and `commands::revision_token`. They were keyed
by a document counter, and the review asked for counter and changed-input
tests for each. Main's memos cover the scene and the pick lines. A panel
cache comes back only with a measurement and an input key.

**Hand-resolved hunk of the second refresh (main at `ed4a9940f`).**

- `egui_app/tests.rs` module list: both sides added one module at the
  same place (`highlight_perf` and main's `pocket_no_adaptive`). Both are
  kept. #2484 (shared pick names) merged without a conflict: its
  `geo_label` status lines in `interact.rs` and its chip names in
  `state.rs` stay as main has them.

**Counters split.** The outline cache counted the viewport hover and the
row hover in one counter. Each now has its own (`hover_builds`,
`row_hover_builds`), so each slot has its own pin.

**Cost to change later.** Low. Each kept cache is one module with a counter
test and changed-input tests:

- `frame_cache_tests.rs`: the world-vertex cache.
- `pick_highlight_tests.rs`: the outline cache (row hover and viewport
  hover, each with its own counter).
- `pick_highlight_mesh_tests.rs`: the screen-mesh cache. For each of the
  three slots, a still frame tessellates once, and an orbit, a pane
  resize and an ink change each tessellate again with moved or recoloured
  painted vertices.

**Not done here (review non-blockers, left open).** The vertex cache keeps
one entry for each pose of a live body (bounded at 32), the vertex cache
hit still clones the vertex vector, and the law tests of
`interact::hover_features` / `row_hover_segments` use
`pick_highlight::project_segments`, not the production projection in
`pick_highlight_mesh`.

## #2201 - the path overlay and the region are cached across frames

**Decided.** The overlay lines of each drawn toolpath are built once per
input and kept in `crate::path_overlay::PathLineCache` on `State`. The key
is the path's content signature (`Toolpath::path_sig`), its move count,
its warnings, the palette, the viewport ground, the dim and the chevron
arm. The chevron arm is kept under each model's facet allocation and pose,
so `model::solid_world_aabb` runs only when a model changes. The region of
a shown operation (`frame_memo::region_of`) is kept across frames under
the operation value and its `operation::op_stamp`. The op page and the
browser read the path through `model::with_toolpath` and do not clone it.

**Why.** The measurements on the windowed release build showed that the
CPU, not the GPU, is the cost. With an 8100-move path, `world::collect`
took 5-6.5 ms per frame (the path lines about 3 ms), and a selected or
previewed operation built its region two times per still frame. The GPU
encode was about 0.3 ms. So #2525, #2526 and #2607 (GPU draw work) are not
linked to this fix.

**Dropped.**
- A key on `doc_version`: crates/ui/AGENTS.md "Frame cost" forbids it, and
  the counter is bumped by hand, so a missed bump shows a stale picture.
- A `History` revision counter: it does not exist, and a new one has the
  same weakness.
- Measurement on the maintainer's project `testdata/models/fig8.camproj`:
  the worker brief forbids to read it. The numbers come from synthetic
  fixtures of the same size (about 8100 moves).

**Cost to change.** The two caches are local to `crates/ui`. A new display
input of the path must be added to the `Look` key, or the lines show the
old look until the path changes.

## #2285 - Read the Probe op's pick in the setup frame

**Chosen:** Read the picked feature's placement in `operation::probe_pick`
through `setup_align::pose_in(world, entity, setup)` instead of
`model::transform_of`, and carry the setup name through the three seed
helpers (`probe_seed`, `probe_from_picks`, `probe_account`) as
`setup: Option<&str>`, the shape #2276 gave the Slot helpers. Add Probe to
the verified aligned-setup mill kinds and to the supported kinds named in
the refusal message. Require a proof: a pick on a box turned about two
axes must seed the touch against the part as the setup holds it, cut the
same path and post the same byte-identical program as a part with that
turn baked into its mesh, while the part as modelled must seed another
touch and cut another path. Add a second test for the safety law: a probe
target written in the model frame in a turned setup drives the stylus
through the part, and the protected-move law convicts it with a
post-blocking warning. Four sentinels that pinned Probe as refused now
name kinds that are still unverified.

**Validation:** The proof test fails with the old seed read: the turned
case seeds the touch on the model top (`the turned seed: [20.0, 15.0,
10.0]`) instead of the turned part's top, and the stylus law convicts the
same path with `Gouge` at moves 3 to 6. It passes with the fix, and the
baked twin posts the byte-identical program. The conviction test holds in
both builds: it pins the safety law that makes the wrong frame visible
rather than silent. The quick gate ran the touched app test binaries and
clippy.

**Why:** Generation already speaks the setup frame: `operation::generate`
passes the setup-frame facets of the source to `probe_op::generate_probe`,
and the stylus law judges the path against those facets. Only the pick's
seed read the model frame. The two reads disagreed, so a Probe in an
aligned setup posted a cycle that sought a surface 10 mm inside or in front
of the real one, with no diagnostic - the silent wrong answer the Prime
Directive forbids. Probe's `KindInfo` sits in `Section::Drilling`, so its
family is Mill: `verified_mill` admits it on `Mill` and `MillTurn`, which
is where probe ops already run.

**Dropped:** Transforming the seed result inside `probe_pick` after the
seed - that would apply the pose twice, because the facets the seed queries
would already carry it. Adding Probe to `verified_turn` - Probe is not a
turning kind, and the lathe voice refusal for it stays. Removing the
refusal before the turned-versus-baked posting proof existed - the safety
floor of #2276. Re-tuning the stylus slack to catch a deep burial - the
protected-move law already convicts the descent from the safe plane, which
crosses the turned part's top face.

**Cost to change later:** A new Probe world read must keep the setup-frame
contract: the facets it queries and the placement it applies must both come
from `setup_align`, and the proof tests must cover each new source or mode.
The verification entry can be withdrawn if that contract cannot be proved;
the refusal then blocks aligned generation by name.

## #2292 - Show the post script file path in the Post dialog

**Decided.** The desktop Post dialog's scope line (the weak small label at
the top right of the "Post" window) names the post script, and the full
path of a shipped script shows as a tool tip when the label is hovered:
`C:\...\assets\posts\fanuc.cps`.
It reuses the existing `posting::builtin_post_path` (which resolves
`assets/posts/<name>.cps` at run time from `camcraft_post::data_dir`, and
returns `None` on the browser build) through a new `posting::post_path`
helper. A user file already names itself through `posting::post_ref_label`
(the label is the path), so `post_path` returns `None` for it and only
registry entries (built-in / named) get the tool tip; a registry entry
that is gone gets none, since `script_source` refuses it anyway.

**Why.** Issue #2292 asks that a user can see which post script will run.
The path is already available (`posting::builtin_post_path`) but was never
shown. Showing it in the dialog scope line keeps the change small, touches
no posted output, and leaves the program header byte-identical so no
goldens change.

**Considered and dropped.**
- A dedicated "Script path" row in the Setup -> Post section
  (`crates/ui/src/egui_app/pages.rs`): redundant, since the post dialog is
  where a user reviews what will post, and a row there would duplicate the
  file name a user file already shows as its label.
- Showing the path for user files too: `post_ref_label` already returns
  the file path as the label, so `post_path` returns `None` for a user
  file and the tool tip stays unset.
- Computing the path from `BUILTINS` text (`assets/posts/<name>.cps`)
  instead of `posting::builtin_post_path`: the disk-resolved path is the
  single source of truth and already handles the wasm `None` case.

**Scope notes.** No command, MCP tool, project file, or posted output
changes. `posting::post_path` is `pub` so other panes can reuse it.

**Cost to change later.** Low. One small pure helper in `posting.rs` and
one label line in `post_dialog.rs`.

## #2303 - a generic LinuxCNC mill post (3-axis), separate from PathPilot

**Decided.** A new built-in post "LinuxCNC" (`assets/posts/linuxcnc.cps`)
and a generic machine "LinuxCNC 3-axis" (`assets/machines/linuxcnc-3axis.mch`),
written from the public LinuxCNC 2.9 G-code and M-code references. The
structure is our own `tormach.cps` (same interpreter); the PathPilot
assumptions are removed: no "machine Z0 is the top" convention, no G30
before each tool change, no belt-range notes, no 1-1000 tool range, no
4th axis. Options (declared post options):

- `retractMode` (default `g53`): `G53 G0 Z<safe_retract>` from the machine
  file; `g28` / `g30` write `G91 G28 Z0` / `G91 G30 Z0` then `G90` (Z only,
  to the stored position); `none` writes no retract (the control's INI
  tool-change position or M6 remap moves Z). With `g53` and no stated
  `safe_retract` - also with no machine at all - the post refuses by name.
  The generic machine file states no `safe_retract`, so a user must state
  it or pick another mode (#435 / #495: never assume Z0 is the top).
- `writeToolLength` (default on): `G43 H<n>` after `T<n> M6`. Off when the
  M6 remap applies the length; then the section safe block also drops
  `G49`, so a repeated tool keeps the length the remap applied.
- `pathControl` (`G64 P<blendTolerance>`, default 0.025 mm, or `G61`).
- `programEnd` (`M30` or `M2`) and `percentDelimiters` (`%` first and last).
- The PathPilot post's sequence-number, header and `useRadiusArcs` options.

Tapping: a rigid tap is `G33.1 Z<bottom> K<pitch>` (pitch = feed / rpm),
written only when the machine file states `rigid_tapping: true` (the
reference requires an encoder on `spindle.N.index-enable`). Otherwise it
is refused by name. A floating-holder tap is `G84` (the reference says G84
is not spindle-synchronized, F = rpm x pitch), so the post declares
`floatingTapping = true`. G33.1 is one move, not a modal cycle: the tool is
seated on R over the hole first and every hole seats again.

Engine: the machine mirror read `rigidTapping` as `true` when the file
states nothing (the unstated-limit law). The post cannot use that as "an
encoder is present", so the engine now also publishes
`machine.rigidTappingStated` (true only for a stated `rigid_tapping: true`).
No other post reads it.

Refused by name: control compensation (G41/G42), a tilted move (3-axis
only), a trip home after an operation, tool numbers that are not positive
whole numbers, G73/G83 with Q <= 0 (the reference makes it an error).

File extension `.ngc` (LinuxCNC's native extension).

**Dropped.** A post option for the G53 Z value (the machine file is the
machine's truth; one place to state it). Expanding a rigid tap into plain
moves (a tap cannot follow unsynchronized moves). G84 for rigid taps (not
synchronized in LinuxCNC). A G0 A indexing 4th axis (not in the issue;
the PathPilot post keeps it). Writing G41/G42 (LinuxCNC supports them,
but no golden or interpreter check exists for them here yet).

**Not verified on a control.** The output was not run in a LinuxCNC sim.
The reporter offered a LinuxCNC 2.9 sim run and an air cut.

**Cost to change.** The post and its goldens
(`crates/app/tests/golden/nc/linuxcnc/`, `synth_linuxcnc.nc`,
`crates/post/tests/recorded/golden/linuxcnc/`).

## #2339 - Save and restore panel setups

**What was decided**

- **Several named setups.** A saved panel setup is one named arrangement.
  The user types a name, saves the arrangement under it, and gets a row per
  saved setup with `Load` and `Delete`. One setup alone could not keep the
  maintainer's "setups" plural, and a name is what makes the list a list.
- **Stored in the application settings, not the project file.** The setups
  live in `panel-setups.json` in the per-user config folder, beside the
  theme and colour-vision preferences (`camcraft_app::prefs`). A setup is
  the screen's, not the part's: it survives New and Open, and it never
  marks the document changed. A file of its own (not a key inside
  `prefs.json`) was chosen so a corrupt or older setups file can never take
  the theme down with it, and because `prefs.json`'s `camcraft-prefs/1`
  tag would have had to change.
- **Auto-load is on by default, and the user can turn it off.** The last
  setup that the user saved or loaded is the one that comes back at the
  next start. The window has one tick box for this. A corrupt saved setup
  at startup is refused by name on the status line and the default
  three-pane layout stands.
- **`Reset to default` stays the View door's existing `Reset layout`
  command**, and the window carries a second door to it. No second reset
  command was added.
- **A load is not undoable.** It is view state, like the dock itself: the
  dock lives beside `State`, never in the world, and the history holds
  commands on entities. A saved-setup load rides the same one-frame
  mailbox that the View door's toggles use (`PanelSetupAsk`), so Ctrl+Z
  still undoes the last document edit and never a panel move. A test pins
  that no command is queued and the history stays empty.
- **The arrangement is the dock's own JSON.** egui_dock's `serde` feature
  is now on (a feature of an existing pinned dependency, not a new
  dependency), and `Tab` derives `Serialize`/`Deserialize`. This keeps
  exactly what the user can arrange by hand - split sides and fractions,
  leaf sizes, tab order, the active tab, collapsed leaves and float rects -
  which a hand-written summary of the default three panes would have lost.
- **The file carries its own version tag** (`camcraft-panel-setups/1`). An
  older or unknown tag is an empty store with a diagnostic, and the dock
  starts as the default. A setup whose dock this build cannot read is
  dropped at the load, and a load that fails puts the default layout back.
- **A saved dock is validated against the permanence law**: exactly one
  viewport, docked in the main area, and a main area with a root. A dock
  that breaks it is refused by name, never handed to egui_dock's asserting
  `split`.
- **Unlaid-out rects are saved as a placeholder.** An infinite `Rect`
  (`Rect::NOTHING`, a fresh float or split) becomes `null` in JSON and
  cannot be read back; `layout::setups::encode` replaces it with a
  320x240 placeholder, which the next frame recomputes.

**Why**

The maintainer asked: "we should be able to 'Save' panel setups what is
opened, where they are attached and how." A saved arrangement that lost
its float position or its split size would not be the arrangement the user
made. The command law stops at the document: the dock is deliberately not
in the world, so a save or load is a mailbox ask, not a history entry.

**Considered and dropped**

- One unnamed setup only. Dropped: the plural was asked for, and a list of
  names makes "load the one I use for roughing" possible.
- Storing the arrangement in the project file. Dropped: the issue's open
  point recommends application settings, and a per-part dock would move
  when a part is opened.
- A hand-written arrangement summary (open panels, a side, a size). Dropped:
  it cannot keep a user's own multi-split dock, so a load would rearrange
  their layout.
- Saving the arrangement automatically on every dock change. Dropped: the
  user asked for a save, and a silent rewrite of the file would make the
  saved setup move under them.
- Undoable saves and loads. Dropped: the dock is not document state, and
  Ctrl+Z after a panel drag is not the expected law here (the existing
  `layout` module's decision).

**What it would cost to change later**

- A different file format (for example our own summary instead of the
  dock's JSON) is a format tag bump: older files then load as the default
  with a diagnostic, which is already the tested path.
- A named setup as a project file field would contradict the store law
  above and would need a new project-file version.
- Making a load undoable would need a command that carries the whole dock
  as its payload; nothing in the current design blocks it, but the history
  would then hold view state.

## #2343 - Rotary Parallel leaves the end face of a held end

Sources: chuck and tailstock practice from machine-tool handbooks; our own
raster, link and stock code. No Fusion or HSMWorks material was consulted.

- **Decided: Rotary Parallel reads the setup stock and leaves the end face of
  a held end.** Where the stock goes on past an end of the model along the
  fitted axis by more than one tool diameter (plus the tolerance), that end is
  a held end: the bar goes on into a chuck or onto a centre. At a held end the
  centre of the ball does not go past the end plane of the model. The
  operation adds a note that names the end and the distance. A free end, where
  the stock ends with the model, is cut as before. **Why:** the end-face pass
  at a held end is a slot one tool diameter wide from the skin of the bar to
  its axis. That parts the bar. The post blocked it only for a tool with a
  short flute. The stock already says where the bar goes on, so the generator
  can know this without a new setting.

- **Decided: the limit is one tool diameter.** Stock that goes on by one tool
  diameter or less is a facing allowance. The end-face pass removes all of it
  and leaves no disc on the bar. That case does not change. More than one
  diameter leaves a disc that the pass cuts off, so it is a held end.

- **Decided: the centre of the ball stops on the end plane.** The turned
  surface is then finished to its end, and the verification reports no rest
  there. Half of the ball goes past the plane. There it cuts no deeper than
  the surface that it rides on, so the bar past the model keeps the radius of
  the model's end or more. **Dropped:** the centre one radius inside the
  plane, so that the ball never crosses it. I built this first. It left a
  strip one tool radius wide with the fillet of the ball, and the example got
  a scallop warning of 0.749 mm against a gate of 0.520 mm. The model was not
  finished to its tolerance, and the user had no way to finish it.

- **Decided: a sloped entry does not start past a held end.** With the
  sloped-entry law (a tool that is not centre-cutting), a ramp whose top is
  past the plane is not used. That infeed stays a radial plunge, and the
  centre-cutting guard judges it as before.

- **Decided: a model with no length between two held ends is refused by
  name.** No pass fits there.

- **Dropped: a new setting** (an axial window with two stations, or "leave
  the end faces"). It needs a parameter, a project-file version, a UI field
  and an MCP field. It is a `feat` and waits for the maintainer. With it, a
  user could also keep the pass off a free end face, or cut a held one.

- **Dropped: a refusal at each held end.** It makes the job impossible on a
  held bar, which is the usual way to hold rotary work.

- **Dropped: a warning only.** The program would still part the bar.

- **Not changed: Rotary Contour and Rotary Offset.** They read their heights
  as stations and already have an axial window.

- **Limit.** The generator knows only the stock that the setup states. If the
  stock ends where the model ends but the real bar goes on (the kit job of
  #2342), CamCraft reads air there and cuts the end face as before. The guide
  pages say this. A model with a domed or coned held end is still cut on that
  dome or cone, up to the end plane.

- **The #1904 example.** The example project and program are generated again.
  The program has no feed move past X-1.25. A 1/2 in flute now posts, because
  the shank refusal came from the cut that is gone. The guide page drops its
  "air cut only" limit and keeps the air cut as the first run.

- **Cost to change later.** A setting can replace the stock reading: `held`
  then returns the window from the two stations. `clip` and the callers stay.

## #2373 - Isolate the live theme between parallel unit tests

**Decided:** Keep the production live theme in its process-wide
`OnceLock<RwLock<Tokens>>`. Under `cfg(test)`, use a thread-local
`Cell<Tokens>` initialized to `Tokens::DARK`. Extract the storage helper to
`theme/live.rs` so the theme table stays near the 400-line limit.

**Why:** Rust's unit-test harness runs tests on separate threads. A test
that selects Light must not change the ground colors another test uses
when scanning overlay colors. Color-vision selection already belongs to
each world, but `palette_of` also reads the live theme's ground. Isolating
that shared input lets the existing tests run in parallel without changing
the application's runtime theme behavior.

**Considered and dropped:** Adding `snapshot_guard()` around every theme
reader and writer would serialize the tests and rely on every future
consumer remembering the lock. Using thread-local storage in production
would change runtime behavior across threads. Running all tests serially
would hide the interference instead of isolating their state.

**Limits and later cost:** This test-only isolation does not prove that
production theme access is safe across a sequence of operations on several
threads. A future unit test that renders on another thread must explicitly
install its tokens there. Changing the storage policy later is a small,
local helper change; callers keep the same `current` and `set_current`
interface.

## #2374 - A machine file names the post that writes its programs

**What was decided:** A `.mch` file may state `controller.post`, the name of
a built-in post. `Machine.post` carries it. `posting::post_offer` returns a
`PostOffer { post, why }`: the machine's named post (`OfferWhy::Machine`)
when it is a registry post that serves the mount and is not the setup's
post, else the kind offer as before (`OfferWhy::Kind`). The Setup page's
banner says which. Taking the offer queues the existing `SelectPostNamed`,
so it rides undo. The reader refuses anything but a non-empty string; the
validator also refuses an unknown name and a post that does not serve the
machine's kind, at `controller.post`.

The MCP tools say the same (a QA run on the issue): `post_offer_for` asks
for any setup, and `post_offer` is the active setup's. `load_machine`
replies with `post_offer` for the setup it mounted to, and `get_job`
gives each setup's `post_offer`: the post, why, and the
`set_setup_post` call that takes it. `null` means no offer. The mount
still changes nothing. The `post` tool's description lists every name in
`BUILTINS`, not a hand-written list that had lost "Tormach PathPilot".

The Machines pane's file editor gives a user's own machine its post: a
Post row in General is a dropdown (`Field.choices`) of the built-in posts
that serve the file's kind, the validator's rule, plus "(none)", which
takes the key out. A stated name off the list stays in view with its
refusal. Only built-in posts are offered: a `.cps` file has no stable
name for a machine file to state.

**Why:** `default_post_for` takes only the machine's kind, so for every
mill it offered Fanuc, and a setup on the grblHAL machine was never pointed
at the grblHAL post. The pairings existed only as comments in `MACHINES`.
In the file, a user's own machine can state its post too. `controller` is
the section about the control, and the post speaks the control's dialect.

**Shipped files:** 32 state their post, where the pairing is written in
`MACHINES`, a machine's issue or its post: the PathPilot mills, routers,
lathes and plasma table; grblHAL and the Sienci AltMills; TinyG; the
Makera machines; the Doosan DNM 5700s; the Haas machines. The generic
machines (`vmc`, `tilthead`, `millturn`, `lathe`), the Sodick ALC400G and
the Mach3-era Tormach PCNC 770 and 1100 mills state none: no pairing is
written for them, and a Mach3 control is not PathPilot. The sinker
template states none either: its kind's default is already the sinker
post, and the EDM suites share a byte copy of the file.

**Considered and dropped:**
- A table of machine-to-post pairs in code next to `MACHINES`: a user's
  own machine could not state its post.
- Changing the post on mount: a mount never re-points the post (#343,
  #388), and the maintainer repeated it on #2374.
- The reader refusing an unknown name: the registry is the app's, so the
  post crate would need it passed in. The validator refuses it in the
  catalogue and at save, and `post_offer` offers only a registry post that
  serves the mount, so a stranger name is never offered.
- A `PROJECT_VERSION` bump: `Machine` is `#[serde(default)]`, so an older
  reader drops the field. That loses only the offer, never a posted line.

**Cost to change later:** Local to `post::machine::post_name`,
`app::machine::validate`, `app::posting::offer` (`posting_offer.rs`),
`app::mcp::post_offer_view` and the Setup page's banner. The MCP field
names are a reply shape agents read: renaming one is a visible change. Moving the registry into `camcraft-post` (#924) moves the
validator's registry check with it.

## #2384 - Home button and the recent projects start page

**Decided:**

- A **Home** button in the top band (the workspace tab row), left of
  Donate. A click shows the start page; a second click, or **Back to the
  project**, hides it.
- The start page stands in for the dock in the central area: the ribbon
  and the status strip stay. It lists the recent projects (the #662 list,
  newest first, from the user's settings file), then **Open project…**,
  **New project** and **Back to the project**.
- A click on a project queues `OpenRecent`, the command of the ribbon's
  Open list. The unsaved-changes prompt and the refusals are Open's own.
  A gone file is greyed, reads "(missing)", and takes no click; its hover
  names the refusal.
- The page remembers the `doc_version` that it opened over
  (`State::home_page`). It closes when the document changes: an open, New,
  an import or any command. A refused open or a cancelled prompt leaves
  the document as it was, so the page stays.
- The page shows at a start with no file on the command line
  (`home::at_start` in the native window). A fresh `State` has no page, so
  the harnesses, the snapshots and the browser build start as before.
- The version label was already the rightmost toolbar item (#556). It
  stays where it is; a test pins that it is painted at the right.
- The page shows each path without the Windows verbatim prefix
  (`home::shown_path`): the list stores canonical paths, which carry it.
  The open still uses the stored path.
- The action row uses the form seam's `action_bar`. The list rows are
  plain buttons and labels: the form helpers have no list-row helper yet
  (#1122).
- The glyph is Tabler's home outline (MIT), with its SVG master in
  `assets/ui/svg/home.svg` and its notice in `assets/ui/LICENSES.md`.

**Why:** the maintainer asked for a Home button that goes to a recent
projects page and for the version in the top bar (#2384). The page and
its door are view state, so they need no command and no MCP tool; the
open goes through the existing `OpenRecent` command.

**Dropped:**

- A separate start window. The single-window law keeps extra surfaces as
  in-app panels, and a page in the central area needs no new window.
- Close the page on each click on it. A cancelled prompt would then drop
  the user on a document that they wanted to leave.
- A second version label in the top band. The toolbar already shows it at
  the right, with the build on hover.
- The start page in the browser build. That build has no recent files.

**Cost to change later:** low. The page is one file
(`crates/ui/src/egui_app/home.rs`) and one branch in `shell_layout`.

## #2394 - Example case turning/cone-thread: a cone with a threaded end

**What was decided**

1. **Two models, one axis.** The case imports the turned blank
   (`cone-blank.obj`: collar, cone, a plain 10 mm journal) and the finished
   part (`cone-thread.obj`: the same with the neck and the thread grooves).
   Face, Profile Rough and Profile Finish cut to the blank. The neck groove,
   the thread and the part-off cut to the finished part.
2. **A sixth operation for the neck.** The issue lists five operations. The
   neck is an undercut that the turning insert cannot reach, so a Groove
   Finish with the 3 mm blade cuts it (one plunge).
3. **G32 passes, not the G76 cycle.** The document keeps the default
   threading output.
4. **A custom threading insert.** `TD-1200-60`, 60 degrees, 1.2 mm wide,
   is given as a tool definition in `build.camscript`.
5. **The thread ends flush with the end face.** The groove centres are at
   Z63.9 + 1.5 k. The band of the last groove (Z76.8 to Z78.0) ends on the
   end face.
6. **A sharp shoulder.** The model has no fillet between the collar and the
   cone. The profile window starts on the collar at Z18, not on the shoulder
   plane at Z20.
7. **The pin reads the committed program.** The test
   `turning_cone_thread_case_posts_the_taper_and_the_thread` asserts the
   operation order, the taper slope of each finish block on the cone, and
   the thread passes. The two suite tests that iterate all cases give the
   regenerate, verify and byte-for-byte checks.

**Why**

1. The Threading kernel needs a modelled thread (V grooves). Profile Finish
   reads the valleys and the neck step as rest and blocks the post (#2880).
   No single model serves the two.
2. Without it the neck stays uncut and the thread has no relief.
3. The G76 start point is inside the part length. A Fanuc-type control
   moves to each pass depth at rapid at that point (#2878, filed P1). The
   G32 output plunges at feed. The issue asks for "the threading cycle";
   the program shows the threading passes instead, and the README says why.
4. The kernel requires `width < pitch - 2 * tolerance` and a reach of the
   thread depth. For M10x1.5 that is 1.01 mm to 1.4 mm. The catalog inserts
   are 0.866 mm and 1.732 mm wide (#893).
5. The verdict reads a band that goes past the end face as 5 mm of rest
   (#2879). A band that ends on the face is the nearest legal position.
6. A fillet's steep first chords send the ride out to X354 on a 30 mm bar
   (#2881). A window that starts on a shoulder plane starts on the same
   kind of degenerate station.
7. The byte-for-byte test fails on each change of the program, but it does
   not say what the program must show. The pin states the "Done means" of
   the issue.

**Considered and dropped**

- One model with a Profile Finish window that stops before the neck: the
  thread's major diameter stays at the rough allowance (10.5 mm). A wrong
  part.
- The G76 cycle as the issue's words suggest: not shipped as an example
  while #2878 is open.
- A copy of `TD-1732-60` with a changed width, made in the script from
  `list_tool_catalog`: shorter, but the reader does not see the insert.
- A catalog row for a 1.5 mm pitch insert: a tool library change, out of
  the scope of an example case (#893 covers the insert model).
- A fix of the kernel defects in this PR: they are motion and post changes
  under the safety floor, each with its own issue (#2878 to #2882).

**Cost to change later**

Low. When #2878, #2879, #2880 or #2881 is fixed, the case can go to one
model, the G76 cycle and a filleted shoulder: edit the generator and
`build.camscript`, run `cargo xtask catalog --case turning/cone-thread`,
and update the pin's thread asserts. When #2882 is fixed, the committed
`.nc` changes; rebuild the case in that PR.

**Review fix (PR #2883).** Keep both meshes embedded in the saved project.
After the imports, `build.camscript` uses `set_model_link` with `path: null`
to remove the source link. The UI checks relative source paths from the
process directory, which can differ from the case directory. An absolute
path would tie the example to one checkout. A change to the product path
resolver is outside this example fix.

The tests `every_catalog_case_opens_regenerates_verifies_and_posts_byte_for_byte`
and `every_catalog_case_rebuilds_from_camscript` pin the embedded meshes and
absent links for both models in the committed and rebuilt projects.
The UI test `catalog_cases_open_and_frame_cleanly` checks opening from
`crates/ui`.

## #2397 - the tool body and profile editor opens in its own window, and the old tool editor is removed

**Decided.**

- Properties shows the tool settings only: the label-left property grid of
  #2014, the one side preview of #2017, and one button, `Edit tool shape`.
- The tool shape editor is its own in-app modal window (`pages.rs`
  `tool_shape_editor_window`, state `State::tool_shape_editor`). It holds
  the holder library first, then the Body / Profile tabs, then the body
  mesh tools or the spun profile. The holder library is above the tabs, so
  a holder is the first thing the user sees and not a row under the
  profile table.
- The old combined tool editor window is gone. `State::tool_editor`,
  `pages::tool_editor_window`, `actions::open_tool_editor` and
  `close_tool_editor_window` are removed or renamed. No door opens a
  second settings surface.
- `New tool…` in the Tool library starts a blank numbered draft in
  Properties (`actions::begin_new_tool`, state `State::new_tool_form`). The
  empty `UiTarget::Tool` is the destination; the flag says which face of it
  shows - the pointer to the library, or the draft. A retarget drops the
  draft.
- Each shape control still queues the same undoable command as before:
  `Apply profile`, `Apply holder`, `Apply body`, `Clear body`, `Apply
  cutter`. No MCP tool changes.
- The shape window is a fixed frame with a scrolling body and a Close
  button that stays under it. The profile and cutter sections use two
  columns - the outline controls on the left, the points table and the
  side view on the right - so no row or button is clipped at the bottom.

**Why.** The maintainer reported that the tool page had two editors for
one tool and that the holder was only reachable under the profile table
(#2007, reopened). One surface for the settings and one window for the
shape matches how the user described the work: set the numbers, then edit
the shape. The two-column window also answers the "right half is mostly
empty" half of the report without a new layout law.

**Dropped.**

- A settings field inside the shape window. It would put a second
  editable surface back on screen; the window is the shape only.
- Removing the side preview from the shape window. #2017 keeps one side
  preview on Properties, and the shape window needs its own picture while
  it covers the dock. Two surfaces, one preview each.
- A single "Apply" in the shape window for the profile, the holder and the
  body at once. The three commands are separate undo steps today; one
  button would either hide that or merge three commands into one.
- A landing that keeps the Properties draft when the shape window closes.
  The shape drafts (body, profile, cutter) still reset on close; the
  settings draft in `State::tool_ui` now survives, because it belongs to
  Properties.

**Cost to change.** The window is one function in `pages.rs`; the shape
body is `tool_profile_page::editor` with the two columns in
`profile_section` and `tool_cutter_page::cutter_section`. The state field
is `State::tool_shape_editor`, closed by `State::close_tool_shape_editor`
and by the ghost law in `State::drain_actions`. The new-tool form is
`actions::begin_new_tool` and `State::new_tool_form`.

## #2400 - Dogbone and T-bone inside-corner relief for 2D pockets and slots

**What was decided:**
- Add `CornerRelief` (`kind`, `tbone_direction`, and per-corner `overrides` matched by XY) to `OpParams::Pocket`, `OpParams::Adaptive2D`, and `OpParams::Offset2D`, with empty/off defaults.
- Refuse non-empty `CornerRelief` on `Adaptive2D` with `AdaptiveMethod::Trochoidal` by name in both `sane` and `generate`.
- Compute each spur in `machining2d::corner_relief` from the raw boundary loop (collapsing micro-fillet chords within `FILLET_CHORD_COS`): place the cutter center along the inside bisector (`Dogbone`) or tangent to the selected wall (`TBone`) to offset `tool_radius + stock_to_leave`, then splice `[start, end, start]` into pocket passes (`corner_relief_spur`) and seed corner-blend bans at spur anchors.
- Enforce safety guards before emission (`operation::corner_relief`): refuse unreachable corners, wall crossings, unmatched overrides, stock exits, `Exclude` / open far-side crossings, `DoNotTouch` keepouts, kept/neighbour steel hits, and multi-height thin-wall punch-throughs.
- Declare bounded `verify::CornerReliefZone` corridors (`radius <= tool_radius`, `z_bottom..=z_top`, inside stock) for `verify` and `stock_sim::credit_corner_reliefs`, reconstructed live from current geometry in `operation::corner_relief_sim::zones_for_op`.

**Why:**
- Keeping `CornerRelief::default()` as off and omitting it from parameter digests and JSON DTOs when off preserves all existing operation digests and saved project files.
- Splicing continuous spurs onto pocket passes avoids separate plunge retracts while letting pocket entry, links, and stepdowns govern the whole cut.
- Bounding verification grants strictly to cutter radius, cut floor, stock boundary, and live CAD slices ensures real gouges and wall breakthroughs still fail.

**What was considered and dropped:**
- Emitting separate plunge or drill moves for corner reliefs: dropped because discrete plunges break cut continuity and bypass pocket link/entry guarantees.
- Expanding the input `Region` with Boolean ears before pocketing: dropped because inner island/keyway geometry can still block cutter approach or create slivers that Clipper rounds away instead of reaching the true corner vertex.
- Supporting `Adaptive2D::Trochoidal` corner relief silently or via perimeter re-cuts: dropped because trochoidal loop paths do not follow corner passes cleanly; an explicit refusal prevents silent omissions.

**Cost to change later:**
- Low to moderate: planning is isolated in `crates/motion/src/machining2d/corner_relief.rs` and `corner_relief_spur.rs`, verification is isolated in `crates/sim/src/verify/corner_relief.rs` and `stock_sim/corner_relief.rs`, and saved projects skip serializing default reliefs.

## #2407 - Post-defined tool-change macros

**Decided:** A post may declare `toolChangeMacros = { before: "M100\nM101", after: "M102" }`.
Both fields are optional strings and default to empty.
The engine emits their literal NC lines immediately before and after `onToolChange` for the first TOOL record and every later tool-number transition.
It still calls `onToolChange` for every TOOL record, but repeated records with the same tool number emit no macros.
Returning to an earlier tool number emits the macros again.
The resulting lines belong to that TOOL record in the preview trace and line map.
An absent or empty macro preserves existing output.

**Why:** The issue allows configuration in a machine file or a post, and its acceptance criterion asks for a post with macros.
A post manifest meets that criterion through the existing posting and preview path.
The existing Tormach post suppresses M6 for repeated TOOL records with the same number.
Suppressing the macros on those records prevents an aggregate head from unlocking and locking when its tool has not changed.
The engine checks the object and string types and rejects control characters other than newlines, tabs and CRLF by name.
It escapes macro text as data rather than evaluating it as JavaScript.
The post author remains responsible for choosing valid controller instructions and a safe machine sequence.

**Considered and dropped:** Adding machine-file fields now would also require changes to the typed Machine parser, mirror and persistence surface.
That broader configuration path is deferred.
Inserting macros inside individual post hooks would require changes to every post and leave the insertion point inconsistent.
Wrapping the existing hook gives all posts the same lifecycle boundary.
Executing macro text as JavaScript was rejected because the requested content is controller code.

**Cost to change later:** Machine-file configuration can reuse the validation and emission rules after adding explicit parser and mirror fields and defining override precedence.
Moving a macro inside a particular post's tool-change sequence requires a separate placement contract and new ordering tests.
Custom posts that force a physical tool change for a repeated tool number would need a future explicit placement contract rather than the current tool-number transition rule.

## #2437 - a Face does not lift over a hole that is below the cut plane

**What was decided.** Under the default `FaceHoles::Lift` law, the Face arm
of `generate` now gives the facer the outline of the material that stands
at or above the cut plane (`material_source::standing_at`). The facer
(`face_holes::beside`) bridges a hole of the region only when that material
stands in the hole or within 0.05 mm of it. A hole that no such material
touches opens below the cut plane. The row cuts straight across its column.

**Why.** A model source gives the facer the silhouette of the whole part.
A through-hole in a low flange is a hole of that silhouette at each height.
The facer lifted over it also when the cut plane was 5 mm above the hole's
rim. The lifts made rapids and plunges for no reason. Their row ends stood
within a tool radius of the open outer rim, and verify law (b) reported
each one as `cuts past the finish surface`. The 16 findings of the issue
were false: no part material stands above the cut plane there.

**What stays the same.**
- A boss in a hole is lifted over (the boss is material above the plane).
- A bore whose rim the cut plane reaches is lifted over, as M13.11 set it.
- `CutAir` and `Through` do not change.
- With no material outline (the slice refuses, or a direct `face` /
  `face_over(.., None)` call) each hole is lifted over, as before.

**Considered and dropped.**
- *Cut across each air hole under `Lift`.* That makes `Lift` equal to
  `CutAir` and changes each existing Face on a plate with holes at the cut
  plane. Dropped: larger than the issue.
- *Change verify law (b) so that an open region rim is not a wall for a
  law point.* The probe showed that a lifted row end within a tool radius
  of the open outer rim is still reported when the hole is at the cut
  plane (a plain plate, hole 5 mm from the edge, 10 mm tool). This is a
  second defect with its own cause in `sim::verify::section::tangency`. A
  change there relaxes a gouge law and needs its own issue, pins and
  review. Dropped from this PR and reported on the issue.
- *A new field on `FaceParams`.* The facer already takes `solid` beside the
  parameters. Reading it under `Lift` needs no new parameter and no
  project-file change.

**Cost to change later.** Small. The law is one match arm in
`face_holes::forbidden` and one arm in the Face arm of `generate`. Remove
the two arms to get the old behaviour.

## #2445 - Import the Solidcraft extension alias

**What was decided.** Treat `.solidcraft` as a case-insensitive alias of
`.sc` in `format_from_path` and the native `MODEL_EXTENSIONS` list shared
by the model dialog and viewport drop. List both names in the MCP import
path description. Both extensions use the existing checked cached-body
importer. The browser filter continues to omit Solidcraft designs because
the browser has no native Solidcraft importer.

**Why.** The two names contain the same design container. Routing both to
one importer preserves its validation and avoids duplicate parsing logic.
The successful MCP alias pin imports the existing sample, including its
thumbnail JSON and PNG entries, which the importer ignores.

**Considered and dropped.** A separate parser would duplicate the same
format. Renaming user files would retain the reported workaround instead
of supporting the saved name. Enabling browser imports requires a browser
reader and is outside this extension-alias fix.

**Cost to change later.** If the formats diverge, update the routing,
native filter, MCP description and regression pins together. Four pins
cover extension routing, named MCP refusal, successful MCP import and GUI
drop classification. Restoring either old routing path makes its pins
fail; restoring the fix makes them pass.

## #2462 - Open a model or project file that is given on the command line

**What was decided.**

- `camcraft-ui <file>` opens one file. A model file (`.stl`, `.obj`, `.step`,
  `.stp`, and a Solidcraft `.sc` on native builds) queues
  `CommandKind::ImportFile`. A `.camproj` file queues
  `CommandKind::OpenProjectFile`. These are the commands of the Model and
  Project dialogs and of a drop, so the worker, the update-or-spawn decision
  and the refusals are shared, not copied (`crates/ui/src/launch_file.rs`).
- The file arguments come from the same walk over the arguments as the
  option check (`cli_options::files`). Thus an option's value (`--gpu
  nvidia`) is never read as a file. A bare `-` is not a file. Arguments that
  `parse` refuses give no file.
- More than one file, an extension that CamCraft does not read, and a path
  that is not a file are refused by name on the status line
  (`open refused: ...`). The app then starts with an empty project. It does
  not exit: a user who double-clicks an unreadable file still gets the app.
- `--headless` ignores a file. The headless run is a self-check of the 3D
  view, not a document session. (Changed by #2648: a headless start now
  opens the file or refuses it by name; `2648-headless-file.md`.)
- `--help` shows `Usage: camcraft-ui [options] [file]` and a `File:` section.

**Why.** Solidcraft proposes a "Send to CamCraft" command (Solidcraft RFC
0001, phase 1; tangency-labs/solidcraft#18936) that starts CamCraft with the
design's path. The operating system's "Open with" needs the same argument.

**Considered and dropped.**

- Several files at once (import each model): the issue asks for one file,
  and a mix of a project and models has no clear meaning. A later issue can
  add it.
- A running window that takes the file from a second start (single
  instance): out of scope in the issue; it needs an IPC channel.
- macOS: `open -a CamCraft part.sc` delivers the file as an Apple Event, not
  as an argument. This change does not read Apple Events. Starting the
  binary inside the bundle with the path works.

**Cost to change later.** Small. The rule lives in `launch_file::command`
and `cli_options::scan`; the tests in `launch_file_tests.rs` pin it.

## #2463 - Linked model: import a model again when its source file changes

**What was decided.**

- **A model records its source** (`schema::ModelSource`: path and SHA-256,
  `crates/app/src/model_source.rs`). `ImportModel::within` records it after
  the parse; a mesh handed in and a browser pick record none. The record
  rides `UpdateModel` (traded with the facets, restored by undo; a repair
  that keeps the fidelity keeps it), `DeleteEntity` (delete and undo) and
  `ImportFixture`'s update. Generated meshes (vise, plate, accessory,
  profile fixture edits) update without a source, so they unlink: their
  facets are no longer the file's.
- **Project v72** (`project/source_dto.rs`): an optional `source` on a
  model row. Absent is not linked, so a v71 file steps up unchanged. A
  source on a row that is not a model, an empty path, a digest that is not
  64 lowercase hex digits, or an unknown key in it is a corrupt file. An
  older CamCraft refuses a v72 file by name (`unsupported project version
  72`), as for every version step: it would otherwise save a linked model
  back unlinked without a word.
- **The check** (`crates/ui/src/model_link_watch.rs`) runs in the app
  window about once a second (`INTERVAL`), and the frame timer comes back
  for it while a model is linked. A file is read again only when its size
  or modification time moved. When its SHA-256 is not the model's, the
  file is imported again through `CommandKind::ImportFile`; `finish_import`
  lands a file that a model is linked to on that model, whatever the file
  is called. The landing is the existing re-import: one `UpdateModel`, one
  undo step, the operations go Stale. Nothing regenerates or posts.
- **Undo stays.** The check remembers the digest it last imported for each
  model and does not import the same bytes again. An undo of the import
  thus stays until the file changes once more.
- **A missing or unreadable file** leaves the model as it is. The status
  line says it one time, by name; the check says nothing more until the
  file is readable again.
- **Unlink**: the Browser's model menu shows "Unlink from <file>" on a
  linked model (`CommandKind::UnlinkModel`, `SetModelSource`, one undo
  step). The MCP tool `set_model_link` links (to a path, recording its
  digest now, no import) or unlinks (`null`); `get_job` shows
  `models[].source`.
- **SHA-256** is the kernel's FIPS 180-4 implementation, re-exported as
  `camcraft_geometry::solidcraft::sha256_hex` (native only). No new crate
  dependency: geometry already depends on the kernel on native builds. A
  browser build records no link: it has no file to check again.

**Why.** Solidcraft proposes "Send to CamCraft" (tangency-labs/solidcraft
#18936, Solidcraft RFC 0001 phases 1 and 3). Each save in Solidcraft writes
the `.sc` file again; with this, CamCraft updates the part after each save.

**Considered and dropped.**

- An OS file-watch crate (`notify`): a new dependency, and the once-a-second
  check of size and time costs nothing while the files do not change.
- Hashing on the import worker: the STL importer streams the file, so the
  digest is a second read after the parse. A file that changes between the
  two reads records the newer digest; the next change imports it again.
- Regenerating Stale operations after an update: refused by the issue. The
  user regenerates and posts.
- Import on open: a project opened while a linked file changed is updated
  by the first check, the same way, and says so on the status line.

**Cost to change later.** Moderate: the project key is a format step (v72).
The check's rules live in one module and its tests pin them.

## #2474 - WCS flip: a flipped Z stays refused, with the exact reason

**What was decided.** A flipped Z does not post. The refusal stays at the two
doors (the verification gate, `app::setup_wcs_flip`, and the post engine,
`post::wcs_flip`). It now names the exact reason instead of a general one.
The two doors read the reason from one constant (`post::wcs_flip::Z_REASON`).
The issue permits this result: "or the refusal names the exact reason and the
decision is recorded".

**The exact reason: the tool-length word.** A flipped axis reads the same
physical point with the other sign. For X and Y the mirror is complete in the
program: signs, G2/G3 and G41/G42 follow from geometry. For Z, one word does
not follow from geometry: the tool-length word.

- The tool is on the physical "up" side of its tip. On a control that reads Z
  reversed, "up" is the control's -Z.
- A register that holds a preset length (a positive number from a presetter)
  then needs the subtracting word, G44.
- A register that holds a length touched off on that control already has the
  control's sign. It needs the adding word, G43.
- The project states only "Z is flipped". It does not state how the tool
  lengths were measured. The two cases need opposite words.
- The wrong word moves the tool by twice its length, toward the work in one of
  the two cases. A note in the program cannot make that safe (Prime Directive).

**The second reason: canned cycles.** A drilling cycle states an R plane and a
hole bottom. A mirrored Z puts the R plane on the far side of the hole bottom.
The public standards (RS-274 / NIST RS274NGC, ISO 6983) define the cycles with
the R plane above the bottom, and some controls refuse the other order. The
post engine names this only for a section that has a canned cycle.

**The open questions of the issue.**

- "Is a flipped Z a real machine setup?" Yes, it can be: a machine whose Z+
  moves toward the work (some routers), or a fixture frame that points down.
  The first is a machine property (`"direction": -1`, #374), and that door
  refuses Z for the same reason. The decision does not depend on the answer:
  the two cases have the same unknown tool-length word.
- "Which dialects can state a negative tool-length direction?" Fanuc and Haas
  have G44. LinuxCNC has G43 only. Heidenhain and Siemens do not use the word
  pair. This is from general machining knowledge and was not checked against
  each manual. A carry by G44 alone cannot cover each built-in mill post.

**What was dropped.**

- *Mirror Z and keep G43, with a program note.* Wrong by two tool lengths for
  preset registers.
- *Mirror Z and swap G43 to G44 (the geometric rule, as G41/G42).* Wrong by two
  tool lengths for touched-off registers, and not available in each dialect.
- *Expand the canned cycles into plain moves for a flipped Z.* It solves the
  second reason only. It has no use while the first reason refuses.

**What a carry needs (the maintainer decides).** One new statement from the
user: how the tool lengths of the flipped setup are measured (preset, or
touched off on the control). With it, the post can select the word, or refuse
a dialect that cannot state it. That is a new parameter with its command, MCP
tool, project-file field and one equivalence test for each dialect
(`crates/post/tests/wcs_flip.rs`, a reader with Z flipped that models the
tool-length word). The setup sheet, the travel check and the viewport envelope
need no change while Z is refused.

**Cost to change later.** Low. The refusal is one branch in each door and one
shared constant. The X and Y mirror (`invert::translate_rules`) already
negates Z coordinates when asked; the cycle branch and the tool-length word
are the open parts.

## #2475 - Each mill post carries a flipped WCS axis and an inverted machine axis

**Decided:** each mill script declares `axisInversion = true`: Mazak, Doosan
DNM, Siemens 840D, Heidenhain, Mach4, grblHAL, Tormach PathPilot, TinyG,
Carvera, and LinuxCNC. LinuxCNC is not in the issue's list (the script is
newer than the list), but the issue's "Done means" says "each mill script".
No script has a recorded reason why it cannot.

**The evidence.** `crates/post/tests/wcs_flip_dialects.rs` posts the mirrored
stream of `wcs_flip.rs` through each script (Fanuc and Haas too, to calibrate
the reader). A new reader, `tests/mirror_trace`, reads the program as a
controller whose X, Y or X and Y run reversed. It compares the physical cut
runs with the CAM path point by point at equal fractions of the run length.
It also compares the physical compensation side, and it checks that no rapid
ends over an X Y that the CAM path does not visit. The standard program read
by the reversed controller must stray, for each script and each case.

**What each dialect changes under a mirror, and how it is read.**

| Dialect | Arc words | Compensation | Drilled hole |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mazak, Doosan DNM, Mach4 | I/J/K increments, G17/G18/G19; R words with `useRadiusArcs` (not Mach4) | G41/G42 | G81 |
| Siemens 840D | I/J/K increments, G17/G18/G19 | `G41 NORM` / `G42 NORM` | G81 |
| Heidenhain | an `I J` block as the absolute centre, then planar G02/G03; XZ and YZ arcs as 1 um chords; native XY helices refused | refused by the script | G200 with an M99 call |
| Tormach, LinuxCNC, grblHAL | I/J/K increments (G91.1); R words with `useRadiusArcs` | refused by the script | G81 |
| Carvera | I/J/K increments | refused by the script | plain moves |
| TinyG | XY arcs in half turns, XZ and YZ arcs as 5 um chords | refused by the script | plain moves |

No script computes a direction, a side or a centre from anything but the
record's own mirrored fields (`CircularDirection`, `IJKIncrement`, `Start*`,
the end point, the compensation side) and the mirrored `Origin*`. That is why
the same engine pass is correct for each of them. The scripts read no other
parameter with an X or Y meaning.

**Why a new reader and not `inverted_support::controller_events`.** That
reader compares event by event. It needs one posted block for each stream
record. TinyG splits arcs, Heidenhain and TinyG write chords, Carvera and
TinyG expand the hole, and each dialect has its own first-traverse blocks. A
comparison of dense polylines is independent of these forms. The reader
panics on a G word that it does not model, so a `G91`, `G68` or mirror word
cannot pass as a trace.

**Each script also writes the two notes** that Fanuc and Haas write: the
section note `WCS X FLIPPED - PROGRAM MIRRORED` (#1649) and the header note
`MACHINE X+ MOVES LEFT - INVERTED AXIS` (#375), in the dialect's comment form.
Doosan DNM and Mach4 had the header note already.

**Kept refused:**
- Heidenhain native XY helices, with or without a WCS flip. The trace and
  golden use the planar fixture for this dialect. A separate test pins the
  named refusal. The reader rejects a Cartesian G02/G03 that changes Z.
- Probing in a flipped WCS (the maintainer's decision of 2026-11-18, engine
  level).
- Probing on an inverted machine axis through the ten scripts. They do not
  declare `probeAxisInversion`; that needs the macro interpreter proof of
  #392 for each dialect. A test pins the refusal.
- A flipped Z, a flipped and rotated WCS, tilted moves, turning, EDM and
  plasma sections (engine level, not changed).

**Refusal texts.** The hint "(Fanuc, Haas)" in the three refusals for a
script without the flag is now "(each built-in mill post does)". A lathe
script and a user's script without the line are still refused; the two
refusal tests use those.

**Dropped:**
- A golden for each of X, Y and XY for each dialect. One X golden for each
  dialect pins the full text; the trace test covers the three cases.
- A trace of tapping, peck and bore cycles on the mirrored stream. These
  cycles take the same mirrored X Y as G81; their other words (Z, R, Q, P, F)
  have no X or Y meaning. Not exercised.
- The line in `.claude/skills/camcraft-mcp/SKILL.md` that says "Fanuc and
  Haas are". The worker session could not write to `.claude/skills`. The MCP
  tool description in `wcs_flip_tools.rs` has the new text.

**Review correction:** the HEIDENHAIN TNC 640 ISO Programming User's Manual,
ID 892909-25, pages 271-272, specifies a helix in polar coordinates. The
Cartesian `G02 X Y Z` form is not a verified helix form for this control.
The post now refuses a native XY helix by name before it writes the arc.
This applies to plain sections and to flipped sections. Planar XY arcs and
the existing XZ/YZ chord paths keep their trace proof.

**Chosen:** refuse the unsupported helix. **Why:** the mirror flag must not
permit a path that the control manual does not document. **Dropped:** add
native polar helix output in this review fix. That needs its own output
implementation and control-reader proof. The present fix limits the post
to its verified forms.

**Cost to change later:** to withdraw one script, delete its
`axisInversion = true` line and its row in `POSTS`. The engine then refuses
that script by name again.

## #2476 - Carry a WCS XY flip with a Z rotation

**What was decided**

- Keep the existing pass order: WCS flip, WCS rotation, then any
  machine-axis inversion. Bake mirrors the existing setup/table
  coordinates. Control rotates those mirrored coordinates using the yaw
  expressed in the mirrored frame. The existing passes carry arc
  centres, starts and stock bounds with the moves.
- Reverse the controller's G68 / ROT angle when exactly one of X and Y
  is flipped. Keep its sign when both are flipped. Keep that composition
  in the shared Rust passes so every rotation-capable dialect receives
  the same transformed stream.
- Allow a Z-yaw WCS through the app's flip validation. Keep named refusals
  for other rotations and nonfinite placements: "only a finite Z rotation
  is supported with flipped axes". Keep refusals for flipped Z, probing
  and the operation types the mirror does not carry. Keep the existing Control
  capability checks and its refusal with inverted machine axes. A non-XY
  arc in a rotated WCS remains refused by the rotation pass.
- Keep the existing travel and setup-sheet behavior. Travel judges the
  mirrored table-frame path after the controller rotation, independently
  of the output mode. The sheet states the setup's original yaw and its
  flipped axes.

**Why**

A reflection and a rotation do not commute. Write the XY mirror as `F`,
its determinant as `d`, and the original yaw as `a`. The flip pass states
`a1 = d * a`. The rotation pass then produces
`R(-a1) F (p - O) = F R(-a) (p - O)`. The controller applies `R(a1)`
in its mirrored frame, so the physical path is
`F R(a1) R(-a1) F (p - O) = p - O`. One flipped axis has `d = -1`;
flipping both XY axes has `d = 1` and preserves the angle sign. The
existing mirror also carries the arc-direction and cutter-compensation
side changes.

**Considered and dropped**

- Reorder rotation before reflection. A mutation that restored the old
  pass order still passed the Control pin: conjugating the yaw in the
  flip pass makes that order equivalent. The reorder adds no behavior,
  so it was dropped.
- Keep refusing every combined flip and yaw. The existing rotation and
  mirror passes can carry the supported milling cases with the
  conjugated yaw.
- Add separate mirror-angle rules to each post script. A shared stream
  transform gives each dialect the same geometry and avoids duplicated
  rules.
- Add dependencies or another placement representation. The existing
  WCS flags, yaw parameter and record transforms express the operation.

**Cost to change later**

The angle parity and composed physical path are part of the posting contract.
Adding another controller rotation convention must preserve the traced
physical path. Extending flipped Z, probing, tilted work or inverted
machine axes in Control mode still needs its own proof and named
capability handling; this change does not remove those refusals.

## #2481 - Grbl 1.1 post (3-axis mill)

Sources: the public Grbl 1.1 wiki pages "Commands" and "Interface"
(supported G and M words, the serial line limit, the M0 program pause).
Behaviour only. The script is derived from our own `grblhal.cps`. No
vendor post or vendor output was consulted.

- **Decided: drill cycles post as G0/G1/G4 moves, never G73/G81-G89.**
  **Why:** Grbl 1.1 has no canned cycles. The engine already sends the
  expanded hole moves next to the CYCLE record, so the post passes them
  through, as `tinyg.cps` does. A dwell (P > 0) is a G4 at the hole bottom.
  **Dropped:** an expansion in the script - it would repeat the engine's
  expansion and could drift from it.
- **Decided: BORE and TAP are refused by name.** **Why:** an expanded bore
  needs a spindle stop before the rapid retract, and a tap needs a
  synchronised spindle. Grbl 1.1 has neither as a cycle. A refusal is
  safer than a program that drags the tool out of the bore or breaks a tap.
- **Decided: tool change is M0 with comments, no M6, no G43/G49.** The
  first tool gets `(LOAD T<n> AND SET Z ZERO BEFORE THE START)`. Each
  later tool gets a retract, `(TOOL CHANGE - LOAD T<n> - SET Z ZERO -
  RESUME)` and `M0`. **Why:** Grbl 1.1 ignores M6 and has no tool table;
  the operator sets Z again after each change.
- **Decided: a line is at most 79 characters.** Comments are cut to fit.
  A motion line that does not fit refuses the program. **Why:** the Grbl
  1.1 serial line buffer is 80 bytes with the terminator; a longer line is
  rejected by the control. Cutting a motion word is never safe.
- **Decided: no G41/G42 control compensation.** Grbl 1.1 has no cutter
  radius compensation, so an op set to control or wear compensation is
  refused, as on TinyG.
- **Machine:** `grbl-3axis.mch` is a copy of `grblhal-3axis.mch` with the
  model "Grbl 3-axis". The user edits the limits for the real machine.

Not exercised: no reading on a real Grbl 1.1 control. The pinning tests
check the goldens and the dialect (`grbl_dialect.rs`: line length and
banned words) only.

Cost to change later: low. The script and the machine are two assets and
one registry line each.

## #2502 - Split contour entry from shared band generation

**Chosen:** Stack on PR #2460 at `ceac40dd9` and move the single-region
entry functions, `PartRef`, and `contour_impl` into `contour_region.rs`.
Keep `PreparedBand`, `prepare_band`, `emit_band`, `finish_contour`,
`air_side`, and `unit` in `contour.rs`. Re-export the entry functions
through `contour.rs` to preserve the public API.

**Why:** The band extraction in #2460 left `contour.rs` at 514 lines.
The split follows the domain seam between single-region orchestration and
band generation shared with `contour_whole`. It leaves `contour.rs` at
396 lines and `contour_region.rs` at 132 lines without changing behavior.

**Considered and dropped:** Moving the emission body would disturb the
tab-handling lines changed by PR #2486. Keeping that body in place makes
the split smaller and avoids that overlap. Existing tests remain untouched
as the issue requires. A temporary external structural pin checks the
400-line limit without adding a repository test or review evidence.

**Cost to change later:** A different module boundary would require moving
the functions and adjusting internal imports. The public re-exports keep
callers independent of this layout; no project format or toolpath behavior
changes with the split.

## #2508 - Move handle cleanup

**Chosen:** Release the centre cache's facet `Arc` and cached centre when
`handles` finds no draggable part and Rotate has no eligible selected part.
Keep the cumulative `computes` counter. Keep the cache while Rotate uses
the selected, visible part.

**Why:** An inactive handle mode must not keep a deleted part's mesh alive.
Move and Rotate share this cache. Clearing it during every Rotate frame
would make Rotate walk the facets again each frame.

**Dropped:** Clear the whole cache on every failed Move query. That would
discard the counter and break Rotate's cache reuse. Replace the retained
facet reference with a weak reference. That would change the cache key's lifetime guarantee
without a need for that change.

**Chosen:** Move the viewport glyph drawing into
`viewport_bar_glyphs.rs`. Keep the bar layout and button actions in
`viewport_bar.rs`. Keep every existing test. Draw an original Move glyph
with a small rectangular part and three arms with round tips. Keep Pan's
four arrows.

**Why:** The split follows the drawing seam and keeps both source files
below about 400 lines. The part and three arms distinguish Move from Pan
at the button's size. The glyph needs no imported asset or licence change.

**Dropped:** Keep the four-arm Move cross. Its outline remains too close
to Pan. Import another icon set. The original drawing meets this need
with less work.

**Chosen:** Defer the split and CRLF conversion of `shell.rs`. Preserve
its bytes in this patch. Convert its line ends in a separate commit when
few open PRs change it. Split it along its domain seams after that.

**Why:** At the overlap check, PRs #2256, #2149 and #1798 change this file.
PR #1798 has `needs-maintainer`, so this issue must not stack on it.
A whole-file split or line-end conversion would increase those conflicts.
The issue permits a recorded decision for each item. At the start of this
patch, `shell.rs` has 1087 lines and CRLF line ends.

**Dropped:** Split or normalize the shell now. This would mix broad
mechanical changes with active work in the same file.

**Chosen:** Keep the crate-wide formatting check unused for this patch.
Format the new glyph module. Do not reformat unrelated code.

**Why:** A crate-wide formatting commit would include extensive unrelated
changes and conflict with active UI PRs. The focused diff is easier to
check. A future formatting change can run when the UI queue is quiet.

**Dropped:** Format the whole crate in this patch. The formatting changes
do not prove cache release or improve the Move glyph.

**Cost to change later:** The cache policy and glyph are local changes.
The deferred shell split needs a focused patch that preserves its tests.
The CRLF conversion needs its own commit. A crate-wide formatting change
needs coordination with open UI PRs and a fresh gate run.

## #2511 - Uncut-corner check: a note when the check did not run

**What was decided.** When `unreached_corner_note` returns an error,
`keep_law::narrow_noted` now adds a note to the toolpath:
`<kind>: the check for corners of the stock tighter than the tool did not
run (<error>) - look at the stock corners around the part`. The log line
stays. The path is kept and the cut is not blocked, as for the band check
directly above it.

**Why.** The band check already says in a note that it did not run. The
corner check wrote only a log line. Material could stay in a corner and
the user saw nothing (review of PR #2503).

**The pin.** `operation::keep_law::tests::a_corner_check_that_cannot_run_says_so_in_a_note`
is a unit test beside `narrow_noted`, because that function is
`pub(super)`. It uses a tool diameter of 4e12 mm. The erosion then
returns `GeoError::OutOfRange`, so the two checks fail and each must give
its note. No input through the commands gets to this error today; the
test pins the guard for the day one does.

**Considered and dropped.**
- One shared note for the two checks: dropped. Each check names different
  material (bands, corners), and one can fail without the other
  (the corner check has more steps: the dilation and the stock clip).
- A blocking warning in place of a note: dropped. The check is advisory
  and the band check does not block either.
- An end-to-end test in `crates/app/tests/narrow_band.rs`: dropped. No
  legal document makes the corner check fail.

**Recorded, not changed: the 0.03 mm noise threshold.**
`CORNER_HALF_WIDTH` (0.03 mm, `crates/motion/src/machining2d/unreached.rs`)
can hide a real cusp at an obtuse stock corner (review of PR #2503). At a
150 degree corner with a 10 mm tool the cusp is about 0.18 mm deep
(`r * (1 / sin(75 deg) - 1)` = 0.176 mm). By calculation its largest
inscribed circle has a radius of about 0.087 mm, which is above the
threshold; a corner more obtuse than about 162 degrees has a cusp below
it and gets no note. This calculation is not a measurement. The decision
of #2503 accepted this threshold. This PR does not change it. The number
must be reviewed against a measured case before it changes; that review
is open work and needs its own issue.

**Cost to change later.** One format string and one test assertion.

## #2538 - Whole-model 2D Contour: a ring without a floor level gets its own note

**What was decided.** A band of a whole-model 2D Contour that stops at the
next flat level and still emits floor passes now checks each outer ring.
An outer ring that stops at that level and has no floor level above it gets
a note. The note names the ring and its uncut Z range: `whole-model
contour: the ring at (x, y) has no floor level between Z a and Z b - that
wall is not cut; reduce the stepdown`. The check is in the one arm that the
first band and the in-between band share, so one function covers the two
cases of the issue.

**Why.** The band cut the rings that have a floor level and then continued
with a new outline. The ring without a floor level got no pass and no
note, because `forward_band_notes` drops the notes of outer rings when the
contour continues. That is a silent wrong result (Prime Directive).

**A note, not an error.** The band without any floor level already gives a
note and continues (#2436). The same condition on one ring of a band gets
the same class of message. The rest of the program is correct and the note
tells the user what is not cut and what to do.

**Considered and dropped.**
- Forward the `contour_depth::ladder` note of that ring ("meets the part at
  its first level - not walked at any level"). Dropped: that text names the
  skipped flat levels, which the next band does cut. It does not name the
  Z range that stays uncut.
- Refuse the operation. Dropped: it is not consistent with the note of the
  band that has no floor level at all.
- Add the test to `crates/motion/tests/contour_whole.rs`, as the issue
  says. Dropped: that file has 375 lines and the 400-line law applies. The
  pins are in `crates/motion/tests/contour_whole_no_floor.rs`, with the
  same Gate map.

**Not changed.** The first band with no floor level on any ring (for
example a part with only a top chamfer) still gives no note. The issue does
not include it, and a note there changes the output of each chamfered part.

**Cost to change later.** One function (`note_rings_without_floor`) and two
tests. A change of the note text changes the two pins.

## #2561 - a contour tab is checked against every cut of its level

**Decided.** After `tab_bridge::fit_tabs` fits each ring, the new
`tab_clear` reads each tab's line on the ring against every other cut of
the tabbed levels: the other keeps of the same ring, the far part of the
two keeps beside the tab, and every other ring.

- Another cut nearer than the tool diameter `D` cuts into the tab. The
  loop is held: its tabbed levels cut nothing, and a `tabs:` note names
  the tab and the distance. This is the response that `fit_tabs` already
  gives when no bridge fits.
- Another cut between `D` and `W + D` away leaves the tab at its width,
