  with less than the tab width of material beside it. The loop is cut as
  before, and a `tabs:` note names the tab and the width of the strip.
- A picked start that a grown tab covers gets a `tabs:` note that names
  the pick and the point where the tabbed levels start instead.
- `SLACK` stays `1e-6` with no margin for the chord error. A test reads
  the bridge on the posted arcs in chords of `1e-5` mm and pins it to
  `1e-4` mm.

**Why.** The shape-mask measurement on main found tabs with a neck of
0 mm and no note: a tab on the wall of a notch 10 mm wide (6 mm cutter),
and a tab that faces a second part 10 mm away. The return run, or the
other ring, passes 4 mm from the tab and removes it from its stock. A
part can then come free with fewer tabs than the user asked for (Prime
Directive: correct, or refused by name).

The strip case is a note and not a hold. The strip between two kerfs has
the full cut depth, and the tab has only the tab height, so the strip is
not the weak point. The same reading also occurs across a thin wall of
the part itself, which is not a tab defect. A hold there would refuse
common nests.

**Dropped.**

- Move the tab away from the other cut. This changes where the user's
  tabs are, and needs a placement law. Not in this fix.
- Hold only the loops that have no good tab left. The user asked for a
  count; fewer tabs without a refusal is the silent case again.
- Remove a held ring's cuts before the other rings are checked. The
  check uses all cuts as first fitted. This is conservative: a hold only
  removes cuts.
- A margin on `SLACK`. A margin of some microns grows each tab window
  on a straight wall and moves the recorded router example program. The
  measured error on the posted arcs is under `1e-6` mm on the fixtures of
  the test. The flatten step (0.05 mm, 8 samples or more for each arc)
  limits the sagitta to about 0.005 mm in the worst case; the tests
  already accept 0.02 mm.
- The meter in `shape_mask.rs`. That file has 409 lines, so the meter is
  `crates/motion/tests/common/tab_neck.rs`.

**Limits.** The check is local to the tab's line on the ring. It does
not follow the stock strip farther along (a strip that narrows away from
the tab). The two keeps beside a tab count only from where they have
left the tab (`W + D` of walk, then the first point `W + D` from the
line); `tab_bridge` owns the part before that. Tabs of two rings that
face each other at the same place join the two parts and not the stock:
this reads as "cuts into" only when the other ring cuts there.

**Cost to change.** `tab_clear::fit_band` is one function with two
thresholds. A later placement law (move the tab) replaces the hold arm.

## #2561 - review fixes of PR #2705 (takeover by the owner account)

**Decided.**

- `tab_clear::departed` drops only the monotonic exit of a keep beside
  the tab: the pieces whose distance from the tab line keeps growing. A
  piece that comes nearer to the line than the farthest point before it
  starts the counted part of the cut, also inside `reach` and before the
  cut is `W + D` away. A U-turn in a shallow notch beside the tab is then
  read and holds the loop.
- With one keep on the ring, its lead-in and lead-out join the tab at
  both ends. `nearest_other` now reads them through `departed` too, so a
  lead that turns back toward the tab counts.
- `tab_clear::fit_loops` takes the tabbed levels of each loop from the
  depth ladder (`Ladder::ring`). A loop with no tabbed level is not
  checked, and a ring is read against the tabs of ring `i` only when the
  two rings share a tabbed level. With no tabbed level in the band, no
  fit is made.

**Why.** The review of head `edb566d33` found a neck of 0 mm with no note
(an 18 mm deep notch), and a false hold of a deep island beside an island
that stops on a shelf above the tabs. The first is a silent thin bridge.
The second refuses a legal program.

**Dropped.**

- Check the pieces past `reach` against `D - SLACK` only. That reads the
  turn-back but not a strip narrower than the tab width, so the note of
  the strip case would depend on the notch depth.
- Check the adjacent leads for each count of keeps. With two or more
  keeps, `tab_bridge` measures those leads; the brief asked for the
  one-keep case only.

**Limits.** The distance is to the tab line as a segment. Near the ends
of the line this is conservative: a turn-back past the end of the tab can
read as nearer than it cuts. The result is a hold or a note, never a
silent bridge.

## #2561 - the two cuts beside a tab against the tab core (`tab_kerf`)

**Decided.**

- New module `crates/motion/src/machining2d/tab_kerf.rs`. `nearest_other`
  reads the two cuts beside a tab also against the core of the tab line:
  the line without its first and last `D / 2`. The two end kerfs (the
  tool disc at each tab end) remove those parts.
- A point of a cut beside the tab is skipped only while the cut stays in
  the disc of radius `D` about the tab end and goes away from that end.
  In that part, the cut is read against the core outside that disc. From
  the first point where the cut leaves the disc, or turns back toward the
  end by more than `TURN = 1e-3` mm, all of the cut is read against the
  full core.
- A distance under `D - SLACK` holds the loop with a `tabs:` note. A NaN
  distance or a NaN limit holds the loop. The new read adds a hold only,
  never a note. `departed` stays for the "narrow strip" note.

**Why.** The review of head `57756c69a` (comment 7007645147) found a
return run along the tab at a constant distance. `departed` dropped that
run because it does not come nearer to the tab line. The meter read a
neck of 0 mm with no note: a silent thin bridge.

**Dropped.**

- Read the full cut against the full tab line. Each cut touches the tab
  end where it starts, so each tab would hold.
- Skip a fixed length of each cut (`reach`). A short notch puts the
  return run inside that length, and the run is not read.
- Make `departed` stricter only. It measures "comes nearer"; a run at a
  constant distance never does.

**Limits.** The tool is a disc and the cut is its centre line. The read
can hold a loop where the true neck still keeps the tab width (an acute
V-notch, a tab end near a tight fold). Such a hold is safe: the tabbed
levels cut nothing, and a note says so. A bore or a slot narrower than
about two tool diameters keeps its tab-height ring of material uncut,
with a note.

## #2566 - Import and export PathPilot (.csv) and Hurco WinMax (.TCM) tool tables

**Decided:** Add a shared machine tool-table codec layer in `camcraft-tools`
(`crates/tools/src/tool_table*.rs`) with a minimal pure-Rust XML reader/escaper
(`tool_table_xml.rs`, no new crate dependencies) and a document-unit bridge in
`crates/app/src/tool_table.rs`. Extend `LibraryTool` with `number: Option<u32>`
and extend `ImportTools` (`crates/app/src/commands/tool_import/mod.rs`) to preserve
controller `T<n>` numbers, refuse tool-number clashes by name, allow number
swaps and reassignments within Update/Replace imports, and apply everything in one
undo step. Keep `.camtools` JSON (`units: "mm"`, no controller numbers)
unchanged. Default controller table units to the document's active units in GUI
(`state_tool_library.rs`), MCP (`import_tool_library`, `export_tool_library`), and
job scripts (`cam.importTools`, `cam.exportTools`), with optional `format` and
`units` overrides in MCP/scripts.

For Tormach PathPilot `.csv`: require the row-1 `Mill Tool Table` marker, bound
numbers to `1..=1000`, parse optional `Description` tokens (`R:`, `loc:`,
`<n>FL`, tool material, `[part]`), keep `Description` as tool name, ignore
machine `Z offset` placeholders, treat negative `Max RPM` values (such as
`-2.0` on probes) as unstated, skip empty slots, refuse bad rows or non-mill
export kinds by name, and export with zeroed offsets.

For Hurco WinMax `.TCM`: read/write UTF-8 XML with BOM and CRLF under
`<Hurco_Document Version="1.1">`, strictly map documented `#30001` `ToolType`
codes (`0,2,7,11,12,13,14,15,16,18,20,21,22,26`) and refuse unsupported codes
(`1,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,17,19,23` or unknown) by name, map `AbsoluteGaugeLength` onto
holder `gauge_len`, and omit Hurco control state (`UsedTime`, `Flags`,
`GeometryFlags`, probe offset indexes) on export.

**Why:** Keeping parsers/writers in `camcraft-tools` decouples table codecs
from Flecs ECS while sharing tool geometry and sanity rules. Refusing
unsupported Hurco `ToolType` codes and non-mill PathPilot exports by name
prevents silent cutter substitution. Ignoring PathPilot `Z offset` on import
and zeroing exported offsets avoids confusing machine gauge offsets with tool
stick-out or writing stale offsets back to a machine. Omitting WinMax control
state avoids resetting tool life or probe calibration data on import.

**Considered and dropped:**
- Adding an external XML dependency in `Cargo.toml` (dropped for one narrow,
  self-contained XML format).
- Mapping unsupported Hurco cutters such as keyseat or dovetail tools to
  `ToolKind::EndMill` (dropped because wrong cutter geometry is unsafe).
- Adding controller tool numbers to `.camtools` JSON or changing its `units: "mm"`
  contract (dropped to keep native `.camtools` files backwards-compatible).
- Emitting guessed zeroed `UsedTime`/`Flags`/`GeometryFlags` tags in `.TCM`
  exports (dropped so partial exports never clobber controller runtime state).

**Limits and later cost:** Acceptance of exported partial `.TCM` files on a
live Hurco WinMax 9.01 control and live PathPilot Hub UI import still need
machine verification. All format-specific field mappings sit inside
`crates/tools/src/tool_table*.rs`, so adding fields or relaxing version headers
from real machine captures is isolated to that module.

**Decided after review:** Refuse a named slitting saw in PathPilot input until
our tool model can represent its cutting shape. Before PathPilot export,
read the proposed description and rounded diameter through the same reader.
Refuse the export by tool name if the resulting cutter geometry differs.
Keep the description and tool name unchanged. Direct the user to `.camtools`
when PathPilot cannot preserve the geometry. Compare geometry lengths within
`1e-6` mm to allow the seven-decimal CSV diameter rounding.

Use character boundaries for malformed XML entity diagnostics. Limit XML
nesting to 32 elements from the root through the leaf before recursive descent.
Return a diagnostic when the input exceeds this limit.

**Why:** A controller table must not substitute a different cutter or cutting
shape. A malformed table must return an error without a Unicode panic or
stack overflow.

**Considered and dropped:** Rewriting descriptions with new geometry tokens
would change tool names and require a new metadata convention. Preserving
names and refusing a lossy export keeps the existing table contract. Unbounded
XML recursion cannot safely accept untrusted controller tables.

**Limits and later cost:** A future tool model can add slitting saw support.
PathPilot export can accept more descriptions when its reader can preserve
more cutter geometry. Both changes need new geometry round-trip tests. Raising
the XML depth limit requires a bounded parser stack or a checked stack budget.

**Decided after the second review:** Start imported threading tools with zero
pitch. Require a positive recorded `ThreadPitch` for Hurco taps and thread
mills. Refuse PathPilot threading tools by name because CSV has no pitch
field. Refuse Hurco left-hand tap exports by name because the supported
export fields cannot preserve the hand.

**Why:** A guessed pitch can produce an incorrect tapping feed. An export
must not change a left-hand tap into a right-hand tap.

**Considered and dropped:** Guessing pitch from free-form descriptions or
using a default pitch does not establish the cutter's required pitch.
Writing an unverified Hurco hand field cannot establish a safe round trip.

**Decided after the third review:** Refuse Hurco export by tool name for
non-center-cutting bull-nose, chamfer, and ball-nose tools. Keep type 15 for
non-center-cutting flat end mills.

**Why:** The supported Hurco types cannot preserve this restriction for the
three cutter kinds. Changing the flag could permit an unsafe plunge.

**Considered and dropped:** Writing an unverified controller field does not
establish a safe round trip. Support for another field requires verification
and round-trip tests before these exports can be accepted.

**Decided after the fourth review:** Split `tool_table_hurco_export.rs` from
`tool_table_hurco.rs` and verify every exported Hurco tool through the Hurco
reader. Refuse Hurco export by tool name when the holder diameter or length
cannot survive the conversion, and refuse boring bars with a positive nose
radius. Export judged holder dimensions when a tool carries a modelled body.

**Why:** Hurco `.TCM` has no verified holder diameter field and `TipRadius` is
verified only for bull-nose cutters. Shrinking a wide holder or dropping a
boring-bar nose radius changes collision and boring geometry silently.

**Considered and dropped:** Guessing unverified Hurco XML tags or dropping the
holder diameter to zero on import without an incomplete-holder gate. Both
approaches remain reversible if verified controller fields or a general
incomplete-holder gate are added later.

## #2567 - Discover known failures from test markers

**What was decided:** Use one structured ignore marker for a test that is
red on purpose. Discover the marker from the test source. Store owned
known-failure descriptors instead of a fixed list. Put a marker immediately
before the expected failing assertion. Check the panic location and message
line prefix. Check the upstream issue state in both release commands.

**Why:** The release gate must distinguish an expected failure from a crash
or another failed assertion. Source markers keep the exception with its
test. A passing test or a closed issue must fail the gate so the stale
exception is removed. Keep the existing warning if `gh` cannot read the
issue state. The expected failure check still runs in that case.

**Considered and dropped:** Keep the three-test static list. It makes each
new exception require gate code changes. Add a custom procedural macro or a
dependency. The source scanner can read this small marker without either.
Use a blanket ignore. It hides new failures and tests that now pass.

**Cost to change later:** A marker format change must update its parser,
marked tests, gate pins and review rule together. Requiring an issue state
when `gh` is unavailable would also require reliable credentials and network
access in each release environment.

## #2568 - `cargo xtask gate heavy`: the heavy lanes a diff reaches

**What was decided**

- A new gate tier, `cargo xtask gate heavy [--base main]`, maps the diff to
  the release `--ignored` heavy lanes that it reaches and runs only those
  (`xtask/src/heavy.rs`). The steps are the release tier's own heavy steps,
  with the same names and commands, so `--only`, `--failed` and the
  known-fail checks work as in a cut.
- The reach is by crate, through the dependencies between our crates. They
  are read from `crates/*/Cargo.toml` (normal, dev and build dependencies).
  A source change in `motion` reaches every heavy target of `motion` and of
  `app`. A change in `kernel` reaches each heavy lane.
- Narrower cases: a changed suite file reaches its own heavy binary only.
  Shared test code of a crate reaches that crate only. A post script,
  machine file, catalog case or fixture reaches the binaries that read it
  (the quick tier's own mappers). A workspace manifest, `Cargo.lock`,
  `.cargo/` or toolchain file reaches each heavy lane.
- An unreadable crate manifest is an error, not a smaller plan.
- Process rule **Heavy lanes at review** (AGENTS.md "Testing"): the author
  runs the command on the final head before the PR is flagged ready, and the
  review comment lists the lanes that ran. "Not run" is never a pass.
- The reviewer checks heavy reach after either the runner path or local
  tests. A missing, stale or incomplete author result requires a local
  heavy run or a blocker.

**Why**

- The v0.24.0 cut gate was red on a heavy test that no earlier gate ran
  (#2568). The quick tier selects by Gate map and skips `--ignored` tests.
- A Gate map names the modules that a suite covers directly. It does not
  follow a change in a lower crate into the suites of a higher crate. That
  is the case that the issue names, so the heavy reach does not use the
  Gate maps for source changes. A crate-level reach can run too much. It
  cannot miss a lane.
- The runner runs quick and clippy only. A common heavy check prevents its
  result from bypassing the heavy lanes.

**Considered and dropped**

- Narrowing a source change by Gate map (as quick does): dropped, because
  it misses the cross-crate case.
- A flag on the quick tier (`gate quick --heavy` already runs changed
  `#[ignore]`d test fns): kept as it is. It does not reach unchanged heavy
  tests.
- `--diff` as a flag (the issue's example): dropped. The tier always works
  from the diff, with `--base` as in quick.
- The shared lanes of the release executor (parallel queue): not used. The
  heavy tier runs its steps one at a time. A later change can turn them on.
- `pr-test.yml` running the heavy tier: not in this PR. A workflow change
  needs the maintainer (`needs-maintainer`), and that workflow refuses a PR
  that changes `xtask/`. The wrappers `scripts/gate.sh` and
  `scripts/gate.ps1` do not forward `heavy` yet; `cargo xtask gate heavy`
  is the command.

- Keeping the heavy check only in the local test step: dropped, because
  the runner path skips that step.

**Cost**

- A change in `motion`, `geometry` or `kernel` source runs most heavy lanes
  in release before the PR is ready. This is a cost on purpose (maintainer,
  2026-11-18: "yes file all 3 changes and move them to P4"). The rule
  "never hours per change" still holds for each edit: the heavy tier runs
  one time, on the final head.
- To change the reach later, edit `heavy::reached`. The pins are in
  `xtask/src/heavy_plan_tests.rs`.

## #2569 - A light heavy tier, and a local full rerun before the cut gate restarts

**What was decided**

- `cargo xtask gate light` is a tier of its own. It runs the light twins of
  the heavy tests in release: one release build of the crates that hold a
  twin, then one step for each test target with a twin (`<crate> light: lib`,
  `<crate> light: <binary>`).
- A light twin is found from the source. Its ignore reason starts with
  `light lane:` and its name is `<full test>_light`. The planner refuses a
  twin by name when its file has no `#[ignore]`d full test.
- The first twin is
  `the_slot_keeps_its_verdict_under_sub_micron_perturbations_light` in
  `crates/motion/src/machining2d/adaptive/tests.rs`. It plans the slot 2
  times (opening 180 nm deeper, slot 125 nm narrower). The full sweep keeps
  its 20 rows and does not change.
- A red light run prints a note for the PR. The note names each red step and
  the command of its full heavy step
  (`cargo xtask gate release --only "<crate> heavy: <target>"`).
- AGENTS.md has two new named rules: **The light lane** and **Local full
  rerun**.

**Why**

- A marker in the source needs no list in `xtask` that can go stale. The
  known-fail markers (#2567) use the same method.
- The name suffix makes the libtest filter safe. A step passes the twin
  names as filters after `--ignored`. A name that ends in `_light` does not
  select a full heavy test by accident.
- The refusal keeps the rule "the golden asserts stay in the ignored set". A
  twin cannot take the place of its full test.
- Only the crates that hold a twin are built. The tier stays at a few
  minutes while there are few twins.
- The two slot rows are rows that dropped the lifted plan before the #982
  fix on Linux x86-64. The 32 nm row is already a debug test.

**Considered and dropped**

- A flag on the release tier (`gate release --light`). Dropped: the release
  tier has the lanes of the cut, the known-fail issue check and the debug
  suites. A light run needs none of them.
- A fixed name filter (`--ignored light`). Dropped: a substring such as
  `light` also selects tests named `highlight_...`.
- `--exact` with the full libtest path. Dropped: `xtask` would need the
  module path of each test. The suffix gives the same safety.
- A mapping from a light log directory to `gate release --failed`. Dropped:
  the step names differ (`light:` and `heavy:`). The note prints the
  `--only` commands instead.
- The wiring into `/review-prs`, `/merge-ready` and `pr-test.yml`. Dropped
  from this PR: issue #2568 owns when the heavy tests of a PR run.
- The text for the `gate` and `release-cut` skills. Not in this PR: the
  worker session could not write files in `.claude/skills/`. The PR body has
  the text. The rules are in AGENTS.md until a session with that permission
  adds the skill text.

**Cost to change later**

- Low. The marker text and the suffix are two constants in
  `xtask/src/light.rs`. A new twin needs no change in `xtask`.
- The release tier runs the twins too, because its heavy steps run each
  ignored test. That costs about 10 s for each twin at a cut.

## #2575 - A new worktree seeds its target/ from another checkout

**Decided.** Before its first step, `cargo xtask gate` copies the dependency units
(`target/debug/{build,deps,.fingerprint}`) of the checkout with the most units into a new
worktree. Cargo then finds `solidcore`, `flecs` and the build-script crates Fresh. The copy:

- skips each package without a `source` in `cargo metadata` (workspace members and path
  dependencies): their sources are in the checkout, and an older copy can read as Fresh
  with other code;
- replaces a unit that is there already (`cargo xtask` builds its own dependencies first),
  else its newer time makes each copied unit above it dirty;
- keeps the modification times, copies outputs before fingerprints, and renames each unit
  into place, so a stopped copy only causes a compile;
- takes cargo's locks of the two directories without a wait, and passes over a checkout
  where a build runs;
- writes `target/debug/.camcraft-seeded` once. `CAMCRAFT_NO_SEED=1` turns it off.

**Why.** sccache 0.19 hashes the `OUT_DIR` value of each env dependency, the cwd and the
raw arguments of a Rust compile. `OUT_DIR` names the worktree, so each build-script crate
misses, and each crate above it misses too. `SCCACHE_BASEDIRS` applies only to C and C++.
Cargo's fingerprints do not name the worktree, so a copied unit is reused. Measured on an
18-core Mac (APFS clones, sccache warm): the first app test took 107 s without the seed
and 42 s with it (9 s seed, 24 s step). 231 units compiled without it, 14 with it.

**Dropped.**
- A `--remap-path-prefix` in RUSTFLAGS: sccache hashes the raw argument, which names the
  worktree, so all keys would change in each worktree.
- A shared `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` or `build-dir`: AGENTS.md forbids the first, and the two lock
  out parallel gates of other worktrees.
- A change to sccache (normalize `OUT_DIR`): outside this repository.
- Copy only the units that the gate needs: cargo has no stable unit graph to name them.

**Cost to change.** One module (`xtask/src/seed.rs`) and one call in `gate`. Removing it
returns the gate to the sccache-only behaviour.

## #2576 - Stock axis on the Stock page: Along Z / X / Y / Custom

**Decided.** The Stock page gets a "Stock axis" choice: Along Z (the
default), Along X, Along Y and Custom. Custom shows three angles in
degrees (turn about Z, tilt about Y, tilt about X). The choice applies to
a box and to a cylinder. The turn is stored in the stock's existing
`Location.rot`, so the project file does not change and needs no new
version. The page reads a stored turn back: a preset turn shows its
preset, any other turn shows Custom with its angles.

- Apply sends the whole turn through the undoable `SetStock`. The UI has
  a new queue entry `CommandKind::SetStockPose { shape, pos, rot }`. The
  old `CommandKind::SetStock { shape, pos, yaw_deg }` stays as it is,
  because about 96 test sites use it. The two run the same dispatch.
- The MCP `set_stock` tool takes an optional `axis` ("z", "x", "y") or
  `angles_deg` ({yaw, pitch, roll}), not both. It calls the same
  `SetStock`.
- The simulation laws do not change here. `OBLIQUE_STOCK` still refuses
  a stock that the simulation cannot cut. The page shows a plain note
  before any simulation, from the same law (`stock_follow::sim_frame`),
  so the note and the refusal cannot differ. A box or a cylinder laid
  along X or Y is cut (the cylinder since #2758, merged from main), and
  no note shows.
- A DXF profile lies on the stock's top face. That face was read in the
  stock's own frame and ignored a tilt. Now an upright stock (any turn
  about Z) keeps its own top face, a stock laid square is read as the
  same solid unturned (the simulation's law), and a laid cylinder or a
  tilted stock is refused by name (`sketch::NO_TOP_FACE`).

**Why.** The maintainer asked for a cylinder that is not along Z. The
turn already exists in the document (`Location.rot`), and the viewport
already draws it. Only the page could not set it.

**Dropped.**
- An axis field in `StockShape::Cylinder`: it duplicates the turn that
  `Location.rot` holds, and it needs a project-file version step.
- Silent acceptance in the simulation: a laid cylinder would simulate as
  an upright one, which is a wrong answer. The refusal stays until the
  follow-up issue makes the simulation cut it.
- A rename of the old `CommandKind::SetStock` fields: it touches about 96
  test sites for no change in behaviour.

**Cost to change later.** Low. The axis choice is a view of
`Location.rot`. When the simulation cuts a laid stock, the note goes
away by itself, because it asks the simulation's law.

### Fit to Models on a turned stock (review of PR #2773)

**Chosen.** "Fit to models" (the Stock page button and MCP `fit_stock`)
measures the parts in the stock's own frame: each part vertex is turned
back by the stock's turn, the fit is made there, and its base point is
turned onto the setup's frame (`stock_fit::fitted_turned`). A stock laid
along X or Y wraps the parts along its own length. An upright stock uses
the old path unchanged.

**Why.** The review found that the fit put a world-frame size into a
laid stock, and the result did not hold the parts, with no message.
A fit in the stock's frame is exact for each turn, so the button stays
useful for a laid bar.

**Dropped.** A refusal of the fit for each turn that is not about Z: it
is safe, but it takes the button away from the case that the axis choice
was made for.

**Note.** A stock turned about Z only now fits on its own axes too. Before,
it took the world-frame size and could miss the parts at the corners.

## #2579 - 2D Contour tabs: the tab top is a cut level

**What was decided.** A closed-ring 2D Contour with tabs gets one more cut
level at `bottom_z + tab_height`, when the stepdown ladder has no level
there. `ContourParams::ring_levels` adds it. The closed contour
(`contour_region`) and the whole-model contour (`contour_whole`) read it.
A ladder level within 1e-6 mm of the tab top becomes the tab top itself.

**Why.** A level carries the tabs when it is below `bottom_z + tab_height`.
The last level above that plane cuts the whole ring. The tab therefore
stood up to that level: 4 mm with a 4 mm stepdown and a 1.5 mm tab height.
With a level at the tab top, the tab is as tall as the user set, for a
stepdown larger or smaller than the tab height. The issue's "Done means"
asks for this pass.

The snap of a near level has the same cause. Repeated subtraction gives
levels such as `-3.0000000000000004`. That level is below a tab top at
`-3.0`, so it carried the tabs and the tab was one stepdown too tall
(0.2 mm stepdown, 1 mm tab height: 1.2 mm).

**Considered and dropped.**

- A note that names the real tab height, with no new level. The issue
  permits it only "if a level must be skipped". No level must be skipped
  here, and a note leaves the tab too strong.
- A change of the stepdown so that a level lands on the tab top. This
  changes each level of the cut for one parameter. The added level changes
  only the passes near the tab.
- The tab level in `ContourParams::levels` for each caller. The open runs
  (`contour_along_chain`, `contour_open_run`, `contour_open_run_sided`)
  have no tabs. A level there is a pass with no purpose.
- A change to a tab top at or above Top Z. Each level carries the tabs
  then, and no level is added. The tab is as tall as the cut. This is not
  the reported defect.

**Cost to change later.** Small. The rule is one function,
`ContourParams::ring_levels`, with two callers. The test
`crates/motion/tests/contour_tab_height.rs` measures the tab height from
the posted moves.

**Known effect.** A program with tabs whose stepdown ladder had no level at
the tab top gets one more pass. Its G-code changes. A program without tabs
does not change.

The shipped example `examples/first-router-part` is such a program: 4 mm
stepdown, 12 mm depth, 3 mm tabs. Its program gets one whole pass at Z-9.
The project file is the command build, saved again (`WRITE_GOLDEN`, the
decision of #1917). The save also writes what `main` changed since the
last save: file version 68 to 71, the tool numbers, the drill undersize
warnings and the start of the first rapid. A file with only the new pass
does not pass the verification gate of its own test, because the cache
stamp does not agree.

## #2581 - "Mill-turn" in the docs means the live-tooling kind; turning on a mill gets its own term

**What was decided.** The guide keeps the word "mill-turn" for CamCraft's
machine kind: a lathe (multitasking turning centre) that also mills with
live tooling, `millturn.mch`. The other meaning, a mill used as a lathe
(part in the mill spindle, lathe tools on the table, one work offset for
each tool), is called "turning on a mill". A box with the two meanings is
in `operations-turning.md` and in the Mill-turn section of `machines.md`.
The glossary has the two entries. The `load_machine` row of the
`camcraft-mcp` skill names the two meanings and tells an agent to confirm
which one a user means. Each other use of "mill-turn" in the guide and the
README says "(live tooling)" or "(a lathe with live tooling)", or is on a
page with the box.

**Why.** The UI already uses "Mill-turn" and "Mill-turning" for the
live-tooling kind (`MachineKind::MillTurn`, the built-in preset name, the
`mill-turn` kind in `.mch` files). A docs term that differs from the UI
would add a third name. "Turning on a mill" describes the setup without a
vendor name, and #2580 can use it.

**Considered and dropped.**
- Rename the kind in the docs to "multitasking lathe". Dropped: the UI,
  the preset name and the `.mch` kind value stay "mill-turn", so the docs
  would not match the screen.
- A Zola shortcode for the box. Dropped: the site has one shortcode
  (`icon`), and `_index.md` already uses a plain blockquote for a callout.
- Qualify the enum lists (`mill`, `lathe`, `mill-turn`) and the UI filter
  list in `setups.md`. Dropped: those are literal values, and the text
  next to them defines the term.

**Cost to change later.** Low: docs text only, no code or file format.

## #2583 - MachineTree: the `.mch` part tree kept whole

**What was decided**

- `camcraft_post::machine::parse_mch_tree` reads `kinematics.default.parts`
  into a `MachineTree`: a flat, depth-first `Vec<TreePart>` in which each
  part holds the index of its parent. It is a second reader beside
  `parse_mch`. `Machine`, `parse_mch` and the existing checks do not change.
- The moving side follows the rule of the issue: a linear or rotary part
  that is an ancestor of a `head` part is on the tool side; each other axis
  is on the table side. A tree with no head states no side (`None`).
- A file in the mirror form (`3axis-vmc.mch`, `kinematics.static`) states no
  part tree. It reads as an empty tree, not as a refusal. The 3-axis parent
  chain is pinned on `vmc.mch`, which is the same machine in the file form.
- The tree door is strict where the model needs the fact. It refuses, with
  the part id and the key: a part with no `id`, an `id` stated two times, a
  `type` that is not `table` / `head` / `linear` / `rotary`, a `parts` value
  that is not a list, a garbled `axis`, `direction`, `pivot`, `offset`,
  `spindle` or `tool_station`.
- The unstated-limit law is shared, not copied: `rate`, `scale` and
  `mm_factor` of `parse.rs` became `pub(super)`, and `pivot` / `offset` go
  through `trunnion::parse_axis_fields`. A garbled `travel` reads as not
  stated, as in `parse_mch`.

**Why**

- An index to the parent keeps the type plain data (`Clone`, `PartialEq`),
  with no reference between parts and no recursion in the consumer.
- The model must find a part by its `id`. Two parts with one id, or a part
  with no id, would give a wrong joint silently. All 45 shipped files
  state unique ids and only the four types.
- One set of helper functions means that the tree and the flat axis list
  cannot scale a length differently. A test compares the two readers on
  each shipped file.

**Considered and dropped**

- A `tree` field on `Machine`: dropped. The issue says that `Machine` does
  not change, and `Machine` is serialized into project files.
- A nested `children: Vec<TreePart>` type: dropped. The parent chain is the
  fact the model needs, and a flat list gives it without recursion.
- A guess of the moving side from the axis letter (Z moves the head on a
  VMC): dropped. The reader states only what the file states.
- A refusal of the mirror-form file: dropped. `parse_mch` also accepts it
  and reads nothing from it.

**Known limit (not changed here)**

Most shipped 3-axis files hang the `head` beside the axis chain
(`vmc.mch`: `base > col > ram > sld`, and `base > head`). By the rule, all
their axes read as table side. Only a file that nests the head below an
axis (`tilthead.mch`, `sinker-edm.mch`, `millturn.mch`) states a tool-side
axis. A correct machine model needs those files nested as the machine
moves. That is a change to the machine files, not to the reader.

**Cost to change later**

Small. The type has no user outside its tests yet. A new fact is a new
field on `TreePart` and one line in `walk`.

## #2584 - sim: the generated machine model (blocks and cylinders)

**What was decided**

- `camcraft_sim::machine_model` has its own plain input (`MachineSpec`,
  `PartSpec`). `camcraft-sim` gets no edge to `camcraft-post`. The caller
  (#2586) maps `MachineTree` into the input.
- The module is forward kinematics only. A joint `axis` is the direction
  in which the part itself moves or turns for a positive axis value. The
  caller reverses the direction of a part that moves the table.
- A part frame is the parent frame, then the part `offset`, then the
  joint. With no offset and each joint at zero, the spindle nose is at the
  origin and the spindle runs up +Z (ISO 841).
- Sizes come only from stated numbers:
  - a head: a cylinder of the spindle diameter and length over the nose;
  - a linear part: a block as long as its travel span, with a square
    section of 0.25 of the span;
  - a root or table part: a block with the linear travel of the machine
    along X and Y, and a thickness of 0.1 of the larger side.
- Head dimensions generate bodies for fixed, linear and rotary joints.
  A linear head with travel also keeps its slide block above its spindle.
- The tool station gives one more body of its own kind, `ToolEnvelope`:
  the room of the largest tool below the nose. It is not steel. A check
  selects bodies by `BodyKind`.
- A part with no number gets no body and a named note: a rotary part, a
  linear part with no travel, a head with no spindle size, a table with
  no X and Y travel.
- Parts that carry the head stand over the spindle body. All other parts
  hang below Z = 0. Thus the bodies of one stack touch and do not overlap
  at the zero pose.
- Each body has `BodySource::Generated`. `BodySource::judged_on()` gives
  the words "judged on a generated model" for a check.
- `pose` needs one value for each linear and rotary part. It refuses a
  missing value. It does not judge travel limits.
- Round faces are circumscribed polygons of 32 sides, as in
  `crate::chuck`: the drawn body is never smaller than the stated one.

**Why**

- The sign law of a table axis and the rotary conventions are in
  `camcraft-post` (`direction`, `moving_side`, the trunnion fields). A
  second copy of those laws in `camcraft-sim` could disagree with the
  post, and a wrong pose is a silent wrong answer.
- `travel` is in program coordinates, and the file states no machine
  home. Thus the model cannot know where a part is in the machine. The
  `offset` field lets the caller place each branch (work offset, tool
  length) when it knows them.
- A missing pose value that reads as zero would show a body where the
  machine does not put it.
- Accepted spindle and tool dimensions must produce their bodies. The
  joint kind changes their pose, not whether the bodies exist.

**Considered and dropped**

- A named refusal for spindle or tool dimensions on moving parts:
  dropped, because the existing joint frames can pose these bodies.
- A side flag (tool or table) in the input, with the sign applied in the
  module: dropped, because it puts a post convention in two crates.
- A body for a rotary part with a guessed size: dropped, the issue
  forbids a guessed size.
- The tool station as the size of a steel body: dropped. It states the
  largest tool, not steel.
- A check of the axis values against `travel` in `pose`: dropped. The
  limit judgment is #2585.
- `thiserror` error types: dropped. The crate's generators
  (`chuck`, `fixture`) refuse with a `String` that names the part.

**Not pinned**

- `pose` has a last check that each posed vertex is finite. The input
  checks ahead of it stop each non-finite value, so no test can reach it.
  It stays as a backstop.

**Cost to change later**

- The ratios (`SECTION_RATIO`, `BED_RATIO`) and the stack rule are in one
  function each. A change moves the pinned boxes in
  `crates/sim/tests/machine_model.rs`.
- A later restriction on moving heads would change input validation and
  the moving-head pins in `crates/sim/tests/machine_model.rs`.
- #2591 (the optional `body` key) adds a `BodySource` variant. Each
  `match` on `BodySource` then needs the new arm.

## #2585 - Share the machine limit judgment without the ECS world

**What was decided:** Put the pure `MachineCheck` accumulator in
`camcraft-post::machine`. It checks tool count, rpm, tool size, and paths.
Each finding can use an optional `SourceLocation`, with an operation name
or an NC line number. Pass tool length, diameter, and rpm as scalar values.
Add no crate dependency.

**Why:** A stand-alone simulator needs the same machine limit checks as
the app. The post crate already owns the machine definition and move
types. The app keeps the ECS walk, holder resolution, spindle power,
part transfer, and the adaptation of the posted lathe path. It calls the
pure checks in the existing order to preserve its diagnostic output.

**Considered and dropped:** Adding a tools dependency would couple the
checks to a full tool definition when three scalar values are sufficient.
Moving world-specific code would bring document concerns into the post
crate. Changing diagnostic text would make this extraction change app
behavior and weaken comparison with the existing tests.

**Cost to change later:** Additional source kinds require an API change
and tests for their displayed locations. Additional tool properties can
extend the pure input API without moving the ECS walk. Moving the retained
app checks later requires plain inputs and tests that preserve diagnostic
order and text.

## #2595 - the diag event-level test runs in a test binary of its own

**Decided:** `diag_lines_are_tracing_events_at_their_level` moves from the
`diag` unit tests in the `camcraft-ui` lib to `crates/ui/tests/diag_events.rs`.
That binary holds this one test only. The test calls `diag::warn` and
`diag::info` directly. The lib keeps `the_macros_take_println_shaped_arguments`,
which compiles the two macros.

**Why:** `tracing` caches the interest of each callsite for the whole
process. The test installs a thread-local subscriber with
`with_default`. In the lib binary, other tests on other threads call
`diag_info!` through the same callsite. When another thread hits the
callsite first, it registers the callsite with the dispatchers that it
sees at that time. If that registration ends after the rebuild that the
new subscriber started, the cached interest is "never". The INFO event is
then lost, and the WARN event (another callsite) stays. In a binary of
its own, no other thread uses these callsites.

**Dropped:**

- `tracing::callsite::rebuild_interest_cache()` before each event. This
  makes the window smaller, but another thread can still write a stale
  interest after the rebuild.
- A lock shared with each test that emits a `diag` line. Nearly each UI
  test emits one, so the lock would serialize the lib suite.
- A global default subscriber for the lib tests. That changes the output
  of each other test.

**Cost to change later:** low. The test is one file. A second test in
`diag_events.rs` brings the race back; the file header says so.

## #2596 - a no-pick 2D Chamfer leaves the model's sharp edges alone when the model carries a chamfer

**Decided.** A 2D Chamfer with no picks (its source is the whole model)
reads the model's own edges at the top plane:

- If at least one top edge stands over a modelled bevel (a modelled
  chamfer or round), the op rides only the bevelled edges. A sharp edge
  beside them (the pocket rim of #2596) is sharp by design and is not
  cut. To break it, the user picks it.
- If no top edge carries a bevel (a sharp brick, a sharp pocket block),
  the op breaks every top edge as before. This keeps the #303 law: the
  default chamfer on a finished sharp part posts with its declared break.

- If a bevelled edge would lose its nesting when the sharp edge around
  it is left out (a modelled chamfer on a pocket in a sharp plate), the
  op refuses by name and asks for picks. Alone, the region would read the
  rim as a boss, and the ride would travel against its material (#1555).
  The refusal is safer than a ride in the wrong direction.

Verify side: on a model that carries a modelled bevel at any declared
edge (`camcraft_sim::stock_sim::models_a_bevel`), a no-pick chamfer gets
no edge-break credit at all. Its ride is judged against the model, so a
cut into a sharp edge, or a bevel cut wider than the modelled one, is a
gouge. This also catches a ride cached by an older build.

**Why.** The model is the finished part. Where the designer modelled
some chamfers and left other edges sharp, the sharp edges are intent,
and a cut there removes model material (Prime Directive). Where the
model has no chamfer at all, it states no intent, and #303 accepted the
no-pick op as "break every edge".

**Dropped.**
- Refuse every no-pick chamfer on a model with no modelled bevel (the
  strict reading of the issue's "Done means"). It reverses the #303 law
  and its tests (`edge_break_gate.rs`, the L-boss and pocket tests of
  `chamfer_modelled_edge.rs`). That needs the maintainer's word; filed as
  a follow-up.
- An operation parameter "auto edges: modelled only / every top edge".
  The pick list already gives the user the second choice per edge, and a
  new parameter touches the project file, the UI and MCP.
- A user-visible note that lists the edges a no-pick op skipped. The
  op shows only its toolpath; filed as a follow-up.

**Cost to change.** The rule is in `chamfer_ride::ride_loops` (one
fallback line) and in `stock_sim_breaks::program_breaks` (one guard).

## #2597 - Whole-model 2D Contour: a new, larger outline starts at Top Z

**Decided.** In a whole-model 2D Contour, a ring of a deeper band whose tool
sweep reaches outside every sweep cut so far gets every flat level above its
first level. So it is cut from Top Z down, one stepdown at a time, and not
first at the level where its outline appeared. The check is in
`crates/motion/src/machining2d/contour_whole_reach.rs` (`reach_up`). A ring
whose sweep stays inside the cut sweeps (an outline that does not grow) is
unchanged. If such a ring cannot be proven clear of the part at the added
levels (a slice error, or material over it), the operation is refused by
name, with no toolpath, so nothing posts.

**Why.** The contour has no stock outline. The material outside the part can
stand up to Top Z. A first pass at the new outline's level buried the tool by
the full height above it (20 mm on the #2597 part with stepdown 5). The
user's stepdown is the axial limit of the operation, so this is not a new
choice and not a new parameter: each pass is now at most one stepdown under
the pass before it on the same ring. The radial load of the added passes is
not more than that of the first band's passes: each pass engages at most the
tool width, as any contour pass does.

**Dropped.**
- Refuse every growing outline. Safe, but it refuses common parts (a boss
  on a plate) that can be cut correctly.
- A new operation parameter ("start new outlines at Top Z" on/off). The
  other value would post the buried pass again, which the Prime Directive
  forbids. So there is no choice to give.
- Read the stock outline to start each ring where the stock really starts.
  The contour generator gets no stock region today; that is a larger change
  (app and motion), and the Top Z rule is safe without it. It costs air
  passes where the stock is narrow. A follow-up can add the stock region.

**Cost of the rule.** A wall that grows a little at each level (a chamfer)
re-walks the new ring from Top Z at each band: more passes, mostly in air.
A strip narrower than 0.05 mm is taken as offset noise and does not count as
growth.

**Stock over Top Z (review blocker B1 of PR #2659).** When the stock top is
over Top Z (`stock_over`, the predicate by which `cut_levels_under` keeps Top
Z as a level), the material stands up to the stock top, not to Top Z. Then
the flat levels under Top Z are not enough: on the #2597 part with the stock
top at 28, the base ring was first cut at Z 20, 8 mm under the stock top
(stepdown 5). The rule (`upper_levels`) has two cases:
- The stock top is less than one stepdown over Top Z: the growing ring takes
  levels one stepdown at a time down from the stock top, until its first
  level. On that part the base ring is cut at Z 23, 18, 13, 8, 5, 0, and the
  boss ring (band 0) at Z 25, 20, 15, 10. These levels are off the flat grid
  on purpose (see "Dropped").
- The stock top is one stepdown or more over Top Z: band 0 bites that much
  at Top Z (the operation already says "Top below stock"). Only a pass at Top
  Z keeps the bite of the growing ring as small. So the ring takes Top Z and
  the flat levels under it.
- Without stock over Top Z, a level at Top Z removes no material, and no
  level at Top Z is added (unchanged).
- Dropped: add the Top Z level in every case (the review's first proposal).
  Top Z is the plane of the ring that band 0 cut there. On the chamfered
  island of `contour_whole_step` case 1 (stock top 17, Top Z 15) the lead-in
  of that ring crossed the grown ring 1 mm outside it at Z 15. The
  `Crossing` warning blocked the post of a correct part. With the levels from
  the stock top, the grown ring takes Z 13.5 there and shares no plane with
  the ring above it.
- Dropped: refuse the ring when the Top Z level crosses. It refuses a
  correct part that #2436 pins.
- Known limit: in the second case the two rings share the Top Z plane. On a
  part like case 1 with the stock top at 18.5 or higher, the verifier finds
  the same `Crossing` and blocks the post. The result is visible and safe,
  but a correct part does not post. #2677 tracks it.
- The added levels are proven by the same `ladder` as before. A ring that
  cannot be proven clear at them is refused by name.

## #2598 - Drill and Thread ops take the tool's feed; a feed above it is refused at the post

**What was decided.**

- A new Drill or Thread operation takes its feed from its tool: the
  cutting-data row for the material in force, else the tool's running
  feed. A Drill sets its feed and its plunge feed to that value. A Thread
  sets its edge feed to it and holds its plunge feed at or under it. This
  runs where every new op is seeded (`cutting_rows::seed_feed_for_tool`:
  the ribbon quick-add, MCP `add_operation`, the feature recognizer).
- Giving an op a new tool (`EditOperationLinks`, MCP `set_tool`) seeds the
  same way, inside that command. Undo restores the old feeds.
- A program with a Drill or Thread op that feeds above its tool's feed is
  refused at the post, by name (`operation::feed_rating::problems`, a
  clause of `posting::verification_report`): "D: feeds 300 mm/min, above
  the 115 mm/min that tool DR-0600 states - ...". A Drill is judged on the
  feeds of its cached path (not tapping cycles, which feed at pitch x rpm).
  A Thread is judged on its stated edge and plunge feeds, because its
  posted arcs are scaled to the tool centre.
- Old project files: nothing changes on load. A file saved with the old
  1200 / 300 seed keeps those numbers, and its first post is refused with
  the line above. The user lowers the op's feed (or raises the tool's
  feed). No project-file field or meaning changed, so `PROJECT_VERSION`
  stays.

**Why.** The Prime Directive: the output is correct, or it is visibly
refused. The cause was the shared seed (1200 / 300) and a feed seed that
moved only milling kinds, only for a named material row. A Drill feeds the
whole tool end axially and a thread mill's feed is stated at its edge, so
the tool's feed is the right number for both. A refusal at the post reads
the op as it stands, so it covers old files, later hand edits and a tool
edit, with no change on load. It has the same per-move form as the
machine's feed ceiling, the existing post law for a feed that is too high.

**Considered and dropped.**

- An advisory `verify::Warning` on the toolpath (like `DrillUndersize`):
  it does not hold the post, and an old file's cached path does not carry
  it, so an old file would still post 2-3x over without a word at the post.
- Rewriting old files' feeds on load: it silently changes a stated value.
- Judging milling kinds against the tool's feed: their feed moves with the
  stepover and chip thinning (`cutting::suggest`); the tool's feed is a
  starting point there.
- Making `suggest_cutting_data` / `apply_cutting_data` speak for drills and
  thread mills: the cutting-data table is a milling table. Not needed for
  this fix; a separate enhancement if wanted.
- Re-seeding the ops when the tool's own feed is edited (`ChangeTool`): it
  would overwrite hand-set op feeds. The post clause judges the new value.
- Re-seeding Drill and Thread ops on a material change (`SetWorkMaterial`,
  `SetStockMaterial`, `ApplyCuttingData`, which use
  `cutting_rows::reseeded_params`): these keep #890's milling-only rule.
  If a new material's row states a lower feed, the post clause names the
  op, and the user lowers its feed.

**Cost to change later.** The clause is one function and one line in the
gate; making it advisory is a change of that line. The seed is one call in
`cutting_rows`.

## #2599 - New tilt angles on a legacy operation take the current frame basis

**What was decided.** `EditOperationParams` steps a tilt's `basis_version`
from 0 (the pre-#2133 frame, kept for a file without the key) to 1 when the
edit changes the tilt's A or B angle (`OpParams::with_stepped_tilt_basis`).
An edit that keeps the angles (feed, depth, origin) keeps basis 0. A loaded
operation that nobody edits keeps basis 0 and posts what it posted before.
The UI page and MCP `edit_operation` both go through this one command door.

**Why.** PR #2157 fixed new tilts (the JSON door and the UI set basis 1), but
a tilt loaded from an old file keeps basis 0, and both the operation page
(it edits the loaded `Tilt` in place) and MCP `edit_operation` (it merges a
partial patch into the loaded fields) carried basis 0 onto new angles. Set
to A0/B180, such an operation posted its plane XY turned 90 degrees
(`G1 X0 Y-10` for a slot from (10,0) to (30,0)), while a new operation at the
same index posted `X10 Y0` - the defect of #2599, still reachable on main.
New angles are a new index, so the old plane coordinates no longer describe
anything the user drew for that index.

**Dropped.**
- Migrate every legacy tilt to basis 1 at load: this silently moves the cut
  of an old file that the user does not touch (a breaking change of what an
  old file posts; `tilt_basis_compat` pins that it must not).
- Refuse a legacy tilt whose basis-0 frame differs from basis 1 at load or
  at post: the old file's frame is the one its preview, its saved geometry
  and its saved program (`examples/first-4axis-part.nc`) use, so it is
  correct for that file. A refusal would also block opening (`is_sane` runs
  at load) or force a re-edit without a cause.
- Step the basis also on `CreateOperation`: a copy of a legacy operation has
  the same angles as its source and must cut the same as the source.

**Cost to change later.** One call in `commands/operation/edit.rs` and one
small file (`operation/types/tilt_basis.rs`). Undo restores the old tilt with
its basis, because the command stores the whole previous operation.

## #2600 - A STEP face's facets are held to its surface

**What was decided.** The STEP importer now measures the mesh it keeps. For
each curved elementary face (cylinder, cone, sphere, torus) it measures the
chord height of every facet edge inside the face against the face's own
surface. An edge that stands more than twice the pass tolerance off the
surface is split at the surface, round by round, until none does
(`geometry/import/step_fit.rs`). An edge on the face's boundary is never
split, so the shell stays closed. A chord height that cannot be refined
away (the facet budget, the round cap) becomes the chord error that the
import reports. The model then carries reduced fidelity (#864) and the
gate refuses to verify against it.

**Why.** The issue says that tilted operations are not judged for gouges.
That is not the cause. A tilted operation is judged at generation, in the
plane's frame, by the keep law (`contain_into`, #1603). The test
`a_tilted_slot_into_a_meshed_bar_is_refused` shows this on unchanged code.
The cause is the reported part. It is a D50 bar with two cross holes, from
a STEP file. The kernel (truck) triangulates a trimmed face in its
parameter plane. A cylinder's parameter grid has two rows, and the two are
on the boundary, so no grid point is inside the face. With a hole in the
wall, each rim edge was joined to the hole's rim a quarter turn away. The
facets ran through the solid, up to 25 mm inside the true cylinder. The
importer reported the tolerance that it had asked for, not the error of
the mesh that it got. Every gouge law (generation, the program sim, the
upright operations too) then judged the cut against a part that was too
small. The slot at A0 was convicted only because the mesh is correct next
to the hole at the top.

**Considered and dropped.**

- *Hold every program that the stock sim does not judge.* This is the
  second option of the issue. It refuses every 3+2 and rotary program,
  although the generator-time laws judge them (`posting_sim.rs`, pinned by
  `post_not_judged.rs`). It also does not fix the report: the upright sim
  reads the same wrong mesh. The maintainer can still decide on an
  override design; this PR does not change that policy.
- *Only report the measured error.* Smaller, but each bar or tube with a
  cross hole is then refused as "imported too coarsely", and a larger
  facet budget does not help. Refinement gives a correct mesh.
- *Stretch the parameter plane of elementary faces* (as #1602 does for
  B-spline faces), or give the triangulation interior rows. This gives the
  better mesh with fewer facets. It changes the triangulation of every
  cylinder face of every model, and its effect on the goldens is not
  known. It is follow-up work.
- *Measure B-spline, NURBS and swept faces too.* Their grid is #1602's
  and one evaluation is more expensive. Not measured here; stated in the
  module header.

**What it costs.** Refinement by edge bisection makes many facets where
the kernel's mesh was wrong: the reported bar goes from 1 084 facets to
about 133 000, and its import takes longer (about 5 s in a debug build). A
face that the kernel meshes correctly is not changed. The slack of two
tolerances keeps a mesh that meets the kernel's own test as it is; a lower
slack would change more meshes.

## #2601 - Preserve separate blind holes and their entry mouths

**What was decided.** Merge coaxial wall components only when their axial
spans touch or overlap. Test finite segments from inside the bore to its
wall ends for a blind floor. Collect triangles in each end plane and within
the fitted bore disc. Connect triangles across full shared edges with the
existing exact-bit vertex keys. Start from triangles with a bore rim edge.
Accept a segment hit on any triangle in the connected floor. Use the opposite end as
the mouth and mark the hole as blind. Keep downward Z holes in `Hole`. Store lower-mouth Z
holes in the existing directed `CrossHole` record. Report directed
findings on mills through the existing detection command.

**Why.** A shared axis does not make two blind holes one through hole.
The solid core between their floors must remain outside both hole depths.
A span check alone does not identify the entry side. Floor evidence gives
each record its own mouth and inward direction. The connected rim edge identifies
the floor as part of this bore, even when subdivision adds interior vertices.
Disconnected interior patches and outer annuli cannot supply this evidence.
An unrelated face that crosses the bore
must not turn a through hole into a blind hole. Finite segments exclude
distant model faces and the opposite hole's floor. Meshes that contain
only walls keep the existing through classification when no floor exists.

Keep the existing generation refusals for mixed lists, radial work on a
plain mill, and Z plunges in the radial generator. Detection can preserve
the findings without sending an unsupported direction to a drilling cycle.
The change adds no dependency and changes no project file format.

The pins use an original closed block and a closed D50 bar with six blind
D5 holes, each 8 mm deep. The bar runs along world Z and, after rotation,
along world Y. The rotated bar includes opposite world-Z entry mouths.
The motion fixture copies the project's original
`punched_bar` helper into the lowest crate that supplies its imports.

**Considered and dropped.** A span check without mouth classification
leaves incorrect lower-side records. Requiring the hit triangle itself to
contain a rim edge fails when a valid floor has interior vertices.
Accepting a hit without checking its connection to the rim admits unrelated
crossing faces. General arbitrary-axis recognition
and indexed drilling need a separate design. They exceed this detection
fix and would require new generation and machine checks.

**Cost to change later.** An indexed drilling implementation can consume
the directed records. It must define setup orientation, dispatch, travel,
and post behavior before it replaces the current generation refusals.

## #2602 - Refuse a machine edit that adds turning capability

**What was decided:** `edit_machine` refuses a change from a non-turning
machine to `lathe` or `mill-turn`. The refusal names the machine and tells
the caller to load a turning machine file. Existing turning machines can
still be edited.

**Why:** Changing the kind does not add a work spindle. The flattened
`Machine` data does not retain the spindle's role. Its axis inventory
cannot prove that a milling spindle can turn the work. A kind edit must
not let the same mill identity authorize turning code.

**Considered and dropped:** Requiring the declared kind to equal the kind
inferred from the axes can reject valid Y-axis lathes. Keeping the edit and
adding a warning still permits turning code under a mill's identity. The
refusal prevents that output before the edit enters command history.

**Cost to change later:** Add explicit work-spindle kinematics and validate
the complete machine conversion. Then permit a kind change only when the
definition proves the required turning capability.

## #2609 - Refuse unsupported G73 and G85 dwell

**Decided:** Add a positive-dwell guard for G73 and G85 in the LinuxCNC,
Tormach, and grblHAL posts. Keep the existing G83 guard unchanged.
The refusal names the cycle and the requested dwell in seconds.
It runs before a cycle block or a modal X/Y continuation can be written.
A zero dwell keeps its existing output.

**Why:** The public LinuxCNC G-code reference gives G73 and G85 no P word.
The PathPilot and grblHAL sources cited by these posts follow that behavior.
The posts must refuse the requested dwell instead of silently dropping it.

**Dropped:** Do not write an unsupported P word. Do not substitute G82 or
G89, or expand the cycle into motions. Those choices change the cycle
behavior and need a separate design.

**Branch:** Stack on PR #2310 because that PR adds the LinuxCNC post.
Change its implementation only to add the dwell guard.

**Cost to change later:** Controller support would need a documented
decision for each dialect and updated pinning tests.

## #2611 - The playhead waits for the stock removal calculation

**What was decided.** While the stock removal before playback is calculated
(`Precalc::Running`, #2181), the transport holds its playhead: `sim.t` does
not advance and the scrub slider is disabled. Play/Pause and Stop still work,
and Cancel stops the calculation (playback then cuts live, as before).

**Why.** The worker publishes no frame until the calculation ends, so the
viewport shows the uncut stock. The transport played on meanwhile, and the
tool moved over stock that showed no cut - on a large block the calculation
takes long enough that the whole program can play with no visible removal.
The transport line already said "playback starts when it is done"; the clock
did not obey it. A headless test of the worker's frames
(`crates/app/tests/stock_play_picture.rs`) showed the published frames do
draw the removal, so the defect is the clock, not the cut.

**Considered and dropped.**
- Publish progress frames from the calculation: the calculation cuts in
  program order, so its stock is at a position other than the playhead's.
  A picture at the wrong position is a silent wrong answer.
- Interrupt the calculation to cut live at the playhead: this is the lag
  that #2181 removed.

**Cost to change later.** Small: `play_precalc::advance_playhead` and the
`held` flag in `egui_app::shell`.

## #2612 - Nesting raster 1: conservative bit-packed rasteriser

**Decided (unattended, issue-worker-high):**

- **Place.** `camcraft_geometry::nesting::raster` (`crates/geometry/src/nesting/raster.rs`
  and `raster/scan.rs`). No new crate, no new crate edge, no new external
  dependency.
- **Integer decisions.** Region vertices are quantized with the `geo2d`
  Clipper-bridge rule (`geo2d::quantize`, 1 unit = 1 um). All cell tests
  are exact `i128` arithmetic with checked multiply and add. No float takes
  part in a cell decision.
- **One algorithm, two outputs.** Two integer passes: (1) "touched" - each
  cell whose closed square touches a closed boundary edge (row slabs, with
  the x extent of the edge in the slab rounded outward: floor of the
  minimum, ceiling of the maximum); (2) "centre inside" - even-odd parity of
  a +x ray at each cell centre, with the half-open edge rule of
  `geo2d::Loop::contains_xy`, in doubled coordinates so that the centre is
  an integer. Over = touched OR centre inside. Free = centre inside AND NOT
  touched. Why this is safe: a closed square that meets the region but no
  boundary edge is fully in the interior, so its centre is inside; a square
  that no edge touches and whose centre is inside is fully in the interior.
- **Rounding direction.** Always outward for "touched": a value on a cell
  line touches the two cells; the x extent in a slab is widened to whole
  units. This can mark one extra cell, never one fewer.
- **Cell packing.** Rows of `u32` words, `ceil(width / 32)` words for each
  row. Cell `i` is bit `i % 32` (least significant bit first) of word
  `i / 32`. Padding bits are always zero. `u32` matches a WGSL storage
  buffer word for the later GPU slice.
- **Grid origin.** `RasterGrid::covering` snaps the origin down to a multiple
  of the cell size (the global lattice), so that part and sheet rasters at
  the same cell size share one lattice and a placement moves in whole cells
  (research comment 2 on #2525, rule 3). `RasterGrid::new` takes any origin.
- **Cell-size default.** `DEFAULT_CELL_UNITS` = 1 mm (the coarse level of
  the coarse-to-fine search of #2525).
- **Cell limit.** `MAX_CELLS` = 2^24 (4096 x 4096, one fine tile of #2525)
  and `MAX_SIDE` = 2^16 on a side. A 3000 x 1500 mm sheet at 1 mm (4.5e6
  cells) fits. A larger grid is `RasterError::GridTooLarge`.
- **A part that does not fit is refused.** `rasterize_over` returns
  `RasterError::RegionExceedsGrid` when the region bounds are not in the
  closed grid extent: a clipped part raster is no longer an
  over-approximation. `rasterize_free` clips freely: a cell outside the
  region is never free, which is the safe side.
- **Empty region.** `RasterGrid::covering` refuses it (`EmptyRegion`); the
  two rasterize functions return an all-zero raster for it.

**Dropped:**

- Float scanline with an epsilon: not exact, and an epsilon can lose a
  touched cell.
- Rasterize the Minkowski-inflated part here: the spacing inflation belongs
  to the placer slice; this slice takes the region that it is given.
- `u64` words: `u32` is the native word of a WGSL storage buffer.

**Cost to change later:** the bit layout is internal to the raster and the
later slices; a change touches only `nesting::raster` and its tests.

## #2619 - CPU facet grid for the drop-cutter support scan

**Decided.**

- The support facets and their grid are one type, `SupSet`
  (`crates/motion/src/finishing3d/grid.rs`). `build_sups` returns it. Each
  `&[Sup]` parameter in `finishing3d` became `&SupSet`.
  - `SupSet` derefs to `[Sup]`, and `for s in sups` still reads every facet.
    The loops that are not point queries (shadow region, crease, rings,
    bridge, gap link) did not change.
  - `support_at`, `support_grad`, `ball_clear`, `column_clear` and
    `edge::fold_best` read `sups.near(x, y)`: the facets of the one cell that
    holds the query point.
- Each scan keeps its own padded-box reject. The grid only removes facets
  that the reject drops. The same f64 code runs on the same facets in the
  same order, so each answer has the same bits.
- The cell map is `floor((v - origin) / cell)`, clamped. The same map bins
  the boxes and places the query. Each step is monotone in IEEE-754, so a
  facet whose box holds the point is always in the point's cell. Each cell
  lists its facets in ascending index, one time each (CSR arrays).
- Cell size: half of the mean padded box, not finer than the extent / 1024.
  The size doubles until the cells are at most `4n + 64`, each axis at most
  1024, and the binned entries at most `32n + 65536`.
- Fallback to the full scan, never a guess: a non-finite box coordinate
  (the old reject never drops such a facet), a non-finite query point, an
  extent that is not finite, more than `u32::MAX` facets, or no size that
  fits the caps.
- The old scan stays as the reference: `SupSet::full_scan` (no grid). The
  parity tests run the same functions on the two sets.
- The parity and superset tests are lib unit tests
  (`finishing3d/grid_tests.rs`), not files in `crates/motion/tests/`. The
  issue named a motion test. The scan functions are `pub(super)`, and an
  integration test cannot reach them without a new public API.

**Why.** The issue asks for bit-equal goldens. The wrapper type keeps every
call site's code and changes only the parameter type. A cache keyed by the
slice address was refused: a freed and re-used address could give a stale
grid, which is a gouge.

**Dropped.**

- Parallel raster lines (the issue's optional item). A follow-up can add
  them; this slice keeps the output order and the thread model as they are.
- A grid shared between `build_sups` and `flat`'s floor set: `flat` builds
  its own (the boxes are the same; the build is O(n)).
- A query for a box (more than one cell). Every scan asks about one point.

**Readings.** Release build, parallel finishing, a height-field mesh, tool
diameter 6, tolerance 0.01, one run each (a temporary harness, not
committed):

| Facets | Before | After | Output hash (same before and after) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1800 | 13.161 s | 13.908 s | `a629dd9f259d227d` |
| 7200 | 162.915 s | 161.515 s | `c719175f144437ae` |

The grid gives no measurable gain on this job. The point scans are not the
hot path here. The grid is kept: it is the CPU reference for the GPU filter
of #2526, its cost is O(n) at build, and the output is the same. A profile
must find the real hot path before more speed work (follow-up issue).

**Cost to change.** The grid is private to `finishing3d`. A different cell
law changes `grid.rs` only. The GPU filter of #2526 compares against
`SupSet::full_scan` and the grid.

## #2624 - Show move arrows and rotate rings together

**What was decided:** The Move button shows arrows and rotate rings together.
The existing Rotate button remains available as a shortcut. The named
`Move value` and `Rotate value` controls select the typed editor only.
Both sets of handles stay visible. A drag selects its corresponding editor.

The change stacks on PR #2662 and uses its typed values and Shift snapping.
The angle snap step keeps the existing configurable default of 90 degrees.
An edge-on ring consumes a press without starting a turn. It shows a hint
to orbit the view. Its accessibility node is disabled. A face-on ring stays
available.

The existing `TurnModelBy` path uses `MoveModel` for the undo step and the
operation staleness checks. The existing MCP tool supplies the same turn.
This change adds no command or MCP tool.

**Why:** The part must turn from its movement gizmo without a mode switch.
Separate typed editors keep distance and angle inputs clear while both
sets of handles remain available. The existing command path preserves undo
and marks toolpaths stale after a turn. The edge-on refusal prevents an
inert drag and tells the user how to make the ring usable.

**Considered and dropped:** Removing the Rotate toolbar button would expand
the change and overlap other toolbar work. A duplicate command or MCP tool
would repeat the existing turn behavior. Guessing an angle from screen
motion on an edge-on ring would make the result depend on an ambiguous
projection. Changing the snap default would alter the behavior from #2662
without a requirement to do so.

**Cost to change later:** Removing the Rotate shortcut requires toolbar and
layout test changes. A different snap default requires a local constant
and test update. A different edge-on interaction requires a new drag law
and behavior tests. These choices change no saved project format.

## #2625 - Separate WCS feature picks by role

**What was decided:** Show four rows for Origin, X axis, Y axis and Z axis. Each row has its own Pick and Clear controls. The picks remain ephemeral UI state until Apply. Clear below the table discards the draft without changing the setup.

Apply uses the existing `align_roles` result and one undoable `SetWcs` command. The active setup check stays in place. The existing MCP tool keeps the same command. Arming a role clears `wcs_ui.pick_circle` and `wcs_ui.pick_anchor`, because those modes otherwise take viewport clicks before the role draft.

**Why:** Each button names the role that receives the next pick. A new pick replaces only that role. The table keeps the accepted `Face`, `Patch`, `Chain` and `Vertex` kinds. It also keeps the existing rule: two axes define the frame, with an optional origin.

**Considered and dropped:** Keeping the role dropdown would keep the extra selection step. Do not add a second WCS derivation, an origin-only rule, direct world writes, or a new command or MCP tool. The existing alignment law and command already provide the required validation and undo behavior.

**Cost to change later:** Changes to the controls require UI code and tests. Extensions to the alignment rules require separate app work and tests.

## #2626 - GPU stock sim S1: the f32 cut twin and the brick work list

**What was decided.**

1. The twin sets the f32 arithmetic that the S2 WGSL kernel must copy.
   No WGSL exists yet, so the twin follows the f64 order of
   `field_sweep::Sweep::dist`: the capsule closed form for the ball; for
   the upright flat, the level closed form, the plunge closed form and a
   32-step golden section on every other move.
2. The tile is the brick (8 cells a side). The CPU subtracts the brick
   origin in f64 and rounds once to f32. A cell center is
   `(local + 0.5) * cell` in f32.
3. The twin adds a margin to each distance before it claims:
   `TWIN_ULPS = 32` f32 epsilons of the tile scale (reach + r + flank +
   8 cells), plus `1e-6` of the path length on the flat path (the f64
   golden-section bracket). The f32 cut is therefore never above the
   f64 cut. The parity test checks this with no tolerance, because the
   f64-to-f32 pack rounding keeps order.
4. The max law runs on the order-preserving key (flip all bits of a
   negative, set the sign bit of a positive). The GPU can then use an
   unsigned atomic max.
5. The work list uses the f64 window of each chord (`Sweep::window`),
   clipped to the lattice box of `pack_cut`. It is made in f64 on the
   CPU. The items are sorted brick-major, then by chord.
6. The twin refuses, by name, every tool other than the ball and the
   flat end mill, an arc move, a tilted axis (also for the ball) and a
   zero-length feed move. The f64 cut accepts a zero-length move as a
   station; the issue asks the twin to refuse it.
7. The twin writes the cut layer only. The ray-entry layers
   (`cut_ups`, `cut_downs`) stay out: the issue makes S1 a display
   reference and S2 writes only the cut layer.
8. The parity test compares values after a clamp at `-cap` on the two
   sides. A cut under `-cap` never shows (the mesh layer is at least
   `-cap`), and a claim that sits at the `cap` threshold on one side
   only must compare by its visible value.

**Why.** The issue asks for one-sided parity ("never more removal") and
for a refusal by name. A margin in the kernel gives the one-sided bound
by construction. A tolerance only in the test would not.

**Dropped.** A ball on a tilted axis (easy, but the issue names upright
tools); a direct copy of `flat_tie` (the twin is conservative on the
tie, and the f64 tie only claims more); a public change to the f64
kernel (the twin reads the f64 window through the crate-internal API).

**Cost to change later.** If S2 needs a different f32 order, change
`cut_twin.rs` and keep the parity tests; the margin then follows the
new error bound.

## #2636 - "Wireframe, see-through" display mode

**What was decided**

- This work is stacked on PR #2835 (#2818). That PR adds "Shaded" (faces, no
  edges), the Display menu, the draw list (`draw_list::plan`) and the saved
  display mode. This PR adds only the mode that #2835 left out:
  "Wireframe, see-through".
- The mode is a fifth entry of the Display menu, after "Wireframe". The
  labels of the other entries are those of #2818. The mode has no control in
  the Browser pane, because #2818 moved the display choice to the viewport
  menu.
- The draw list of the mode has no face step: no lit faces and no depth-only
  faces. It draws the cached model edges, the cached stock edges and the
  region fills. The depth buffer stays empty, so the model hides nothing: not
  the stock, not a fixture, not a toolpath.
- All edges draw in the same wireframe ink.
- In the mode, a click asks the feature pick for `through`, as the "Pick
  through" switch does. The rule is the existing rule of `pick_bodies`: the
  edge nearest to the cursor wins; at the same distance from the cursor, the
  edge nearest to the camera wins. The switch itself stays as the user set it.
- The wireframe switch of the toolbar shows as active in the two wireframe
  modes. One press in either gives "Shaded, with edges".
- The stored key is `wireframe-see-through`. An older build reads an unknown
  key as the default mode (#2835), so the file stays readable in both
  directions.

**Why**

- #2636 asks for the mode in the maintainer's words: "wireframe \"see thru\"
  as well".
- A depth prepass would hide the toolpath behind the model. The issue says
  that the model must not hide what is behind it.
- The pick rule already exists and has tests. A second rule for one display
  mode would give two answers for the same click.

**Considered and dropped**

- Hidden edges in a lighter tone. The issue says "may". It needs a depth
  prepass and a second edge pass, and the prepass hides the toolpath lines
  behind the model. "Shaded, with hidden edges" (#2835) already shows the two
  tones on a shaded model.
- Box selection that takes hidden edges in the mode. The issue names only the
  click. The box follows the "Pick through" switch, as before.
- Four radios in the Browser pane, as #2636 first described. #2818 is the
  later instruction and moved the choice.
- A new pick order (camera depth first). The issue's sentence agrees with the
  existing order, and the test states it.

**Cost to change later**

- The lighter tone for hidden edges is one more `Pipe` step and one pipeline.
  The draw list test of the mode then changes.
- A rename of the stored key needs a reader for the old key.

## #2648 - A headless start opens the file named on the command line

**What was decided.**

- `camcraft-ui --headless <file>` takes the same file list as the window
  (`cli_options::files`) and the same check (`launch_file::command`). A
  refused file (two files, an extension CamCraft does not read, a path that
  is not a file) is said by name and the run exits with 2, the code of a
  bad argument. No adapter is touched.
- A file that passes the check is opened through the same command as the
  window (`ImportFile` or `OpenProjectFile`) on a new state, in place of the
  seeded proof document (`crates/ui/src/headless_open.rs`). The run waits
  for the import (`State::settle`), frames the document (`FrameAll`) and
  draws it with the same View3D readback.
- The run fails (exit 1) and names the file when it does not open: a model
  file that gives no model geometry, or a project whose open is refused.
  The pixel check (at least 5% of the frame drawn) applies when the opened
  document has part geometry; a project without a part opens and draws
  without it.
- The last line of the run says what was drawn: `opened part.sc: 1
  model(s), N facets`, or the seeded document as before.
- `--help` and `docs/user-guide/start-options.md` say what `--headless`
  does with a file.

**Why.** The review of #2542 found that `--headless part.sc` ignored the
