**Cost to change later:** The budget constants and their boundary tests must change together.
A post that legitimately expands records beyond this allowance needs evidence and a revised finite budget.
The change adds no dependencies or user commands and changes no recorded G-code or CL golden files.

## #3004 - A tilted plane reads its stock cap only in its own frame

**Decided.** The tilted (3+2) verify branch in `operation/generate.rs`
starts its local stock cap at negative infinity. The cap is the maximum
local height of the projected corners of the stock box and the model box.
The world stock top (`stock_top_z - oz`) is no longer a lower bound.

**Why.** The world top is a height along world Z. On a side plane (A +90 or
A -90), the local cap is the extent of the blank toward the tool (30 on a
60 x 60 x 70 blank). The old start value held the cap at 70. The shank law
then named a shank 11 mm over the side face a `ShankHit`. The first-traverse
law named a clearance 10 mm over the face low. The corner projection is
already an over-report of the true cap (an affine map takes its maximum at
a corner), so a real collision still convicts.

**Dropped.**
- Recheck `ShankHit` against the exact solids in `stock_top_law`. That
  keeps the wrong cap for the other laws (first traverse, rapids), and it
  is a second law where the cause is one wrong start value.
- A fallback to the world top when no box exists. The model box is always
  projected, so the branch cannot run without a box.

**Cost to change.** Low. The change is one start value in one branch.
The conservative box cap for an oblique face is a separate limitation
(see the issue) and is not touched here.

## #3019 - A seam lead turns only when it crosses its own ring

**Decided.** At the seam of a closed contour ring, the lead-in and the
lead-out keep the walk's own end tangents, except when the full lead
along that tangent crosses a feed move of the ring. The check uses the
verifier's crossing law (`arc_cross::moves_cross_prior`: proper crossing,
a shared end is a touch). Only then is the tangent mirrored across the
other end's tangent. The mirrored lead is used only if it does not cross.
The change is in the new module
`crates/motion/src/machining2d/lead_seam.rs` (`seam_tangents`).
`lead_fit.rs` calls it from `both_fit` and `plan_leads`.

**Why.** The first fix (#3053) mirrored the tangent on each closed ring
that bent to the air side at the seam. That condition is also true at a
sharp corner of a plain rectangle. There it moved the reseated start,
reversed the vertical entry arc and dropped the chord-fan entry (#3111,
reverted in #3114). A gate on the real fault, "this lead crosses its own
ring", changes nothing where no crossing exists. So all other rings keep
their seam, leads, entry and posted G-code.

The issue's crossing does not come from the tabs. The same crossing
occurs with no tabs on the R6 plate (pinned). So the gate is on the
crossing, not on the tab count. The maintainer's reopen comment asked for
"only where a tab needs it". The crossing gate is narrower than "each ring"
and covers the untabbed case of the same fault.

**Dropped.**
- Gate on `tab_count > 0`. It leaves the same crossing on an untabbed
  round-cornered plate.
- #3053's bend-direction law. It changed rings that had no crossing.
- Relax the crossing law for leads. It would hide real lead crossings.
- Shrink a crossing lead. The crossing is next to the seam, so each
  halving still crosses, and the lead would be refused.

**Cost to change.** Local to one function. The check builds the ring's
moves once for each call. A lead that crosses after the mirror too keeps
its tangent, and verify still holds the post (no silent change).

## #3020 - Judge a shallow spot with its cone radius

**What was decided:** Keep the tangency law. Use the matching real cone's
radius at the stock top for linear axial moves with no explicit tool pose.
Apply this radius only in Boundary contexts with declared drill rims and no
supplied model. Use the deepest endpoint to bound both the plunge and the
retract. Keep the nominal radius when the cone top or the shank enters.
Keep the nominal radius for model sections, tool poses, arcs, lateral moves,
other shapes, and missing or mismatched cutter geometry.

**Why:** A 6 mm drill with a 120-degree point reaches a radius of 1.732 mm
at a point depth of 1 mm. That cone stays inside a hole with a radius of
2.5 mm. The nominal 3 mm radius stays above the stock surface. The solid
check, stock simulation, and post checks still refuse actual gouges.

**Considered and dropped:** Suppressing all spot gouge warnings would hide
real wall cuts. Changing the tool diameter would describe the wrong tool.
Reducing the section radius for all operations would weaken other wall
checks. Extending the change to posed tools or other profiles would need
additional geometry proofs and tests.

**Cost to change later:** Extend the footprint calculation for tool poses
or other profiles only with separate safety proofs and pinning tests.
This change adds no dependencies and changes no process files.

## #3021 - Zigzag pockets close with the wall and island rings

**What was decided.** Each 2D pocket that cuts as Zigzag (strategy
Zigzag, or Auto that resolves to Zigzag) now uses the rest pocket's pass
plan: the rows stand 0.01 mm inside the cutter-center area, and one
closed ring follows each boundary loop of that area (the outer wall and
each island). The row points stand on the 1 um lattice.

**Why.**
- Rows alone touch a side wall or an island only at their ends. Between
  two ends the cutter leaves a cusp over the full depth. With a 6 mm tool
  and a 2 mm stepover, the cusp is about 0.17 mm on a straight wall and
  0.75 mm on a rounded corner. Verify had no law for that material, so
  the program passed as clean.
- The rest pocket already had this plan (`pocket_zigzag::rest_passes`).
  The 0.01 mm gap keeps the row ends from crossing the ring.
- The gap puts the row ends off the lattice. A helix entry snaps its
  centre and its turn ends to the lattice. Two levels' helices at one
  off-lattice start then differed by 3.5e-7 mm, and the post check read
  their chords as crossings (`setup_align`). Lattice row points remove
  that. The snap moves a point by less than 0.5 um, inside the 10 um gap.

- With blended turns, a row-turn fillet or a ring-corner fillet can
  cross the other pass. The Zigzag pocket now holds its blends to the
  crossing law (`hold_crossings`), as the rest pocket does. A fillet
  that would cross stays a sharp turn. The ring corners of a square
  pocket then stay sharp.

**Dropped.**
- A verify law that names unfinished walls. The cut is the defect; a
  warning on every Zigzag pocket is noise.
- An Auto that resolves to Offset rings when the pocket has an island.
  It changes the strategy that the user sees, and an explicit Zigzag
  pocket keeps the cusps.
- The same rings in `pocket_avoid` (Do not touch) and in the 3D pocket
  levels. They use other pass plans; a follow-up issue tracks them.

**Cost to change later.** Low. One condition in `pocket_over_with_relief`
selects the plan. The goldens of `pocket_zigzag_plate_with_island` and
the two `first-part` sample programs hold the output.

## #3022 - A move into another setup keeps the program order

**Decided.** `SetOperationSetup` (`crates/app/src/commands/setup.rs`) gives
the moved operation a position at the end of its target setup. It uses the
same `append_position` helper as `CreateOperation`. That helper also pins the
target's siblings at their current positions, and undo restores them. A move
that does not change the effective setup (the implicit `None` to the first
setup, or the reverse) keeps the position of the operation.

**Why.** The old command cleared the position (`order = None`). The program
order puts an operation without a position after the others, in name order.
Operations moved one by one into a new setup thus came out in name order: a
tap came before its tap drill. The issue asks that the program order stays
the user's. An append in move order keeps the relative order of a batch of
moves. It also is what a new operation does, so the rule is the same for
both commands.

**Dropped.**
- Keep the old position value. Positions count inside one setup, so the old
  value has no meaning in the target and would interleave the operations at
  random places.
- Insert the moved operation at its old index in the target. The target has
  different siblings, so that index is not defined.
- Append also when the effective setup does not change. The first move of
  the issue's case (implicit to the first named setup) would then send each
  operation to the end, one at a time. The order would be correct only after
  the last move.

**Cost to change.** Low. One command and its tests.

## #3023 - Threading refuses a helical modelled thread by name

**Decided.** Threading now refuses a model with a HELICAL thread, with a
message that names the helical thread, its pitch and its hand, and that
tells the user to model the thread as revolved V grooves. The refusal
comes before the slice of the job region and before the axis fit. These
two steps refused the issue's part with messages that named other causes
("the mesh is open ... dangling chord ends", "every axis fits this model
equally").

The detector (`camcraft_motion::multiaxis::axis_helix::helix`) uses the
normal lines of the facets. About a candidate axis, each inclined facet
gives the screw parameter `h = (n x u) . (o - p) / (n . u)`. A revolve
gives zero. A helical thread gives one common nonzero `h` on its two
flanks. The gates: the agreeing area is at least half of the inclined
area and 2% of the part, and it goes all the way round the axis (the
coarseness skip of `axis.rs`). The pitch is the area-weighted mean of
the agreeing band, because the two triangles of one twisted quad read
`h` low and high by the ratio of two radii (1.356 and 1.665 for a 1.5
pitch).

**Why.** The issue's "Done means" accepts a refusal that names the
helical thread. The kernel's own design already reads a modelled thread
as a revolved V section and cannot find a phase on a helix (its
silhouette is a flat crest). So the honest output today is a clear
refusal, not a toolpath.

**Dropped.**
- Read a helical thread (find its phase from the helix). This is a new
  algorithm (effort:max) and changes posted G-code. It needs its own
  issue.
- Repair the STEP tessellation of helical faces so the slice closes.
  That is an importer defect, separate from Threading; the refusal now
  comes first, so Threading does not depend on it.
- Make the axis fit accept helical facets. That changes every rotary
  and turning kind, not only Threading.
- Use the median `h` as the pitch. It lands on one side of the truth
  (about 10% low on the test shaft).

**Cost to change.** The refusal is one call in the kernel and one in the
app arm. A later helical-thread reader replaces the refusal with a
phase read and keeps the detector.

**Not tested.** The QA files of the issue (`q03-turn-shaft*.camproj`,
the STEP and `.sc` models) were not on this machine. The pins use a
procedural shaft of the same shape (M16x1.5 helical V, Ø24 body, Ø30
head, 70 long), closed and with gaps.

## #3024 - Clip pick outlines before screen projection

**What was decided:** Clip each highlight segment in homogeneous clip space before the perspective divide. Use the renderer's near plane, `z >= 0`, and a positive `w` limit. Keep the visible portion of each crossing segment. Join only adjacent surviving segments. Preserve the seam of a fully visible closed outline. The selected, viewport-hover and row-hover highlights use the same path.

**Why:** Point rejection removes visible portions of edges that cross the near plane. A point close to the eye can also project far outside the viewport. Segment clipping keeps the outline complete and prevents a false connection across its hidden portion.

**Considered and dropped:** Stroke width and anti-aliasing changes do not correct the projection. Dropping a whole crossing edge leaves gaps. Changing the camera matrix or the GPU projection extends the scope beyond pick highlights.

**Evidence:** Seven tests cover clipped rectangle edges, stroke bounds, the near plane, separate runs, closed seams, invalid points and the positive `w` boundary. Five fail on the unchanged baseline; all seven pass with the fix. Restoring the old code, removing the near-plane guard and removing the positive `w` guard each make the relevant pin fail. Restoring the fix makes them pass. The quick gate and UI clippy pass. No golden files change.

**Cost to change later:** A different renderer depth convention requires a matching clip-plane change and updated analytic projection tests. The display cache and the camera API need no change.

## #3028 - A symlinked camcraft-cli finds the shipped posts

**What was decided.**
- `camcraft_post::data_dir::DataFiles::from_process` resolves the
  executable path with the new `real_exe` before the assets lookup. If the
  path is a symbolic link, `real_exe` calls `std::fs::canonicalize` and the
  lookup starts beside the installed file. A plain path is not changed.
  The posts and the machines use this lookup, so the two kinds are fixed.
- The refusal of a copy of the executable now ends with `COPY_HINT`. The
  hint says to start the program from its install folder, or through a
  symbolic link to the installed executable. There is no setting or
  environment variable that points at an assets folder, so the hint names
  none.

**Why.**
- `std::env::current_exe` gives the path that started the process on macOS
  and on Windows, and that path can be a link. On Linux it reads
  `/proc/self/exe`, which is already the real file: a release build made
  before this change posted through a link on Linux (readings on the
  issue).
- Only a link is resolved because `canonicalize` on Windows adds the
  `\\?\` prefix. Each path in a message would then change for all Windows
  users, also for those who start the program without a link. A link to a
  folder needs no resolution: `<link folder>/assets/posts` follows the
  folder link to the real folder.
- A link that does not resolve keeps the link path. The lookup then fails
  with a refusal that names the folder of the link, as before. It never
  panics.

**Considered and dropped.**
- `canonicalize` on each executable path: dropped for the Windows prefix
  above.
- A walk of two candidate sets (the real file first, then the folder of the
  link): dropped. Assets beside a link are not a shipped layout, and two
  sets make the refusal longer with no gain.
- An environment variable for the assets folder: dropped for this fix. The
  module doc of `data_dir.rs` rejects a second source of shipped files
  that can shadow them with no warning (review of #2293). A variable needs
  its own decision.

**Cost to change later.** Low. The resolution is one function in
`crates/post/src/data_dir.rs`, with its pins in `data_dir_tests.rs`.

## #3043 - The catalog timing line is one write; the contract test runs its cases in order

**Decided.** `within` (`crates/app/tests/example_catalog/support.rs`) makes
the whole timing line into one `String` (`timing_line`) and writes it with
one `write_all` on the locked stderr. The contract test
`two_broken_cases_report_both_names_and_times` runs its inner test binary
with `--test-threads=1`. Its asserts do not change.

**Why.** The post-merge run 44780029308 failed at `contract.rs:59`. The
inner run started the two broken cases in parallel. Stderr has no buffer,
so the formatted timing line went out in pieces. The default panic hook of
the other case thread wrote its message between the pieces:

```
catalog 2d/contour-tabs regenerates
thread '<unnamed>' panicked at crates/app/tests/example_catalog/support.rs:68:5:
2d/first-part: missing model/
 elapsed=0.000s budget=60.000s
```

The assert looks for the contiguous text `catalog {case} {action}
elapsed=`, so it failed. This is a race. It occurs more on a loaded Linux
runner. The one-write change also keeps the timing lines whole in normal
parallel gate logs. The one-thread inner run makes the contract test
deterministic.

**Dropped.**
- A retry of the inner run: it hides the race and does not remove it.
- A looser assert (find `catalog {case} {action}` and `elapsed=` apart):
  it weakens the contract that each case reports its name and its time on
  one line.
- Only one of the two changes: each change alone removes this failure, but
  the one-write change protects the real gate logs, and the one-thread run
  protects the test from other writers to stderr.

**Cost to change.** Low. Two test files only; no product code.

# 3050 - bore heavy-lane pins after the solidcore mesh

- Chose: Windows x86_64 pin becomes (3158, 3130, 1141), equal to the Linux
  x86_64 and macOS arm64 pins already on main (via 2903f4dda / 4be274f79).
- Measured (release, `pocket3d_hsm -- --ignored --exact
  the_users_bore_roughs_adaptive_level_by_level_and_verifies_clean`) at
  upstream main d66400b78: Windows x86_64 (3158, 3130, 1141); macOS arm64
  (3158, 3130, 1141); Linux x86_64 (3158, 3130, 1141) by sn3ro on 3c761b5bb
  (comment on #3050).
- Why: PR #2904 changed this fixture's mesh from 952 to 6228 facets at the same
  chord cap; the planner is unchanged. On Windows the verify-clean,
  every-level-cuts, no-fallback and no-budget assertions all passed before
  the count pin failed, so the plan still verifies clean; only the counts moved.
- Considered and dropped: a band for Windows (the pin stays exact per
  platform); loosening any assertion (none touched).
- Added `the_windows_x86_64_bore_count_pin_is_exact`, which rejects the old
  triple and every off-by-one.

## #3069 - Generic starter tools for hobby routers

**Decided:** Add 22 unbranded cutters to the embedded tool catalog. Include
up-cut, down-cut, compression and ball nose cutters at 3 mm, 6 mm, 1/8 in
and 1/4 in. Include sharp-point 60 and 90 degree V-bits with 6 mm and
1/4 in shanks. Include 25 mm and 1 in surfacing bits. Store all lengths in
mm. The inch names retain the exact conversions of 3.175, 6.35 and 25.4 mm.

Each tool states a nominal flute length and stick-out. The existing model
stores stick-out as flute length plus exposed shank length. These generic
dimensions and the holder dimensions must match the actual assembly before
machining. The cut direction appears in the name. The model does not state
the compression transition height.

Use positive baseline spindle speeds and feeds because the tool reader
requires them. Use 18000 rpm and 600 mm/min for the small cutters. Use
12000 rpm and 600 mm/min for the surfacing bits. These values are not
verified settings for a real cut. Leave material-specific cutting rows
empty until the wood cutting data in #3068 lands. Mark the surfacing bits
as unable to cut through their centre.

**Why:** The existing catalog powers the library picker and the normal
library import. Data additions make the starter set available without a
new command, dependency or file format. Separate tests preserve the legacy
tool order and check the router shapes, reach and import command.

PRs #2714 and #2836 touch other catalog rows. PR #2714 also extends the
legacy `ORDER` constant. This change keeps that constant intact and changes
the validation function. Each touches the same file, different function or
row; whichever merges second refreshes.

**Considered and dropped:** Vendor libraries remain in the community
repository. Flat-tip V-bits wait for #895; these entries describe only sharp
points. A new helix or compression transition field needs separate model
work. Wood cutting rows must not use a metal material as a substitute.
Changing the library reader or the picker adds no value for this set.

**Cost to change later:** Low for nominal sizes and baseline values. A
compression transition or a flat-tip profile needs model and validation
work. Material-specific cutting rows can follow the wood data change.

## #3070 - Guided sheet job: one checklist over stock, WCS and a post floor

**What was decided.**

- One undoable command, `SetSheetJob`, holds the existing `SetStock` and
  `SetWcsOrigin` commands and writes a new `SetupDef::sheet_job` record.
  It applies them in order and inverts them in reverse. One undo restores
  the stock, the origin and the record.
- The record keeps these values: length (X), width (Y), thickness, Z zero
  (`top` or `spoilboard`), XY zero (four corners or `centre`, default
  `front_left`), the through-cut allowance, and the clamp clearance. All
  values are in mm. The record saves additively (no version step). The
  loader refuses a value that the command would refuse.
- The post gate gets one clause, `sheet_job::program_problems`. For each
  operation of a sheet-job setup, it refuses the post by name when:
  - a move goes below the sheet bottom minus the allowance;
  - a rapid that moves in XY is below the sheet top plus the clamp
    clearance;
  - the stock thickness or the WCS Z no longer match the job (an edit
    after the checklist).
- The stock stays where the setup's stock was: the same XY centre and the
  same bottom face, or the origin if the setup has no stock. The WCS
  rotation becomes identity, because a sheet lies flat on the bed.
- The command acts on the active setup, because `SetStock` acts on the
  active setup. The UI refuses Apply on the page of an inactive setup and
  names the setup to activate.
- The MCP tool `set_sheet_job` requires `allowance` and `z_zero`, so an
  agent always states them. `{"clear": true}` drops only the record.
  `get_job` shows the job. The live gate puts the tool in `LimitEdit`,
  because the allowance is a safety floor.
- The UI is a "Sheet job" group on the Settings page of a milling setup.
  It shows the allowance row every time, with the default 0.3 mm, and one
  summary line ("deepest Z...").
- The allowance is 0..5 mm. The clamp clearance is 0..200 mm. These limits
  catch typing errors.

**Why.** The issue asks for a checklist over the existing undoable
commands, not a second copy of the settings. A post-time floor is the
only place that sees each operation's real depth. Per-operation heights
stay with their operations, and the gate refuses a depth that is not
safe. It does not change the depth silently.

**Considered and dropped.**

- Rewriting the bottom and clearance heights of each operation from the
  checklist. Dropped: this is a hidden edit of many operations. The user
  could not see it, and a later edit of the operation would undo it
  silently. The gate refusal says which height to raise.
- A judgment of every rapid, including vertical plunges, against the
  clamp plane. Dropped: a vertical rapid down to the retract height over
  the part does not cross a clamp. Only XY travel can hit one.
- A job on the implicit (undeclared) setup. Dropped: the record needs a
  `SetupDef`, so the command asks for a setup first.
- A machine-bed limit from the machine file. Dropped: no machine file
  gives a bed Z. The spoilboard is the bed that the user can see.

**Cost to change later.** The record is one optional setup field. More
answers (for example, a spoilboard thickness) are additive keys. A move
from a post refusal to height rewriting would need a new command for each
operation kind.

## #3077 - The first traverse of a cross drill on a lathe or a mill-turn

- **What was decided** (issue workers, unattended; the maintainer can change it):
  1. **The premise is the maintainer's (#2987, #2997).** The unknown start is the top of the machine's travel: on a lathe the turret's index position (the tool-change position), at the top of the X and Z travel. This is the same premise as the upright law and the 3+2 table law. NOT covered: a program that starts with the tool low near the work, for example after a manual jog.
  2. **The lathe post's real first move is judged.** `fanuc-lathe.cps` `liveMove` writes `G00 C` with the turret at the index position, then `G00 X Z` to the first motion record. The record stream (`camcraft_post::post::dump`) writes each move's END only; the first move's start goes out only as the `StartX/Y/Z` parameters, and `liveMove` does not move there. So the first G00 X Z goes to the END of move 0: the R-plane point of the first hole, not the kernel's standoff (`crates/motion/src/drilling/cross.rs`: the path starts at the standoff, move 0 is the rapid to the R plane). `tormach-lathe.cps` states no `liveTooling` and refuses a live section. A G00 moves each axis at its own rate (RS-274 / ISO 6983), so the tip can pass any point of the box between the index position and the first point: every radius from the first point's radius out, at every height from its Z up.
  3. **The law** (`camcraft_sim::verify::live_first_traverse`). The tool lies along the station's radius, its tip inward. The swept solid is read in the part frame about the spindle line through the work offset (`u` the first point's radial direction, `v` across it, `s = u - r`): `u >= r`, `|v| <= W(s)`, `z >= z - W(s)`. `W(s)` is the widest band of the tool stack (`ToolGeom`: flute, shank, holder) within `s` of the tip. Past the stack's end the widest band runs on, because the turret is not modelled. The move's end is judged, then its start (on one station line the start's swept solid lies inside the end's).
     - Work and turning steel stand at the C angle the post states before X and Z move, so they are read exactly: each facet (a box as its twelve facets) is clipped by each band's planes. Work: the source (the part, or the stock on a stock source), the kept parts, the neighbour parts, and the setup's stock (its facets, or its box when it has no facets). Turning steel: the chuck (`fixture::workholding_for` `.0`).
     - Fixed steel (a tailstock, the machine table) stands in the machine frame at an angle the part frame does not state. It is read revolved about the spindle: its nearest and farthest radius against each band, and its top against the band's floor. That holds at any C.
     - **A touch passes.** A face within `Z_TOL` (1e-6 mm) of the swept solid's boundary is clear, as in the other traverse laws: the tip slides down a face flush with the R plane and does not enter it. The work's model excess (a coarse model) follows the law of #1053, as the other cross-drill laws do: it tightens the tolerance while a positive one is left, and past that the law reads the facets untightened (the program gate refuses the coarse model by name). The steel is never tightened.
  4. **A refusal by name, not a warning.** The cross branch of generation refuses the drill (`GenError::Invalid`): "cross drill: the first rapid comes from the turret's index position ...". The refusal names the solid and how far out from the spindle it reaches, at which Z. No toolpath, so nothing posts. A start or a tool stack that cannot be read is refused by name too.
  5. **A mill-turn answers to two laws.** Its default post is the mill post (`posting::default_post_for`: `Kind::MillTurn` gives the builtin Fanuc mill post). That post sends Z to the clearance height, then X/Y from an unknown X/Y, then the full block with the rotary words (decision #2965 item 1). So a mill-turn cross drill also answers to the upright law (`first_traverse::judge` with the cross drill's lifted start). The live-tool law also judges it. A mill-turn that posts through a lathe post is judged by both laws, which is stricter than its own post.
  6. **Cache.** The cross drill's op stamp takes one more word, `live-traverse-3077`. Such a cache reads Stale once and the post refuses it until a regenerate.
  7. **One test fixture was unsafe and is changed (coordinator decision, recorded by the worker).** `drilling_cross::recognition_finds_the_bar_two_holes_and_they_generate`: its 44 mm box stock (`cross_support::cross_world`, `Location::default`) stands at X/Y +-22 and Z 0..44, over the bar. Its first hole (the through hole at (15, 0, -10)) has its R plane at radius 20 (clearance 20 over top 15). The Z leg of the first rapid at radius 20 passes 2 mm of uncut stock from Z 0 up. The law is right and the fixture is wrong. Chosen: that test's clearance is 30, so the R plane stands at radius 30, outside the stock. What the test pins stays: the recognition finds the bar's two holes, and they generate Ok. It is a test fixture, not a shipped example, a catalog case or a golden. Dropped: a rule that this stock is not there (it is uncut material in the setup), and a move of the stock (the clearance can be raised, so the fixture keeps its shape).
- **Why.** The lathe post's move order is the fact that the law must follow. C is in position before X and Z move, so the work and the chuck have a known angle; the fixed steel has none in the part frame, so it is read at every angle. The tool's own stack, not its widest band everywhere, is what the rapid carries past the work: a wide shank 30 mm behind the tip cannot meet a lump 3 mm beside the drill's line.
- **Pinning tests.** `crates/app/tests/lathe_cross_drill.rs`: `a_cross_drill_over_its_chuck_has_a_clear_first_traverse` (lathe and mill-turn: clear), `a_cross_drill_under_a_wide_tailstock_is_refused_by_name` (lathe and mill-turn: refused), `a_thin_tailstock_centre_is_clear_on_a_lathe_and_convicts_a_mill_turn`, `a_turning_collar_flush_with_the_first_point_is_clear_and_one_proud_of_it_is_refused`. The sim unit tests in `crates/sim/src/verify/live_traverse_tests.rs` pin the tool width, the touch, the coarse excess (#1053), the shank band behind the flute, the station's half-plane, a square bar's face and diagonal, the clipped facet, the spindle line off the origin, the fixed steel read revolved, and a start or a tool that cannot be read. The shipped cross-drill suites stay green unchanged (`coarse_cross_drill`, `drilling_cross_box` and the others), except one test fixture (item 7).
- **Known limits.**
  - The law does not use the stated X and Z travel. It reads every height from the band's floor up, and every radius out. Steel beyond the travel top is read as in the way. That is stricter.
  - The turret itself (its body and the other stations) is not modelled. Past the tool stack the widest band of the stack runs on; a turret wider than that is not read.
  - The tool's cross-section is read as a square of its band's half-width about its axis, not a disc. That is stricter by the corners.
  - A lathe whose index position is at the low Z end (toward the chuck) is not this premise. The shipped machines and the lathe convention of this project put the free end of the bar at +Z.
  - The other kinds on a mill-turn (milling, axial drilling) still answer to no first-traverse law (`is_mill` is false). That is outside #3077: #3083 owns it.
- **What was considered and dropped**:
  - A new `Warning` variant: it needs mappings in the UI, MCP and the warned moves, and `FirstTraverseLow` says "unknown X/Y", which a lathe does not have. A refusal by name in the cross branch needs none.
  - The work and the chuck read revolved too (the first draft): it refused every legal cross drill on a square bar or a box stock (the corner radius stands over the face's station), 22 tests in the cross-drill suites. The swept solid reads them at the angle the post states.
  - One slab as wide as the widest band (the second draft): it refused a wide shank that stands 30 mm behind the tip (`drilling_cross_box::a_wide_shank_on_box_stock_is_proven_clear_along_the_line`).
  - A touch read as a hit (the second draft took the tolerance off the radius): it refused a flange flush with the R plane at full fidelity (`coarse_cross_drill`), which no other traverse law refuses.
  - The excess as a growth of the work (the third draft): it refused the flush flange on the coarse model (`coarse_cross_drill`), against the #1053 law that every other cross-drill law follows.
  - Judging only the kernel's standoff (move 0's start): the lathe post never moves there.
  - Vertex samples in the station's half-plane: a large facet can cross the band with no vertex in it. Each facet is clipped instead.
  - Judging only the mill law on a mill-turn: a mill-turn can post through a lathe post, and the last block goes down at the station's radius.
- **Cost to change later**: low. One sim law (`live_traverse.rs`), one app seam (`operation::cross_traverse`), one call in the cross branch and one flag at the upright judge.

### Refuse an item with no unit context when the file states a non-radian angle unit (#3079)

**What was decided:** The STEP model read refuses each solid item that no
representation gives a unit context when a context of the file states a
plane angle unit that is not the radian. The refusal names the item and
the angle unit. An item is listed when a representation with a context
lists it, or when it is a piece of such a solid (the reader gives a piece
the context of its solid). The check is `UnlistedAngles` in
`crates/kernel/src/step_units_guard.rs`. The seam applies it to the solids
that the reader builds, and to the items that the reader fails to read.
For a failed item the unit reason replaces the read message, because the
wrong angle unit is the first cause of the failure.

**Extended at the takeover review:** an item whose context states no plane
angle unit is refused the same way, when the file states an angle unit that
is not the radian. The reader gives that item the default units too, so its
angles are read in radians. The refusal names the item and its context.
`UnlistedAngles` now keeps each item's context by the reader's rules (the
first representation that lists it with a context; a piece of a solid in
that solid's context) and the contexts that state a plane angle unit. This
is the same shape as the length rule of #2919
(`crates/kernel/src/step_length_units.rs`). An item is kept when its
context states an angle unit, or when every stated angle unit is the radian,
or when no angle unit is stated. Pins:
`item_in_a_context_with_no_angle_unit_in_a_degree_file_is_refused_by_name`
and the control
`item_in_a_context_with_no_angle_unit_in_a_radian_file_is_kept`.

**Why:** The reader gives an item with no context the default units: its
angles are read in radians. In a file that states degrees, the item then
has wrong geometry. That is a silent wrong answer (Prime Directive). The
issue asks for the rule of the length unit: keep such an item only when
every stated angle unit is the radian, or when no angle unit is stated.

**Considered and dropped:**
- Stacking on PR #2927, which edits the solid build loop of the same
  function. It has `needs-rework` and `conflicts`. This change adds its own
  lines before the failure loop and does not touch the lines of #2927.
  Whichever PR merges second refreshes.
- Refusing only items that use an angle (a cone, a torus). The issue asks
  for the item rule. An angle can hide in many entities, and a missed one
  is a silent wrong answer.
- Refusing the whole file. The other items of the file have a context and
  read correctly. The importer already refuses a file that reads only in
  part, by name.

**Cost to change later:** Remove the check when the pinned reader gives an
item with no context the units of the file. Keep the three pins in
`crates/kernel/tests/step_short_units.rs`.

## #3081 - A 3+2 tool axis that points down toward the table gets a verdict that blocks the post

- **What was decided** (taken unattended; the maintainer can change it):
  1. **A new verdict, `Warning::FirstTraverseUnderTable { at, height_mm, limit_mm }`.** Past a 90-degree head tilt the tool axis points down toward the machine table (`axis_z < 0`). A higher plane along that axis stands lower in the world, so the repair is the opposite of the `FirstTraverseLow` repair. The new variant says "lower the clearance plane to Z<limit> or under it" and never "raise". It blocks the post (it is not in the advisory list of `Warning::blocks_post`). It replaces the note of #2987 ("...the tool axis points down toward the table...").
  2. **The same premise as #2987 (premise (b), maintainer decision of 2026-11-20).** The unknown start is any point of the X/Y travel at the tool-change height, the top of the Z travel (table top plus `stroke`). The worst start is the one with the LOWEST reading `low` along the axis: the move from it to the plane drops `(plane - low) * -axis_z` in the world. The plane is refused when that drop is more than `stroke + Z_TOL`. The highest plane that every such move keeps over the table top is `limit = low + stroke / -axis_z`, and the verdict names it.
     - **NOT covered:** a program that starts with the tool low near the table or the work, for example after a manual jog. The operator must send the machine to its tool-change height before the program starts, as for the upright law and #2987.
  3. **Two verdicts can stand together.** The stock and fixture verdict (`FirstTraverseLow`, "raise") and the table verdict ("lower") are judged apart and both go into the warnings. When the limit is under the stock top along the axis, no plane is clear from the tool-change height, and the two verdicts say so together. The UI folds the new verdict on its own line, key 224: the opposite repair of key 221. Key 222 is taken by open PR #2836 (`UndercutLift`) and 223 by open PR #3062 (`DrillUndersize`), so 224 collides with neither.
  4. **Tilted caches read Stale once.** The post gate trusts the warnings that a cache carries. A tilted cache judged under the old law holds the note and no verdict, so `current_stamp` writes the salt `first-traverse-table-3081` for each operation with a tilt (`OpParams::tilt()`). Only those operations regenerate; the global salt stays.
  5. **MCP.** `mcp/job.rs` `finding` names the kind `first_traverse_under_table`, with `blocks_post: true`. No new command, so no new MCP tool.
- **Why.** A refusal must name the right repair (Prime Directive: a visible refusal, never a silent pass). The note of #2987 did not block the post, so a first rapid into the table on a past-90 head tilt could post.
- **Considered and dropped.**
  - Refuse with the `FirstTraverseLow` "raise" verdict: its height is wrong for a down-pointing axis, and a refusal with a wrong repair misleads.
  - A new boolean field on `FirstTraverseLow`: the enum is a file format (project v3 cache), and a new field breaks old caches. A new variant is additive.
  - Bump the global stamp salt (`camcraft-op-stamp-v5`): every cache in every project reads Stale for a law that only reads tilted planes.
  - Keep the note beside the verdict: the verdict says all that the note said, and the repair too.
- **Not judged (known).** As #2987: the law runs at generation only; a mixed machine and a head tilt with a vertical work C keep the #2987 limits.
- **Cost to change later**: low. One arm of `table_read` and the push in `judge` (`operation/first_traverse.rs`), one `Warning` variant and its text.

## #3083 - On a mill-turn, the mill kinds answer to the first-traverse laws of a mill

- **What was decided** (taken unattended; the maintainer can change it):
  1. **The same laws, from the post's real order.** A mill-turn posts a milling tool through the mill post: `posting::default_post_for` gives `MillTurn` the built-in Fanuc mill post, whose first move is `G00 Z` to the clearance (`traverseZ`), then `G00 X Y` at that height (`xyFirst`, `assets/posts/fanuc.cps`). That is the order that the first-traverse laws read. So `first_traverse::mill_order(kind, lathe_tool, params)` is true on a mill and on a mill-turn for a milling tool, and the three calls in `generate.rs` (`turned_axis` and the two `judge` calls) read it in place of `is_mill`. The planar, 3-D, hole (axial and cross) and multi-axis kinds on a mill-turn get the upright law, the 3+2 table law (#2987, #3081) and the tip law (#2965), with no change to the laws.
  2. **The premise of the maintainer (decisions #2965, #2987, #3081).** The unknown start is at the top of the Z travel (the tool-change height). **NOT covered:** a program that starts with the tool low near the work, the chuck or the table, for example after a manual jog. The operator must send the machine to its tool-change height before the program starts.
  3. **The steel of the mill-turn.** The laws read the steel that the setup holds: each tagged workholding model (a chuck, a tailstock or a steady rest model, split turning and fixed by `fixture::workholding_for`) and the box from the stated X/Y/Z travel. The machine file states no chuck, tailstock or turret body (`millturn.mch` has none), so an untagged chuck is not judged - as an untagged vise on a mill is not. The turret holds the tools; the tool's own stack is not steel to its first traverse.
  4. **A rotary kind on a mill-turn stays out (follow-up #3096, P1).** There a rotary kind (`Mode::Rotary`) turns the bar on the spindle C under a radial live tool. Its first rapid comes from the turret index position, not from an upright tool over an unknown X/Y. With a vertical C, the swept law of #2965 reads the start at its height along the spindle against the bar's top, so a radial contour that cuts under the bar top is refused (for example the C-axis tests, whose clearance Z 25 stands under a 34 mm bar stock). The right law is the live-tool reading of #3077 (`verify::live_first_traverse`); #3096 extends it to the rotary kinds after #3077 merges. Before #3083 no law judged these kinds either, so nothing that was refused now posts.
  5. **The struck-link planner stays mill-only** (`generate.rs`, `fixture_route::plan_links`). On a mill-turn the post gate judges each link against the steel (`posting::fixture_problems` -> `fixture_struck::op_hits`, no kind gate) and refuses a struck one, so no link posts unjudged. The planner would route the link over the steel, which changes the mill-turn's posted program: an enhancement, not this P1 fix.
  6. **The mesh steel stays mill-only** (`generate.rs`, `mesh_steel`). The mesh only acquits a box hit (`verify::mesh_refined`), so the box verdict that a mill-turn keeps is the stricter one. No hit can pass.
  7. **Mill-turn caches read Stale once.** The post gate trusts the warnings that a cache carries. `current_stamp` writes the word `first-traverse-mill-turn-3083` for each operation that `first_traverse::newly_judged_on` names (a judged mill kind on a mill-turn setup). No mill's stamp moves, and the global salt stays. No shipped example or catalog project mounts a mill-turn (scout read of `examples/` and `docs/tester-kits/`), so none reads Stale.
  8. **The overlap with #3077.** #3077 routes the mill-turn's cross drill into the upright `judge` with its own flag (`mill_post_cross`). `mill_order` already includes that drill, so the merged flag is `mill_order || mill_post_cross`, and its live-tool law stays beside it.
- **Why.** Prime Directive: a first rapid through the stock or the steel must be refused by name. A mill-turn's mill kinds post the same first move as a mill's, so they must answer to the same laws.
- **Considered and dropped.**
  - Change `is_mill` in `job.rs` to include the mill-turn: it also gates the mesh steel, the planner and the cross-drill refusal ("a mill with no turret"), and each of those must stay as it is.
  - Judge the rotary kinds with the mill premise: it refuses the legal C-axis live-tool work of each shipped test, a false refusal for each program.
  - Refuse every mill kind on a mill-turn until a mill-turn law exists: a refusal of legal work, and the mill laws apply as they are.
  - A lathe post on a mill-turn mill op: `default_post_for` gives the mill post. A lathe post can send X first; that order is not judged here (as #3077 states).
- **Cost to change later**: low. `mill_order` and `newly_judged_on` in `operation/first_traverse.rs`, one stamp word.

## #3084 - The first traverse over work that the machine's rotaries can leave at any pose

- **What was decided** (issue worker, unattended; the maintainer can change it):
  1. **The premise (maintainer, PR #2997).** The unknown start is at the top of the Z travel (the tool-change height), as for #2901, #2965 and #2987. A program that starts with the tool low near the table or the work (for example after a manual jog) is NOT covered.
  2. **The post order is the basis.** The post sends Z, then X/Y at that height, then the move with the rotary words (`fanuc.cps` `traverseZ`, `xyFirst`, `onRapid`). So during the X/Y traverse each rotary that turns the work stands where the previous program left it. The operation does not state that pose.
  3. **Where the lines are.** Each line of a work-turning rotary passes through the WCS origin. This is the indexed post's setup law that the index-swing clause already reads (`posting_index_swing.rs`). No shipped machine file states `pivot` or `offset` (#1962), and no code places nested rotaries from them.
  4. **What the law reads** (new law `sim::verify::first_traverse_low_posed`, seam `operation::first_traverse_posed`):
     - Two or more work-turning rotaries: each turn moves the other's line. The only figure that every pose keeps is the distance from the WCS origin. Each point of the start stock and of the part, and each corner of each tagged fixture, is read on its sphere about the WCS origin (top = origin height + distance).
     - One work-turning rotary that tilts: a full turn about its line through the WCS origin (`posed_top`, the same circle as `swept_top`).
     - A full turn and a full sphere contain every stated turning range. So the read is never lower than the true top. The turning range is not read.
     - Heights are read along the path's frame axis (`+Z` upright; the 3+2 frame's axis and origin in a tilted frame).
  5. **Who answers.** A milling operation (`mill_order`) of a multi-axis or rotary kind (`Section::MultiAxis` or `Mode::Rotary`), on a mounted machine with a tilting rotary that states `turns_part: true`:
     - a rotary kind on a machine where two or more rotaries turn the work (case 1 of the issue);
     - a multi-axis kind on a machine where one or more rotaries turn the work (case 2 of the issue).
     - A rotary kind with one work-turning rotary keeps #2965's swept law about the fitted axis.
  6. **The traverse height.** The higher of the clearance and move 0's own height in the path's frame (`traverseZ`). A rotary kind's move 0 is a radial pose, so it reads the clearance alone: the post never traverses under it. With no clearance, move 0's height.
  7. **Steel.** Each tagged fixture is read as turning with the work (a superset: a box's swept top is never under its plain top). The machine table stays under the rotaries and is not read.
  8. **The verdict.** The same blocking `Warning::FirstTraverseLow`. It replaces each first-traverse verdict at a lower top, so one verdict names the highest top that the clearance must clear.
  9. **Refusal by name.** A lone tilting work-turning rotary with no usable line (no stated axis and no RS-274 letter A or B, or a zero or non-finite axis) refuses generation: "the work-turning rotary Q states no usable axis line, so the first traverse over the work it turns cannot be judged". The sphere case needs no line.
- **Cache.** The op stamp of an operation that the posed law reads (`first_traverse_posed::newly_judged`) takes one more word, `first-traverse-posed-3084`. Such a cache reads Stale once. The salt does not change. No shipped project moves: the only examples on a machine with a work-turning rotary (`first-4axis-part`, `first-continuous-4axis-part`, the microARC 4, one rotary) have slot and rotary-parallel operations, which the law does not read.
- **Pinning tests.** `crates/app/tests/first_traverse_posed.rs`: `two_work_turning_rotaries_read_the_rotary_kinds_stock_on_its_sphere`, `a_tilting_table_reads_a_5_axis_kinds_stock_swept_about_its_line`, `a_work_turning_rotary_with_no_line_refuses_by_name`. Sim unit tests in `crates/sim/src/verify/first_traverse_posed.rs`.
- **Known limits.**
  - A program that starts low (premise, item 1).
  - The setup law of item 3: a work offset that is not on the rotary lines is read as if it were. The index-swing clause has the same premise.
  - The Z word is read as a machine height in the frame of the rotaries at zero, as #2965 reads it. Under a TCP mode that turns the program frame with the table, the post's Z is a height in the turned frame; that reading is not made.
  - A rotary that never stated `turns_part` (a project saved before #804, or a machine built in code) is not read as work-turning. The load names such a machine (#813), and each parsed file states it.
  - A 3+2 operation (`Tilt`) and a cross drill on a work-tilting machine are not read by this law. Their first traverse has the same unknown pose: follow-up #3100.
  - The tool radius is not added (the law reads the tip, as #2901 and #2965 do).
- **What was considered and dropped**:
  - The exact top over the stated turning ranges (branch and bound over the inner angle, with the closed form over the outer one): it needs the order of the rotaries and the position of each line, which no file states. The sphere is exact for a trunnion whose ranges reach 90 degrees, which is the common case.
  - The lines from `pivot` / `offset` / `chain_order`: no shipped file states them.
  - A refusal of every multi-axis operation on a table-tilt machine: it blocks programs that the law shows to be safe.
  - A new warning variant: the #2901 verdict blocks the post and carries both heights; a variant adds four mappings and no information.
  - Edit `first_traverse::judge`: the law stays in its own functions, so the stacked PRs (#3099, #3096) do not conflict.
- **Cost to change later**: low. One law function in `camcraft-sim` and the selection in `operation::first_traverse_posed` (`turn_of`).

## #3089 - Name the operations that need the missing machine

Include the affected operations in the shared default-machine refusal. The
verification pass already knows which setups and operations use that machine.
Listing them in posting order gives the operator the setup, operation and file
to check. Moving the check into each output mode would duplicate the refusal.
A future change to the wording only needs to update this diagnostic.

## #3096 - A rotary kind on the spindle C answers to the live-tool first-traverse law

- **What was decided** (taken unattended; the maintainer can change it):
  1. **The post's real order is the lathe's.** A rotary kind (`Mode::Rotary`: Rotary Contour, Parallel, Offset) whose fitted line is the machine's C gets its path stamped with C (`rotary_gate::stamp_spindle_c`). The stream of that path carries `PARAM LiveTool`, and the post engine refuses by name each post that does not declare `liveTooling` (`crates/post/src/post/engine.rs`). Only `fanuc-lathe.cps` declares it, so the mill post (`fanuc.cps`, the mill-turn's default) never writes such a program. The lathe post's `liveMove` writes `G00 C` with the turret at its index position, then `G00 X Z` to the first motion record. That is the order of #3077's cross drill, so the law is `verify::live_first_traverse`, called from the new seam `operation/rotary_traverse.rs` in the two rotary arms of `generate.rs`, right after the C stamp.
  2. **The premise of the maintainer.** The unknown start is at the top of the travel (the tool-change height: the turret's index position, the top of the X and Z travel), as in #2965, #2987, #3077 and #3083. **NOT covered:** a program that starts with the turret low near the work, the chuck or a steady, for example after a manual jog. The operator must send the turret to its index position before the program starts.
  3. **The work turns with C; fixed steel does not.** C stands at the first point's angle before X and Z move. So the stock, the parts and the turning steel (a chuck) are read in the part frame about the first point's own radius, exactly (#3077's swept solid). The fixed steel (a tailstock, a steady, the table) is read in the machine frame, where the station is the +X half-plane of the spindle line: the convention of `verify::c_steel` (#486) for the same kinds. The seam calls the law a second time with a start on the +X station and the fixed boxes as steel that stands still there.
  4. **Both ends of the first move are judged**, as for the cross drill: the end (where `liveMove` goes) and the start (for a post that goes to the stated start).
  5. **A hit is a refusal by name** (`GenError::Invalid`, the kind's label first). It blocks the generation, so nothing posts. No warning variant, as #3077.
  6. **Which machines.** The law answers where the path states C and `first_traverse::mill_order` is false: a mill-turn or a lathe. A mill keeps #2965's swept law.
  7. **An unstamped rotary kind on a mill-turn takes the mill laws.** A machine file that states no axis line for its rotaries gives no C stamp (`rotary_gate::rotary_letter` answers `None`). That path has no `PARAM LiveTool`, so the mill post writes it in the mill order (Z, then X/Y, then the rotary words), the premise of #2965's swept law. `rotary_traverse::mill_post_rotary` adds it to `mill_order` at the call in `generate.rs`. Before this no law judged it.
  8. **Caches read Stale once.** `current_stamp` writes `live-traverse-rotary-3096` for each rotary kind on a lathe or a mill-turn setup (`rotary_traverse::newly_judged_on`). No mill's stamp moves; the global salt stays. No shipped example, catalog project or golden holds a rotary kind on a lathe or a mill-turn (scout read of `examples/`, `docs/tester-kits/` and `crates/app/tests/golden/`), so none reads Stale. The goldens `c_axis_helix.nc` and `c_axis_unwind.nc` post a hand-made path and do not pass through generation.
  9. **The spindle line has one source.** `rotary_gate::c_center` gives the line that C turns about; the stamp and the law both read it.
  10. **Test fixtures (decided by the coordinator).** The shared C-axis bar fixture (box stock 14 x 14 x 34, top Z34; Rotary Contour clearance 25; BN-0600, r 3) opened with a first record at r 2.000, Z28.000, inside the box stock: the posted `G00 X Z` went into uncut stock, and the law refuses it. The fixtures in `c_axis_live`, `c_axis_fixture`, `lathe_work_spindle`, `lathe_workholding_live` and `rotary_letter` take clearance 40 (as `c_axis_unwind` already did), which keeps what each test pins. `c_axis_unwind::a_rewind_through_stock_is_convicted_by_the_verifier` needs its orbit on a clearance plane inside the stock, and its first record stands on that plane too, so no mill-turn stock can hold the orbit and clear the first rapid. It now asserts the mill-turn's refusal by name, then reads the verifier's orbit conviction (`RapidInStock`) on the same bench declared a mill, where #2965's swept law reports `FirstTraverseLow`. Dropped: move the stock (more readings change); expect only the refusal (loses the verifier coverage); drop the override (changes the test's intent).
- **Why.** Prime Directive: a first rapid through the stock, a part or the steel must be refused by name. Before this, no law judged the first rapid of a rotary kind on a mill-turn.
- **Considered and dropped.**
  - Judge the mill post's order (Z, then X/Y, then C; `fanuc.cps` `xyFirst`) for the stamped path: that post refuses the stamped path by name, so the order is never posted. Judging it would refuse legal work (decision #3083 item 4) and leave the order that is posted unjudged.
  - Read the fixed steel revolved about the spindle (#3077's reading for the cross drill): stricter, but it refuses a steady that stands opposite the station at every C. The station is a fixed machine place (`c_steel`), so the exact read is correct here.
  - Reuse `cross_traverse::judge` with a label: its texts name holes and a chuck/table split that reads the fixed steel revolved. A seam of its own keeps the cross drill's texts and readings unchanged.
- **Known limits** (as #3077): the turret body and its other stations are not modelled (the widest band of the tool stack runs on past its end); the tool's cross-section is read square; the stated X/Z travel is not used.
- **Cost to change later**: low. `operation/rotary_traverse.rs`, two calls in `generate.rs`, one stamp word.

## #3100 - The first traverse of a 3+2 plane and a cross drill on a machine whose table tilts

- **What was decided** (issue worker, unattended; the maintainer can change it):
  1. **The premise (maintainer, PR #2997).** The unknown start is at the top of the Z travel (the tool-change height), as for #2901, #2965, #2987 and #3084. A program that starts with the tool low near the table or the work (for example after a manual jog) is NOT covered.
  2. **The post order is the basis.** `fanuc.cps` sends Z (`traverseZ`), then X/Y at that height (`xyFirst`), then the move with the rotary words (`onRapid`, the `tilt()` words on the same `G00`). A 3+2 plane and a cross drill post in that order too. So during the X/Y traverse each rotary that turns the work stands where the previous program left it, and the #2987 law (which reads the work at the operation's own pose) is not enough.
  3. **Who answers now.** The posed law of #3084 (`first_traverse_posed::turn_of`) reads, besides the multi-axis and rotary kinds, each kind that carries a `Tilt` (the 3+2 planes: Face, Contour, Pocket, Adaptive 2D and the others of `OpParams::tilt`) and the cross drill (`OpParams::Drill` with a cross set). Only in the mill order (`mill_order`, a mill or a mill-turn's mill post), and only on a machine with a tilting rotary that states `turns_part: true`. The pose set, the WCS-origin premise of the lines and the refusal by name of a lone rotary with no line are #3084's, unchanged.
  4. **The machine table.** A table never turns (`fixture::workholding_for`). On a machine where every tilting rotary turns the work, the posed law reads the table fixed where it stands: its top as a machine height over the WCS origin, in the path's height scale (`table_top`). Where a head tilts, the #2987 table law reads it, as before. The coordinator accepted the fixed read (the table does not turn; a swept travel box refuses every 3+2 program). When the stock rests on the table, the stock's posed top is never under the table top (a stock point on the table top keeps at least that height in the pose zero), so this read refuses nothing more today. It keeps the table judged and not silently left out.
  5. **The verdict.** The same blocking `Warning::FirstTraverseLow` (#2901). The higher of the posed work top and the table top is named; it replaces each first-traverse verdict at a lower top.
  6. **The post's declared order (coordinator decision, after the batch gate on #3142).** `tormach.cps` turns A at the safe Z (`G53 G0 Z`, then `G0 A`) at each section's first motion, and only then makes the first X/Y traverse. So under it the X/Y traverse never runs at a pose the previous program left, and the posed law over-read: it refused `tilt_a180_routes` and `tilt_basis0_edited_file` (a 50 x 50 bar on the A line, clearance 10 over its top: the corner sweeps to 35.355 over Z35). The order is now a capability the post script DECLARES, as `liveTooling` is: `rotariesBeforeTraverse = true` (`post::dialect::turns_rotaries_first`). The setup's post is read when the job is collected (`first_traverse_posed::post_order`, once per script text). When the post declares it, the posed law does not read the operation (for every posed kind, the #3084 multi-axis kinds included); the #2987 law reads it at its own pose. A post that does not declare it (every other built-in, every user script without it, a script that does not load) reads the strict way: never looser. Three conditions:
     - **Backed by a pin.** `posting_rotaries_first.rs` posts three indexed slots through `tormach.cps` and asserts, in each section, `G53 G0 Z` then `G0 A` before the first X/Y word. A registry check asserts that Tormach PathPilot is the only shipped post that declares it, so a new declaring post fails until it has its own order test.
     - **A user's own script is taken at its word, never silently.** A `PostRef::File` script that declares it puts a note on the path: "First traverse: judged at the operation's own pose, because the post script declares rotariesBeforeTraverse ... taken at its word".
     - **The stamp follows the declaration.** The #3084 word is written only when the posed law reads the operation (`newly_judged` = the law applies and the post does not declare the order). A change of the setup's post, or of its script's declaration, moves the stamp. A user's own declaring script also writes the word `first-traverse-declared-3100` (Opus safety review of a4d2ac019): an operation generated under Tormach PathPilot reads Stale after the setup takes a user's copy of the script, and its regenerate puts the note on the path. The declaration cache keeps at most 32 script texts.
  7. **Cache.** The op stamp word of #3084 (`first-traverse-posed-3084`) comes from the same `newly_judged` selection. So a 3+2 or cross-drill cache on such a machine under a strict post takes the word and reads Stale once. Under a declaring post (Tormach PathPilot) the stamp of a 3+2 operation is as before this change. So `examples/first-4axis-part.camproj` (Tormach PathPilot) keeps its stamps: the restamp of the first version of this PR is dropped. A #3084 multi-axis kind under Tormach PathPilot on a work-turning machine loses the word and reads Stale once.
- **Test change.** `first_traverse_table.rs` `a_work_turning_rotary_keeps_the_table_under_the_work` pinned "no verdict" for a B 30 face 20 over the plane origin on a trunnion (A and B turn the work). The block's corner now reads on its sphere (29.584 along the B axis), so that plane is held by name (by the stock, not the table). The test now asserts that verdict, and that a plane 30 over the origin passes. Its machine now sets the WCS origin to zero (on the lines). The coordinator accepted this change (a test fixture).
- **Pinning tests.** `crates/app/tests/first_traverse_table_tilt.rs`: `a_3_2_plane_under_the_work_a_turning_table_can_leave_turned_up_is_refused_by_name`, `a_3_2_plane_over_every_pose_of_a_turning_table_passes`, `a_post_that_turns_the_table_first_reads_the_plane_at_its_own_pose`, `a_users_own_post_is_taken_at_its_declared_order_with_a_note` (with the negative: the same script without the declaration is held by name), `a_switch_to_a_users_declaring_post_reads_stale_and_regenerates_with_the_note`. `crates/app/tests/posting_rotaries_first.rs`: `only_the_tormach_post_declares_that_it_turns_the_rotaries_first`, `the_tormach_post_turns_a_at_safe_z_before_each_first_xy_traverse`. `tilt_a180_routes` and `tilt_basis0_edited_file` stay unchanged and pass because the Tormach post declares the order. The changed `first_traverse_table.rs` test. Unit test `the_fixed_table_reads_its_top_in_the_paths_height_scale`.
- **Known limits.**
  - The premise of item 1.
  - A user's own script that declares `rotariesBeforeTraverse` and does not keep that order is not caught: its declaration is taken at its word (with the note). The swing of the rotaries at the safe Z is the index-swing clause's.
  - A cross drill on a mill-turn is read only when its machine states a tilting rotary that turns the work. A spindle C stated along Z does not tilt. The one shipped mill-turn file, `assets/machines/millturn.mch`, states one rotary, C along [0, 0, 1], with the head under it; so no shipped mill-turn reads the posed law, and the cross drill has no end-to-end pin (coordinator decision).
  - An upright operation (no `Tilt`) on a table-tilt machine posts no rotary words, so the table stays where the previous program left it for the whole operation. That is not a first-traverse question and is not read here.
  - The #3084 limits (lines through the WCS origin, the Z word read as a machine height, the tool radius not added) hold.
- **What was considered and dropped**:
  - Read the machine table through every pose (as turning steel): a table box spans the X/Y travel, so its swept top would refuse every 3+2 program, and the table does not turn.
  - Read every pose under every post (the first version of this PR): it refuses legal programs of the shipped microARC 4 with its own post.
  - A check of the post's NAME (skip the law for "Tormach PathPilot"): a user's copy of the script, or a changed script, would not follow it; the declaration lives in the script and is pinned to its real order.
  - Raise the clearance of the two red fixtures: it keeps the false refusal in the product.
  - A refusal of every 3+2 plane on a table-tilt machine: it blocks programs that the law shows to be safe.
  - A new stamp word: the #3084 word already moves each newly judged cache once.
- **Cost to change later**: low. The selection is `first_traverse_posed::posed_kind`; the table read is `table_top` and `table_stays`; the declaration is one manifest flag (`post::dialect::turns_rotaries_first`) and `first_traverse_posed::post_order`.

## #3102 - Heidenhain G205: the retraction feed Q208 is a number, not FMAX

**What was decided.**

- `heidenhain.cps` writes `Q208=+99999.999` in the G205 UNIVERSAL PECKING definition. It wrote `Q208=FMAX` before.
- 99999.999 mm/min is the top of the documented Q208 input range. It asks for the fastest retract that the control permits. The control holds a programmed feed to the machine's own limit.
- The Heidenhain cycle tests now fail on any Q value that is not a signed number. This covers G200, G205, G206 and G207, not only Q208.
- The golden file `crates/app/tests/golden/nc/heidenhain/drill_peck.nc` changes in this one word.

**Why.**

- The user's iTNC 530 programming station (NC software 606425 004 SP20) prefixed the whole `N100 G205` block with `ERROR =` on a DIN/ISO import. With only `Q208=+60` in place of `Q208=FMAX`, the station read the complete block (#3102).
- HEIDENHAIN "iTNC 530 Cycle Programming", ID 670388-25 (NC software 60642x-04), cycle 205: Q208 is the "Feed rate for retraction", input range 0 to 99999.999. The manual lists FMAX, FAUTO and PREDEF as dialogue inputs, but its own NC example writes the number `Q208=99999`.
- The TNC 640 manual that the post was written from (892905-25) also accepts the number. One output is correct for the two controls.
- `Q208=0` was not chosen: it retracts at the plunge feed Q206. That is safe but slower, and it changes the requested retract behaviour.

**Considered and dropped.**

- A machine property for the controls that accept FMAX. No control is known that refuses the number, so the property adds a choice and no safety.
- The machine's maximum feed from the `.mch` file. It is not set on each machine file, and the control already holds the feed to its own limit.
- A refusal of G205 on the iTNC 530. A supported number exists, so a refusal takes a working cycle away.

**Cost to change later.**

- The value is the constant `RETRACT_FEED_MAX` in `assets/posts/heidenhain.cps`, beside `qword`.
- The check on the physical Fehlmann (NC software 340490-03) is still open (#3102). If that control refuses the number too, the post must refuse G205 there.

## #3105 - Check the default-machine refusal separately from logs

**Decision:** Check the per-operation refusal assertions against the CLI refusal line. Set `CAMCRAFT_LOG` to `info` for the child process so the test always includes generation logs.

**Why:** The complete stderr stream includes a valid generation log for `Face1`. The refusal correctly names only the unmounted setup `Setup2` and its operation `Face2`. The test must check which operation the refusal names.

**Dropped:** Disabling logging would hide the regression. Production posting changes are unnecessary because the refusal is correct. A broad exclusion from stderr would also reject valid generation logs.

**Cost to change later:** Update the test if the CLI refusal prefix changes. Production posting behavior does not change.

## #3109 - Circular: keep the helix entries of the rings apart

**Decided.** A flat Circular with a helix entry (or a helix level
transition) turns the start of each later ring to a vertex of that ring's
own polygon. At that vertex, the predicted helix orbit keeps 0.01 mm from
every helix orbit that the earlier rings flew. The prediction uses the
same first rule as the descent: the first of the eight compass offsets
whose disc the cutter-center disk holds. After each ring, the kernel reads
the descents (feeds that change Z) that the ring really flew. It reads
them with the crossing law itself (`verify::crossed_pairs`, at 0.01 mm and
0.001 mm chords) against the earlier rings' descents whose box and band
meet them. If a pair crosses, the kernel refuses the operation by name
("helix entry: the descent at ... crosses the descent of an earlier
ring ...").

**Why.**
- All rings of a flat Circular run the same level ladder. Thus the helix
  of each ring at a level shares its depth band with the helix of each
  other ring at that level, not only the ring before it.
- A helix makes a full turn at least, so a clear orbit circle is a clear
  helix. The circle test is a safe, cheap prediction.
- The reading uses the law that verification uses. The refusal therefore
  fires only where verification would block the post. A first version
  read orbit circles only. It refused a table row that verifies clean
  (`circular_arcs` repro): two half-turn arcs can share a band and still
  miss the points where their circles meet.
- The first ring, and any ring with no conflict, keeps vertex 0. Plunge
  entry, ramp entry and the vault mode do not change. No golden file
  moves.
- A helix that has no clear start is refused by name. The issue permits
  this outcome. Examples: a helix as wide as the cutter in a small circle,
  and three rows of the `circular_arcs` table (helix radius 0.5, radius 4
  and radius 6). Before this change, Crossing warnings held each of these
  rows: 30, 154 and 350 warnings.

**Dropped.**
- The pocket's z-major order (tried on #2898): it removed the crossings,
  but the inner rings then started with an axial plunge that no note
  named. Four ramp-entry tests went red.
- A refusal before generation for `stepover <= 2 * helix_radius`: it is
  simple, but it refuses the common job of the issue (stepover 2, helix
  radius 1). The stagger generates that job.
- A trial generation of each candidate start on a copy of the path
  builder: exact, but the copy grows with the path. The cost is quadratic
  in the ring count.
- A change to the crossing law: the law is a safety check under the
  safety floor, and the issue does not ask for it.
- The stagger in the vault mode: vault rings descend in separate bands,
  so their helices do not share a depth.

**Test change.** `crates/app/tests/circular_arcs.rs`: the three rows
above now expect the named refusal. The radius 4 and 6 rows were also the
table's gouge check. They are judged again with a plunge entry, and they
must still gouge.

**Cost to change later.** Low. The logic is in
`crates/motion/src/machining2d/circular_helix.rs`. `circular.rs` calls
it at two points: the start vertex before each ring, and the reading
after it.

**Also.** The test module of `circular.rs` moved to `circular_tests.rs`
(the `#[path]` pattern of `multiaxis/`). This keeps `circular.rs` under
the 400-line law.

## #3119 - The AI guide test reads a CRLF checkout

**Decided:** `crates/app/tests/ai_guide.rs` changes CRLF to LF after it reads
`site/content/guide/automate/ai.md`. A new test makes a CRLF copy of the
guide and checks that it gives the same `tools/call` examples as the LF text.

**Why:** a Windows checkout with `core.autocrlf` writes the guide with CRLF.
The test split the text on "```json\n", found no fence, and failed. The fix is
in the one place that reads the file, and it works in each checkout that
exists now, with no new checkout or `git add --renormalize` step.

**Dropped:** a `.gitattributes` rule (`site/content/** text eol=lf`). It
makes Git write LF only in new checkouts. An existing Windows clone keeps
CRLF until the user checks out the files again, so the test stays red for
them. The rule also changes the bytes of the site sources for each Windows
author, which is a larger change than a test fix.

**Cost to change later:** low. A `.gitattributes` rule can come later. The
normalization in the test then has no effect, and the test stays correct.

## #3121 - Post-processor API reference

**What was decided:** Add one user reference page for the current CamCraft
post contract. Link it from the posting workflow. Cover manifest values,
hooks, records, properties, helpers, refusal causes, and standalone debugging.
Use an explicitly non-executable trace example with exact output.

**Why:** Users need to diagnose their own posts without reading Rust.
The reference follows our documents and implementation only. It distinguishes
the app's refusal gate from the standalone tool, which still writes output
when warnings exist. The manifest coverage test detects missing reference
rows when the authoring contract changes.

**Dropped:** Do not copy another product's post reference. Do not present
a short example as a machine-safe milling post. Do not change posting
behavior, dependencies, controller scripts, or golden output for a docs task.

**Cost to change later:** Update the reference when the API changes. Extend
its coverage check if the manifest description adopts a different syntax.
The page has its own URL and can later split into linked reference pages.

## #3127 - A work-turning rotary line that does not pass through the WCS origin

- **What was decided** (issue worker, unattended; the maintainer can change it):
  1. **Refuse, do not read.** A work-turning rotary that states a non-zero (or non-finite) `pivot` or `offset` is refused by name. The posed first-traverse law (`operation::first_traverse_posed::turn_of`) refuses generation. The index-swing clause (`posting_index_swing::verdict`) refuses the post.
  2. **One test for both.** `posting::index_swing::off_origin` reads the two fields. A component with an absolute value of 1e-9 mm or less reads as zero. A zero vector (`[0, 0, 0]`) is judged as before.
  3. **Which lines.** A vertical line keeps every height, wherever it stands. So one vertical work-turning rotary with a pivot is not refused. With two or more work-turning rotaries, the sphere about the WCS origin needs every line through that origin, so any off-origin rotary refuses.
  4. **The sibling clause.** `posting_swing_standing` reads the same `Verdict`. It reads only `Verdict::Judged`, so it skips the new `OffOrigin` verdict as it skips `Unlined` and `Leaning`. The index-swing clause has already refused the post.
- **Why.** `pivot` is stated in machine coordinates. The program does not know where the WCS origin is in machine coordinates. So the program cannot place the stated line in the WCS. A read about a guessed line can be too low, and the post is then not blocked. A refusal is visible and safe. No shipped machine file states `pivot` or `offset`.
- **Pinning tests.**
  - `crates/app/tests/first_traverse_posed.rs`: `a_table_line_off_the_wcs_origin_refuses_by_name`, `a_zero_pivot_reads_the_table_line_through_the_wcs_origin`.
  - `crates/app/tests/index_swing_offset_line.rs`: `a_pivot_off_the_wcs_origin_refuses_the_index_swing_by_name`, `an_offset_off_the_wcs_origin_refuses_the_index_swing_by_name`, `a_zero_pivot_and_offset_judge_the_index_swing_as_before`.
- **What was considered and dropped**:
  - Read the swept set about the stated line: it needs the machine position of the WCS origin, which the project does not state. A guess makes a silent wrong answer.
  - Treat `pivot` as a WCS position: the field is documented as machine coordinates (#1962). This reading is wrong for a typical machine.
  - Refuse every rotary with a stated `pivot`, also a zero one: a file that states the default must not lose its checks.
- **Cost to change later**: low. When the project can place the machine frame in the WCS, replace the refusal with a read about the moved line in `off_origin`'s two callers.

## #3129 - Zigzag levels of the avoid pocket and the 3D pocket close with boundary rings

**What was decided.** Two more pass plans now use
`pocket_zigzag::rest_passes` for Zigzag and Auto, as the plain 2D pocket
does after #3021:
- `pocket_avoid` (2D pocket with "Do not touch"), at each level.
- `machining3d::hsm::plan_level`, the 3D pocket's level plan when the
  strategy is not Adaptive and the level has no rotary seam.

The rows stand 0.01 mm inside the level's cutter-center area. One closed
ring then follows each boundary loop of that area: the outer wall, each
island, and each keep-out edge.

**Why.**
- Rows touch a wall or an island only at their ends, so a cusp stays
  between each two ends over the full depth. The pins measured, before
  the change: 0.755 mm on a rounded corner of the avoid pocket (0.919 mm
  with blended turns), and a 2.0 mm strip on the boss wall of a 3D level.
- `rest_passes` is the plan that the plain 2D pocket and the rest pocket
  already use. One plan for all Zigzag levels keeps the wall result the
  same in all three operations.
- The 3D plan already read Auto as Zigzag (`plan_passes`). The change
  keeps that reading.
- `rest_passes` is made `pub(crate)` and re-exported as
  `zigzag_ringed_passes`, so that `machining3d` reads it through the
  `machining2d` door, as it reads `plan_passes`.

- The rotary wrap (Rotary Offset) uses the same `plan_level`, always
  with a seam. Its levels keep the plain rows. The developed area of a
  wrap level ends at the seam, so a ring on each boundary loop would also
  cut the seam line, at both ends of the strip. That is one physical line,
  cut twice, and not a wall.

**Dropped.**
- Rings on the rotary wrap levels in this PR. They need a ring that
  skips the seam edges. Issue #3168 tracks them.
- A change inside `plan_passes`. It has more callers (the 2D Adaptive
  fallback, the 3D rest pass and shells), and #3130 changes its caller in
  `pocket.rs`. A change at the two call sites is smaller and does not
  overlap #3130.
- A crossing-law post for blended turns in `pocket_avoid` (the plain
  pocket's `hold_crossings`). The blended pin shows no crossing pair, and
  `pocket_avoid` rounds its turns with the level area as the legal region.
  If a crossing shows up later, the post check blocks the program, and the
  law can be added then.

- A raw count of posed moves in the Multi-Axis Rough test
  (`posed <= 20`). The closing ring round the boss adds a pose on each
  ring chord. The test now checks that each pose stays within the ball's
  reach of the boss, which is the intent of the old bound.

**Cost to change later.** Low. Each plan selects `rest_passes` in one
branch. The pins in `crates/motion/tests/pocket_wall_finish_levels.rs`
hold the wall result.

### Review correction: plain pocket entries and link assertions

**What was decided.** A restart for a tool that is not center-cutting
now checks its posted entry against prior feed moves. It tries the helix,
then a ramp along the pass. It refuses the operation if neither entry
passes the check. The plain pocket tests keep the inset rows and the
separate closing rings. Their entry counts describe that plan.
The KeepDown test measures the reduction in rapid moves as well as gaps
that contain nonplanar moves.

**Why.**
- A closing ring restart can descend through the same depth interval as
  the rows' earlier entry. Room inside the region does not prove that
  those descents miss each other. The restart now uses the existing
  `moves_cross_prior` check on a staged entry before it posts that entry.
  The `center_cut_law` pocket test checks the crossing pairs directly.
  `a_closing_ring_restart_does_not_cross_the_rows_transition_ramp`
  also requires the round pocket to succeed with a named ramp fallback.
